The Poonen–Rains Heuristics for Selmer Groups

In 2012 Poonen and Rains formulated a precise probabilistic model for the p‑Selmer groups of elliptic curves over ℚ (and more generally for principally polarized abelian varieties). Their heuristic asserts that the isomorphism class of the p‑Selmer group Selₚ(E) behaves like the cokernel of a random symmetric matrix over the finite field 𝔽ₚ, weighted by the inverse of the size of its automorphism group. Concretely, for each prime p the probability that Selₚ(E) ≅ G for a finite abelian p‑group G is proportional to 1/|Aut(G)|. This weighting reproduces the Cohen–Lenstra measure for class groups when p is odd, and for p = 2 it matches the distribution found by Bhargava and Shankar for 2‑Selmer groups of elliptic curves. A striking numerical prediction follows: the expected size of Selₚ(E) equals p + 1. For p = 2 this gives an average 2‑Selmer size of 3, which agrees with the Bhargava–Shankar theorem that the average size of the 2‑Selmer group is exactly 3. The Poonen–Rains model also predicts the full distribution of ranks: the proportion of curves with rank r is the probability that a random symmetric matrix over 𝔽ₚ has corank r, after accounting for the parity constraint coming from the root number. Subsequent work of Bhargava, Kane, Lenstra, Poonen and Rains extended the heuristic to families of abelian varieties and to function fields, where the predictions have been proved in many cases by Ellenberg, Venkatesh and Westerland using homological stability for Hurwitz spaces.

The heuristic rests on two pillars. First, the p‑Selmer group fits into an exact sequence 0 → E(ℚ)/pE(ℚ) → Selₚ(E) → Ш(E)[p] → 0, so its size is the product of the p‑part of the Mordell–Weil group and the p‑torsion in the Tate–Shafarevich group. Second, the local conditions defining Selₚ(E) are given by a collection of maximal isotropic subspaces in a symplectic 𝔽ₚ‑vector space; choosing these subspaces at random yields exactly the cokernel of a random symmetric matrix. The weighting by 1/|Aut(G)| arises naturally from the orbit‑counting method of Bhargava: each Selmer element corresponds to an integral orbit on a prehomogeneous vector space, and the stabilizer of the orbit is Aut(G). This geometric interpretation explains why the same measure appears for class groups (where the relevant space is the space of binary quadratic forms) and for Selmer groups (where the space is the representation of a reductive group attached to the p‑isogeny). The Poonen–Rains conjectures remain open in general, but they have been verified for the 2‑Selmer group (Bhargava–Shankar 2015), for the 3‑Selmer group (Bhargava–Shankar–Tsimerman 2015), and for the 5‑Selmer group in certain families (Bhargava–Shankar–Wang 2022). The heuristic also predicts that the average size of the p‑torsion in Ш(E) is 1, a statement that is still far from proof.

An important refinement concerns the parity of the rank. The root number w(E) = ±1, the sign of the functional equation of L(E,s), forces the rank to have the same parity as (1−w(E))/2. In the random matrix model this parity constraint is implemented by conditioning the symmetric matrix to have a prescribed determinant (or Pfaffian) in 𝔽ₚ. The resulting conditional distribution matches the observed split of ranks in large databases of elliptic curves. The Poonen–Rains framework thus unifies the Cohen–Lenstra heuristics for class groups, the Bhargava–Shankar results for 2‑Selmer groups, and the random matrix models for L‑functions under a single geometric‑probabilistic umbrella.

From an examiner’s perspective, the key take‑aways are: (1) the average size of the p‑Selmer group is p + 1; (2) the distribution is the Cohen–Lenstra measure on finite abelian p‑groups; (3) the parity of the rank is dictated by the root number and is built into the model by a determinant condition; (4) the heuristic is proved for p = 2, 3 and in many function‑field cases, but remains conjectural for higher p over number fields.

Malle’s Conjecture and Its Refinements

In 2004 Gunter Malle proposed a precise asymptotic formula for the number N(G,X) of degree‑n extensions L/ℚ with Galois group G ⊂ Sₙ and absolute discriminant ≤ X. The conjecture states that N(G,X) ∼ C(G) Xa(G) (log X)b(G)−1 as X → ∞, where the exponent a(G) = 1/ind(G) and ind(G) = ming≠1 (n − cycles(g)) is the minimal index of a non‑identity element of G. The power b(G) depends on the number of conjugacy classes in G that achieve this minimal index. For the full symmetric group Sₙ, a transposition has index 1, so ind(Sₙ) = 1 and a(Sₙ) = 1; however, the discriminant of an Sₙ‑extension is a square times the discriminant of its quadratic resolvent, which forces an extra factor of 1/2 in the exponent for n ≥ 3. The refined version due to Türkelli (2017) replaces a(G) by 1/a(G) where a(G) = ming≠1 (ind(g)/|G|) and adjusts the logarithmic exponent to b(G) = r(G) − 1, with r(G) the number of conjugacy classes of minimal index. These refinements resolve several counter‑examples to the original formulation, notably for groups with non‑trivial center.

The conjecture has been proved in a handful of cases. For n = 3, Davenport–Heilbronn (1971) established N(S₃,X) ∼ (1/3) X, and Bhargava (2005) gave a uniform proof for all cubic fields using the geometry of numbers on the space of binary cubic forms. For n = 4, Bhargava (2005) proved N(S₄,X) ∼ C X with an explicit constant, and for n = 5, Bhargava (2010) obtained N(S₅,X) ∼ C X1/2 (log X)b with b = 1. Ellenberg and Venkatesh (2006) provided upper bounds of the shape Xexp(G)+ε for any G, where exp(G) is the exponent of the group, using the geometry of numbers on Hurwitz spaces. More recently, Alberts (2021) proved the conjecture for all nilpotent groups of odd order, and work of Lemke Oliver and Thorne (2022) established it for many wreath products. The constant C(G) is expressed as a product of local densities (the “mass formula”) and a Tamagawa number; its computation involves the same prehomogeneous vector spaces that appear in Bhargava’s parametrizations.

A parallel conjecture exists for function fields: over 𝔽_q(t) the number of G‑extensions with discriminant of degree ≤ d grows like qd·a(G) db(G)−1. In this setting the conjecture is a theorem for many groups, thanks to the work of Ellenberg, Venkatesh and Westerland on homological stability for Hurwitz spaces. The function‑field results provide strong evidence for the number‑field conjecture and illustrate the deep connection between arithmetic statistics and the topology of moduli spaces.

For exam purposes, remember the definition of the index ind(g) = n − cycles(g), the formula a(G) = 1/ind(G) (or its Türkelli refinement), and the fact that the logarithmic exponent b(G) counts conjugacy classes of minimal index. Typical questions ask to compute a(G) and b(G) for a given permutation group (e.g., G = D₄, A₄, or a wreath product) and to explain why the discriminant exponent for Sₙ extensions is 1/2 rather than 1 when n ≥ 3.

Examiner's trap
A question asks: “According to the Poonen–Rains heuristic, what is the predicted average size of the 3‑Selmer group of an elliptic curve over ℚ?” A common mistake is to answer 3, confusing p with p+1.
The Poonen–Rains heuristic predicts that the average size of the p‑Selmer group equals p + 1. For p = 3 this gives 3 + 1 = 4. The value 3 is the average size of the 2‑Selmer group (p = 2). Therefore the correct answer is 4.
Exam‑day strategy
Memorise the three core constants: average p‑Selmer size = p + 1; Malle exponent a(G) = 1/ind(G) (with ind(g) = n − cycles(g)); Keating–Snaith moment exponent = k². Write them on a flash card and rehearse the definitions of ind(G) and the logarithmic exponent b(G) for the groups Sₙ, Aₙ, Dₙ.

The Keating–Snaith Moment Conjectures for L‑functions

In 2000 Keating and Snaith used the characteristic polynomials of random matrices from the classical compact groups to conjecture precise asymptotics for the moments of the Riemann zeta function and of families of L‑functions on the critical line. For the Riemann zeta function they predicted that for any integer k ≥ 1, ∫₀ᵀ |ζ(½ + it)|²ᵏ dt ∼ aₖ · G(k+1)² / G(2k+1) · T (log T)k², where G is the Barnes G‑function (G(1)=1, G(z+1)=Γ(z)G(z)) and aₖ is an arithmetic factor given by an Euler product over primes: aₖ = ∏ₚ (1 − 1/p)k² ∑m=0^∞ ( (Γ(m+k)/Γ(m+1)Γ(k) )² p−m ). The factor (log T)k² reflects the unitary symmetry type of the zeta zeros, while the ratio of Barnes G‑functions comes from the moment of the characteristic polynomial of a random unitary matrix. For families with symplectic symmetry (e.g., quadratic Dirichlet L‑functions) the moment conjecture replaces the unitary integral by an integral over USp(2N) and the exponent of log T becomes k(k+1)/2. For orthogonal families (even or odd) the exponent is k(k−1)/2 or k(k+1)/2 respectively, and the random matrix integral is over SO(2N) or SO(2N+1). These predictions have been verified to high precision numerically for k = 1,2,3,4 and have motivated a vast literature on the “recipe” for computing arithmetic factors aₖ for any family.

The Keating–Snaith recipe proceeds in three steps. First, identify the symmetry type of the family from the functional equation (unitary, symplectic, orthogonal even, orthogonal odd). Second, compute the random matrix moment ∫G(N) |Λ(1)|²ᵏ dμ(N) where Λ is the characteristic polynomial and μ is Haar measure; the large‑N asymptotics of this integral yields the Barnes G‑function ratio and the power of log T. Third, multiply by the arithmetic factor aₖ, which encodes the Euler product of the L‑function and is obtained by a heuristic “Euler product over primes” that matches the local factors of the family. The arithmetic factor is often expressed in terms of the coefficients of the L‑function’s Dirichlet series and can be evaluated explicitly for many families (e.g., for the family of quadratic twists of a fixed elliptic curve, aₖ involves the Satake parameters of the curve).

The conjectures have profound implications. They imply the Lindelöf hypothesis on average, give a precise form of the “moment conjecture” of Conrey and Ghosh, and provide a framework for understanding the distribution of values of L‑functions at the central point. In particular, the conjectured moments determine the full distribution of log |L(½)| via the method of moments, predicting a Gaussian limit with variance (1/2) log log T for the zeta function. The Keating–Snaith formula also connects to the work of Conrey, Farmer, Keating, Rubinstein and Snaith (2005) on the “ratios conjecture”, which gives a recipe for averages of ratios of L‑functions and has been used to derive conjectures for the distribution of zeros, the mollified moments, and the one‑level density.

From an examination standpoint, the essential points are: (1) the exponent of log T is k² for unitary, k(k+1)/2 for symplectic, k(k−1)/2 for orthogonal even, and k(k+1)/2 for orthogonal odd; (2) the random matrix integral yields the Barnes G‑function ratio G(k+1)²/G(2k+1) for unitary, with analogous expressions for the other groups; (3) the arithmetic factor aₖ is an Euler product that can be written down once the local factors of the family are known; (4) the conjectures are proved only for k = 1,2 (Hardy–Littlewood, Ingham) and in function‑field settings (Rudnick, Soundararajan), but remain open for higher k over number fields.

The Parity Conjecture and Root Number Statistics for Elliptic Curves

The parity conjecture asserts that for an elliptic curve E/ℚ the rank of E(ℚ) has the same parity as the root number w(E) = ±1, i.e. rank(E) ≡ (1−w(E))/2 (mod 2). This is a consequence of the Birch and Swinnerton‑Dyer conjecture together with the functional equation of L(E,s). While the full parity conjecture is still open, it is known in many cases: for curves with a rational 2‑torsion point (by work of Monsky, 1996), for semistable curves (by Nekovář, 2006), and for a density‑one set of curves (by Smith, 2017). The root number itself is the product of local root numbers wₚ(E) over all places p ≤ ∞; for a minimal Weierstrass equation it can be computed via the formula w(E) = ∏ₚ wₚ(E) with w_∞(E) = −1. In large databases (e.g., the LMFDB) the root numbers are observed to be equidistributed: exactly half of the curves have w(E) = +1 and half have w(E) = −1, up to negligible error. This equidistribution is predicted by the random matrix model: the family of all elliptic curves over ℚ has orthogonal symmetry with both even and odd types occurring equally often, leading to a 50‑50 split of root numbers.

The connection to random matrix theory is made precise by the Katz–Sarnak philosophy. The family of all elliptic curves ordered by height (or by conductor) has orthogonal symmetry, but the sign of the functional equation is not fixed; it varies with the curve. The symmetry type of the subfamily with w(E) = +1 is SO(even), while the subfamily with w(E) = −1 has SO(odd) symmetry. The one‑level density of low‑lying zeros for each subfamily matches the corresponding random matrix prediction, and the proportion of curves with each root number is exactly the proportion of matrices in the full orthogonal group with determinant +1 versus −1, which is 1/2. This explains the observed equidistribution and also predicts that the average rank of curves with w(E) = +1 is 0 (even rank) and with w(E) = −1 is 1 (odd rank), assuming the rank is as small as possible subject to the parity constraint. Goldfeld’s conjecture (1979) that the average rank of all elliptic curves is 1/2 follows immediately from this picture.

Bhargava and Shankar (2015) proved that the average rank of elliptic curves is bounded (≤ 1.17) and that a positive proportion of curves have rank 0 and a positive proportion have rank 1. Their method uses the 2‑Selmer group distribution, which is modeled by the cokernel of a random symmetric matrix over 𝔽₂. The parity of the 2‑Selmer rank matches the root number, and the random matrix model predicts that the 2‑Selmer rank is 0 with probability 1/2 and 1 with probability 1/2, giving an average 2‑Selmer rank of 1/2. Since the Mordell–Weil rank is bounded above by the 2‑Selmer rank, this yields the bounded average rank result. The parity conjecture would then imply that the actual Mordell–Weil rank equals the 2‑Selmer rank for a density‑one set of curves, so the average rank would be exactly 1/2.

For exam questions, the key facts are: (1) the parity conjecture links rank parity to the root number; (2) the root number is the product of local root numbers and is equidistributed in the family of all elliptic curves; (3) the random matrix model predicts a 50‑50 split of root numbers and consequently an average rank of 1/2 (Goldfeld’s conjecture); (4) Bhargava–Shankar proved bounded average rank using the 2‑Selmer distribution, which matches the Poonen–Rains heuristic for p = 2; (5) the parity conjecture is known for curves with a rational 2‑torsion point and for a density‑one set, but remains open in general.

Higher Selmer Groups and the Bhargava–Shankar–Tsimerman Method

Building on their parametrization of 2‑Selmer groups via orbits on the space of binary quartic forms, Bhargava, Shankar and Tsimerman (2015) developed a uniform method to study the average size of the 6‑Selmer group of elliptic curves. The 6‑Selmer group fits into an exact sequence involving the 2‑Selmer and 3‑Selmer groups, and its size is the product of the sizes of the 2‑ and 3‑Selmer groups divided by the size of the intersection (which is the 1‑Selmer group, i.e. the Mordell–Weil group modulo torsion). By parametrizing both the 2‑Selmer and 3‑Selmer groups using integral orbits on prehomogeneous vector spaces — binary quartic forms for 2‑Selmer and pairs of ternary quadratic forms for 3‑Selmer — they were able to count the number of locally soluble orbits with bounded invariants. The geometry‑of‑numbers argument yields an average size of the 6‑Selmer group equal to 9, which factorises as 3 × 3, the product of the average 2‑Selmer size (3) and the average 3‑Selmer size (4) divided by the average 1‑Selmer size (4/3). This matches the Poonen–Rains prediction that the average size of the p‑Selmer group is p+1 for p = 2,3 and that the Selmer groups for different primes behave independently.

The method extends the orbit‑counting technique of Bhargava to the product of two prehomogeneous vector spaces. The key technical innovation is a “cut‑and‑paste” argument that separates the counting of 2‑Selmer and 3‑Selmer elements while controlling the overlap. The invariants that bound the height of the orbits are the discriminant of the binary quartic form (for 2‑Selmer) and the discriminant of the pair of ternary quadratic forms (for 3‑Selmer). The local solubility conditions at each prime p translate into congruence conditions on the integral orbits, and the product of local densities gives the mass formula that determines the average size. The result also implies that the average size of the 2‑torsion in the Tate–Shafarevich group is 1, and similarly for the 3‑torsion, supporting the conjecture that Ш(E) is finite and its p‑torsion has average size 1 for every p.

Subsequent work by Bhargava, Shankar and Wang (2022) pushed the method to the 5‑Selmer group, using the parametrization of 5‑Selmer elements by orbits on a 40‑dimensional representation of a group of type E₈. They proved that the average size of the 5‑Selmer group is 6, again consistent with the Poonen–Rains heuristic (p+1 = 6). The pattern suggests that for any prime p, the average size of the p‑Selmer group is p+1, and the full distribution is the Cohen–Lenstra measure on finite abelian p‑groups. The ultimate goal is a uniform proof for all p using Vinberg’s theory of θ‑groups, which provides a parametrization of p‑Selmer groups for all p by integral orbits on a single prehomogeneous vector space attached to a graded Lie algebra. This program, initiated by Bhargava and Gross (2013), remains a central open problem in arithmetic statistics.

From an examination perspective, the essential points are: (1) the 6‑Selmer average size is 9, obtained as the product of the 2‑Selmer average (3) and the 3‑Selmer average (4) divided by the 1‑Selmer average (4/3); (2) the method uses integral orbits on the product of the binary quartic form space and the pair‑of‑ternary‑quadratic‑forms space; (3) the result confirms the Poonen–Rains prediction of independence of p‑Selmer groups for different p; (4) the same technique has been extended to p = 5 (average size 6) and is expected to work for all p via Vinberg’s θ‑groups; (5) the average size of the p‑torsion in Ш(E) is predicted to be 1 for every p, a consequence of the Selmer average being p+1 and the Mordell–Weil rank being small on average.

  • Confusing the average p‑Selmer size p+1 with the average p‑torsion in Ш(E) (which is 1).
  • Using the original Malle exponent a(G)=1/ind(G) without the Türkelli refinement for groups with non‑trivial center.
  • Assigning the wrong symmetry type (unitary vs symplectic vs orthogonal) to a family of L‑functions, leading to an incorrect log‑exponent in the Keating–Snaith moment formula.
  • Assuming the parity conjecture is a theorem for all elliptic curves; it is only known for a density‑one set and for curves with a rational 2‑torsion point.
  • Thinking the average rank of elliptic curves is proved to be 1/2; only bounded average rank (≤1.17) is proved, Goldfeld’s conjecture remains open.
  • Mixing up the average 2‑Selmer size (3) with the average 3‑Selmer size (4) when computing the 6‑Selmer average.
  • Neglecting the local solubility conditions in orbit counting; they are essential for the mass formula and for matching the Poonen–Rains measure.

These traps highlight the subtle points that examiners often test.

hand/general-relativity.html:
Experimental Tests of the Equivalence Principle and Post‑Newtonian Parameters

The weak equivalence principle (WEP) has been probed far beyond the classic Eötvös torsion‑balance experiments. The MICROSCOPE satellite, launched in 2016, compared the free‑fall of titanium and platinum test masses in a drag‑free environment and constrained the Eötvös parameter η to |η| < 1.1 × 10⁻¹⁵ at 90 % confidence. This improves ground‑based limits by two orders of magnitude and directly tests the universality of free fall for different compositions in orbit. Complementary lunar laser ranging (LLR) measures the Earth‑Moon distance with millimetre precision, providing a test of the strong equivalence principle (SEP) through the Nordtvedt parameter η_N. Current LLR data bound |η_N| < 4.4 × 10⁻⁴, limiting any violation of SEP that would arise from gravitational self‑energy contributions.

In the parametrized post‑Newtonian (PPN) framework, the metric potentials are expanded in powers of v/c and the gravitational potential U/c². The two most relevant PPN parameters are γ (space curvature per unit mass) and β (non‑linearity in superposition). Solar‑system experiments constrain γ − 1 = (2.1 ± 2.3) × 10⁻⁵ from Cassini radio‑science tracking, and β − 1 = (−1.6 ± 2.0) × 10⁻⁴ from perihelion precession of Mercury combined with LLR. These bounds are consistent with general relativity (γ = β = 1) and severely restrict scalar‑tensor alternatives such as Brans‑Dicke theory, which predicts γ = (1 + ω)/(2 + ω) with ω > 4 × 10⁴ from Cassini.

Laboratory tests of the gravitational inverse‑square law at sub‑millimetre scales search for Yukawa‑type deviations parameterised by a strength α and range λ. Torsion‑balance experiments (Eöt‑Wash) and micro‑cantilever setups have excluded |α| > 10⁻² for λ ≈ 10⁻⁴ m, while neutron‑scattering experiments probe even shorter ranges. Any positive signal would indicate extra dimensions or new light scalar fields, but null results continue to support the standard geometric description of gravity.

Key experimental milestones

  • 1909 – Eötvös torsion balance, η ~ 10⁻⁹
  • 1976 – Lunar laser ranging begins, SEP test
  • 2003 – Cassini superior conjunction, γ test
  • 2016 – MICROSCOPE launch, η < 10⁻¹⁵
  • 2022 – MICROSCOPE final results, η < 1.1 × 10⁻¹⁵

Singularity Theorems and the Cosmic Censorship Conjecture

The singularity theorems of Penrose (1965) and Hawking‑Penrose (1970) demonstrate that, under physically reasonable conditions, spacetime must contain incomplete geodesics — i.e. singularities — rather than being globally regular. Penrose’s theorem requires a non‑compact Cauchy surface, the null energy condition (Tμνk^μk^ν ≥ 0 for all null k^μ), and the existence of a trapped surface. The Hawking‑Penrose theorem relaxes the trapped‑surface requirement, instead assuming a closed trapped surface or a point where the expansion of null geodesics becomes negative, together with the generic condition that every causal geodesic experiences a non‑zero curvature coupling.

These theorems do not specify the nature of the singularity; they only guarantee geodesic incompleteness. The cosmic censorship conjecture, proposed by Penrose in 1969, asserts that singularities arising from gravitational collapse are always hidden behind event horizons, so that the exterior spacetime remains predictable. The weak cosmic censorship conjecture (WCCC) states that no naked singularities form from generic, asymptotically flat initial data. The strong cosmic censorship conjecture (SCCC) further demands that the maximal Cauchy development of generic initial data is inextendible as a regular Lorentzian manifold.

Counter‑examples have been constructed in highly symmetric or fine‑tuned settings. The collapse of a self‑similar scalar field (Christodoulou, 1994) can produce a naked singularity for a set of initial data of codimension one, suggesting that WCCC may hold generically but not universally. In higher dimensions, black‑string solutions (Gregory‑Laflamme instability) can fragment, potentially exposing singularities. Numerical relativity simulations of binary black‑hole mergers and critical collapse have not found stable naked singularities, lending empirical support to WCCC.

Implications for predictability

If cosmic censorship holds, the evolution of fields outside black holes is uniquely determined by initial data on a Cauchy surface, preserving determinism in classical general relativity. Violation would imply loss of predictability, as observers could receive signals from regions where the classical theory breaks down. The conjecture remains unproven in four dimensions; its status is a central open problem linking global differential geometry, partial differential equations, and gravitational physics.

Technique: Identifying the energy condition used in a singularity theorem
A question states: "The Penrose singularity theorem requires the null energy condition. Which of the following stress‑energy tensors violates this condition?" Options: (A) Perfect fluid with ρ > 0, p = 0; (B) Electromagnetic field; (C) Scalar field with potential V(φ) = −½ m² φ²; (D) Cosmological constant Λ > 0.
The null energy condition demands Tμνk^μk^ν ≥ 0 for all null vectors k^μ. For a perfect fluid with ρ > 0, p = 0, Tμνk^μk^ν = ρ (u_μk^μ)² ≥ 0 — satisfied. The electromagnetic stress‑energy tensor also satisfies the null energy condition because its energy density is non‑negative for any observer. A cosmological constant Λ > 0 gives Tμν = −Λ gμν/(8πG); for null k^μ, Tμνk^μk^ν = 0 — satisfied. A scalar field with a negative mass‑squared potential can have negative kinetic energy contributions in certain configurations, allowing Tμνk^μk^ν < 0. Therefore option (C) violates the null energy condition.
Exam‑day strategy
When a question asks which energy condition a theorem uses, recall the hierarchy: null ≤ weak ≤ strong ≤ dominant. Penrose uses null; Hawking‑Penrose uses null plus generic condition; the focusing theorem uses null. Memorise the standard matter models that satisfy or violate each condition — perfect fluids with ρ ≥ 0, p ≥ 0 satisfy all; a cosmological constant satisfies null and weak but violates strong; a ghost scalar field violates null. This quick classification eliminates wrong options rapidly.

Black Hole Thermodynamics: Entropy, Temperature, and the Information Paradox

The four laws of black‑hole mechanics, formulated by Bardeen, Carter and Hawking (1973), map directly onto the laws of thermodynamics when the surface gravity κ is identified with temperature T = ħκ/(2πk_B) and the horizon area A with entropy S = k_B A/(4ℓ_P²), where ℓ_P = √(ħG/c³) is the Planck length. For a Schwarzschild black hole of mass M, κ = c⁴/(4GM) and A = 16πG²M²/c⁴, giving the Hawking temperature T_H = ħc³/(8πGMk_B) and the Bekenstein‑Hawking entropy S_BH = 4πGM²k_B/(ħc). These relations imply that a black hole radiates thermally with a power P ≈ ħc⁶/(15360πG²M²), leading to complete evaporation in a time τ ≈ 5120πG²M³/(ħc⁴).

The generalized second law (GSL), conjectured by Bekenstein and proved in various semiclassical settings, states that the sum of black‑hole entropy and ordinary matter entropy never decreases. Quantum field theory on curved spacetime shows that the renormalised stress‑energy tensor near the horizon yields a negative energy flux into the black hole, balancing the positive Hawking flux at infinity and ensuring energy conservation.

The information paradox arises because Hawking radiation appears thermal and thus carries no information about the initial state that formed the black hole. If the black hole evaporates completely, the final state is a mixed thermal state, contradicting unitary evolution in quantum mechanics. Proposed resolutions include: (i) information is encoded in subtle correlations within the radiation (Page curve), (ii) remnants with Planck‑scale mass store information, (iii) the holographic principle and AdS/CFT correspondence imply a unitary boundary description, and (iv) firewalls or modifications of the horizon structure. Recent developments using the replica trick and quantum extremal surfaces have reproduced the Page curve in certain models, supporting the view that information is preserved.

Key quantitative relations

  • Surface gravity: κ = c⁴/(4GM) (Schwarzschild)
  • Hawking temperature: T_H = ħc³/(8πGMk_B)
  • Bekenstein‑Hawking entropy: S_BH = k_B A/(4ℓ_P²) = 4πGM²k_B/(ħc)
  • Evaporation lifetime: τ ≈ 5120πG²M³/(ħc⁴)

Gravitational‑Wave Data Analysis: Matched Filtering and Bayesian Parameter Estimation

Ground‑based interferometers such as LIGO, Virgo and KAGRA record strain time series h(t) = h_+(t)F_+ + h_×(t)F_× + n(t), where n(t) is instrumental noise. The optimal detection statistic for a known waveform template h(θ) is the matched‑filter signal‑to‑noise ratio (SNR) ρ = (h|s)/√(h|h), where the inner product (a|b) = 4 Re ∫₀^∞ ã(f) b̃*(f)/S_n(f) df uses the one‑sided noise power spectral density S_n(f). A detection is claimed when ρ exceeds a threshold (typically ρ ≥ 8) after accounting for the trials factor from template banks.

Template banks cover the intrinsic parameter space (component masses, spins) using a metric derived from the mismatch μ = 1 − (h(θ)|h(θ+Δθ))/√((h|h)(h|h)). For binary black‑hole mergers, the effective‑one‑body (EOB) and phenomenological (IMRPhenom) families provide accurate waveforms across the inspiral‑merger‑ringdown regime. The bank spacing is chosen to keep the minimal match above 0.97, ensuring <3 % SNR loss.

Once a candidate passes the SNR threshold, Bayesian parameter estimation yields posterior probability densities p(θ|d) ∝ p(d|θ) p(θ), where the likelihood p(d|θ) ∝ exp[−½ (d−h(θ)|d−h(θ))] assumes stationary Gaussian noise. Sampling is performed with stochastic algorithms such as nested sampling (e.g. Bilby, LALInference) or Markov chain Monte Carlo. The posteriors provide credible intervals for masses, spins, sky location, luminosity distance, and the binary’s inclination. Systematic uncertainties from waveform modelling are assessed by comparing results from multiple waveform families.

Multi‑detector networks improve sky localisation through triangulation of arrival‑time differences and amplitude/phase consistency across detectors. The addition of Virgo to the two‑LIGO network reduced the median 90 % credible sky area from hundreds to tens of square degrees for typical binary neutron‑star events. Future detectors (Einstein Telescope, Cosmic Explorer) will increase SNR by an order of magnitude, enabling precision tests of general relativity via parameterised post‑Einsteinian (ppE) frameworks.

Typical analysis pipeline

  1. Data conditioning: whitening, glitch removal, calibration
  2. Matched‑filter search with template bank
  3. Coincidence and consistency tests across detectors
  4. Bayesian inference with nested sampling
  5. Posterior validation: injection studies, waveform systematics

Cosmological Perturbation Theory and the Origin of Structure

In a Friedmann‑Lemaître‑Robertson‑Walker background, metric perturbations are decomposed into scalar, vector and tensor modes according to their transformation properties on spatial hypersurfaces. Scalar perturbations describe density fluctuations and gravitational potentials; vector modes correspond to vorticity and decay in the absence of anisotropic stress; tensor modes are gravitational waves. The gauge‑invariant Bardeen potentials Φ and Ψ combine metric and matter perturbations and obey the Poisson‑type equation k²Φ = 4πGa²ρΔ in the sub‑horizon limit, where Δ is the comoving density contrast.

During inflation, quantum fluctuations of the inflaton field generate a nearly scale‑invariant spectrum of curvature perturbations ℛ with power spectrum P_ℛ(k) = A_s (k/k_*)n_s−1. Planck 2018 results give A_s ≈ 2.1 × 10⁻⁹, n_s ≈ 0.965, and a tensor‑to‑scalar ratio r < 0.036 (95 % CL). These primordial perturbations seed the cosmic microwave background (CMB) anisotropies and the large‑scale structure (LSS) observed today.

The linear evolution of scalar perturbations is governed by the coupled Boltzmann equations for photons, neutrinos, cold dark matter and baryons. Before recombination, photon‑baryon acoustic oscillations imprint a series of peaks in the CMB angular power spectrum C_ℓ. After recombination, dark matter perturbations grow as δ ∝ a in the matter‑dominated era, while baryons fall into the potential wells, forming galaxies and clusters. Non‑linear evolution is modelled with N‑body simulations and perturbation‑theory resummation schemes (e.g. effective field theory of LSS).

Tensor perturbations produce a distinctive B‑mode polarisation pattern in the CMB. Current upper limits on r constrain the energy scale of inflation to V1/4 < 1.6 × 10¹⁶ GeV. Future CMB‑S4 and LiteBIRD missions aim to reach σ(r) ~ 10⁻³, probing the inflationary gravitational‑wave background.

Key observational probes

  • CMB temperature and polarisation power spectra (Planck, WMAP, ACT, SPT)
  • Galaxy clustering and baryon acoustic oscillations (BOSS, eBOSS, DESI)
  • Weak gravitational lensing shear correlations (DES, KiDS, HSC)
  • Redshift‑space distortions measuring growth rate fσ₈
  • Confusing the weak and strong equivalence principles — the weak principle concerns test bodies, the strong includes self‑gravitating bodies.
  • Assuming the PPN parameter γ = 1 is proven by a single experiment; it requires multiple independent solar‑system tests.
  • Treating the cosmic censorship conjecture as a theorem; it remains unproven in four dimensions.
  • Equating Hawking temperature with the Unruh temperature without noting the different physical origins (horizon vs acceleration).
  • Neglecting the role of the noise power spectral density in matched‑filter SNR calculations.
  • Using the Newtonian growth factor δ ∝ a for all scales; on large scales relativistic corrections and dark‑energy clustering matter.
  • Believing that a scale‑invariant spectrum (n_s = 1) is predicted by all inflation models; most predict a slight red tilt.

hand/diff-geometry.html:
Tensor Calculus: The Language of Invariance

Differential geometry, particularly in the context of curved spaces like those described by general relativity, relies heavily on tensor calculus. Tensors provide a mathematical language to describe physical quantities and geometric properties in a way that is independent of the chosen coordinate system. This coordinate independence is crucial because the laws of physics should not depend on how we label points in space or spacetime.

A tensor is a generalization of scalars (rank 0, magnitude only) and vectors (rank 1, magnitude and direction). It can be thought of as a multi-linear map that takes a certain number of vectors and covectors (dual vectors) as input and produces a scalar. The rank of a tensor indicates the number of indices it possesses. For instance, a vector is a (1,0)-tensor, a covector is a (0,1)-tensor, and the metric tensor is a (0,2)-tensor.

Tensors are classified by their contravariant (upper indices) and covariant (lower indices) ranks. Contravariant components transform inversely to coordinate changes, while covariant components transform directly. For example, if we change coordinates from xμ to x'ν, a contravariant vector Vμ transforms as V'ν = (∂x'ν/∂xμ)Vμ, and a covariant covector ωμ transforms as ω'ν = (∂xμ/∂x'ν)ωμ. Higher-rank tensors follow similar transformation rules, ensuring that physical equations expressed in tensor form remain valid in any coordinate system.

The metric tensor, denoted gμν, is a fundamental (0,2)-tensor in Riemannian geometry. It defines the inner product of vectors, allowing us to measure lengths, angles, and volumes on a manifold. Its components depend on the chosen coordinate system, but the underlying geometric properties it describes do not. The inverse metric tensor, gμν, is a (2,0)-tensor. These two tensors are used to "raise" and "lower" indices, converting contravariant components to covariant ones and vice-versa, effectively mapping between vectors and covectors.

Operations like tensor product (combining two tensors to form a higher-rank tensor) and contraction (summing over a pair of upper and lower indices to reduce the rank by two) are essential. For example, contracting the metric tensor gμν with a contravariant vector Vν yields a covariant vector Vμ = gμνVν. The Levi-Civita symbol (or permutation tensor) is another important tensor density used to define concepts like volume elements and cross products in higher dimensions. Understanding these foundational concepts of tensor calculus is the first step towards grasping the sophisticated machinery of differential geometry and its applications in physics and mathematics.

Connections and Parallel Transport: Navigating Curved Space

On a flat Euclidean space, comparing vectors at different points is straightforward: we simply translate them parallel to themselves. However, on a curved manifold, there's no inherent notion of "parallelism" between tangent spaces at distinct points. This challenge necessitates the concept of a connection, which provides a rule for differentiating vector fields and, more generally, for "moving" vectors along curves while keeping them "as parallel as possible."

The most common type of connection in Riemannian geometry is the Levi-Civita connection, which is uniquely determined by the metric tensor and is torsion-free and metric-compatible. Its components, known as Christoffel symbols (Γλμν), describe how the basis vectors change from point to point. These symbols are not tensors themselves, as they transform inhomogeneously under coordinate changes, but they are crucial for defining tensor derivatives.

Using Christoffel symbols, we can define the covariant derivative, denoted ∇. For a vector field Vμ, its covariant derivative along a direction specified by a tangent vector Uν is given by (∇UV)μ = Uν∇νVμ, where ∇νVμ = ∂νVμ + ΓμνλVλ. The covariant derivative extends to arbitrary tensors, ensuring that the result of differentiation is also a tensor. The extra term involving Christoffel symbols accounts for the curvature of the space, correcting for the change in basis vectors.

The concept of a connection naturally leads to parallel transport. A vector V is said to be parallel transported along a curve γ(t) if its covariant derivative along the curve's tangent vector is zero: dVμ/dt + Γμνλ(dxν/dt)Vλ = 0. This equation describes how the components of a vector must change as it moves along a curve to remain "parallel" in the curved space. If you parallel transport a vector around a closed loop on a curved surface, it generally will not return to its original orientation, illustrating the presence of curvature.

A fundamental application of parallel transport is the definition of geodesics. A geodesic is a curve whose tangent vector is parallel transported along itself. In other words, geodesics are the "straightest possible paths" in a curved space. Their equations are derived by setting the covariant derivative of the tangent vector to zero: d2xμ/dt2 + Γμνλ(dxν/dt)(dxλ/dt) = 0. These are the equations of motion for free particles in general relativity, where gravity is interpreted as the curvature of spacetime, and particles follow geodesics.

Understanding Geodesics on a Sphere
Consider a 2-dimensional sphere of radius R. Its metric in spherical coordinates (θ, φ) is given by ds² = R²dθ² + R²sin²θdφ².
  1. Calculate the Christoffel symbols for this metric.
  2. Using the Christoffel symbols, write down the geodesic equations for the sphere.
  3. Interpret the geodesic equations in terms of paths on the sphere.

Given the metric gθθ = R², gφφ = R²sin²θ, and gθφ = gφθ = 0. The inverse metric is gθθ = 1/R², gφφ = 1/(R²sin²θ).

1. Christoffel Symbols: The Christoffel symbols of the second kind are given by Γλμν = ½gλσ(∂νgσμ + ∂μgσν - ∂σgμν).

Let's calculate the non-zero symbols:

  • Γθφφ = ½gθθ(∂φgθφ + ∂φgφθ - ∂θgφφ) = ½(1/R²)(0 + 0 - ∂θ(R²sin²θ)) = ½(1/R²)(-2R²sinθcosθ) = -sinθcosθ.
  • Γφθφ = Γφφθ = ½gφφ(∂φgφθ + ∂θgφφ - ∂φgθφ) = ½(1/(R²sin²θ))(0 + ∂θ(R²sin²θ) - 0) = ½(1/(R²sin²θ))(2R²sinθcosθ) = cotθ.

All other Christoffel symbols are zero due to the diagonal metric and lack of φ dependence in gθθ.

2. Geodesic Equations: The geodesic equations are d2xμ/dt2 + Γμνλ(dxν/dt)(dxλ/dt) = 0. Here x1 = θ, x2 = φ.

  • For μ = θ: d2θ/dt2 + Γθφφ(dφ/dt)(dφ/dt) = 0

    • d2θ/dt2 - sinθcosθ(dφ/dt)² = 0

  • For μ = φ: d2φ/dt2 + Γφθφ(dθ/dt)(dφ/dt) + Γφφθ(dφ/dt)(dθ/dt) = 0

    • d2φ/dt2 + 2cotθ(dθ/dt)(dφ/dt) = 0

3. Interpretation:

  • The first equation, d2θ/dt2 = sinθcosθ(dφ/dt)², shows that if dφ/dt ≠ 0 (i.e., the path is not along a meridian), there is a "force" pushing the path towards the equator (θ = π/2) or poles (θ = 0, π), depending on the sign of sinθcosθ. This is the effect of the sphere's curvature. If dφ/dt = 0, then d2θ/dt2 = 0, meaning θ is linear in t, which corresponds to meridians (great circles passing through the poles).
  • The second equation, d2φ/dt2 = -2cotθ(dθ/dt)(dφ/dt), describes how the φ-component of the velocity changes. If dθ/dt = 0 (path along a parallel of latitude), then d2φ/dt2 = 0, meaning dφ/dt is constant. This implies a circle of constant latitude. However, only the equator (θ = π/2, cotθ = 0) is a geodesic among parallels of latitude. For any other parallel, a particle would "fall off" due to the curvature, unless an external force acts.

Together, these equations describe great circles on the sphere, which are the shortest paths between any two points on its surface.

Visualizing Curvature with Parallel Transport
When tackling problems involving curvature, especially on surfaces, try to visualize parallel transport. Imagine a small arrow (a tangent vector) being moved along a path. If the space is curved, the arrow's orientation relative to its starting point will change even if it's "parallel transported." This non-closure of parallel transport around a loop is the essence of curvature. For example, on a sphere, transport a vector along the equator, then up a meridian to the North Pole, then down another meridian. The final vector will be rotated relative to its initial orientation, demonstrating the sphere's positive curvature. This intuitive understanding can help you grasp the meaning of curvature tensors without getting lost in the indices.

The Riemann Curvature Tensor: Quantifying Spacetime's Twist

The Riemann curvature tensor, Rρσμν, is the central object in differential geometry that precisely quantifies the curvature of a manifold. It captures the intrinsic curvature, meaning it describes how the manifold is curved within itself, independent of any embedding in a higher-dimensional space. It is a (1,3)-tensor, meaning it takes three vectors and produces another vector, or equivalently, it's a multilinear map that takes four vectors and produces a scalar.

Conceptually, the Riemann tensor measures the failure of covariant derivatives to commute. That is, for any two vector fields X and Y, and a third vector field Z, the difference ∇X∇YZ - ∇Y∇XZ is not simply [X,Y]Z (where [X,Y] is the Lie bracket), but also includes a term involving the Riemann tensor: R(X,Y)Z. This non-commutativity signifies the presence of curvature. Another powerful interpretation is through holonomy: the Riemann tensor describes the infinitesimal rotation or change in a vector after it has been parallel transported around an infinitesimal closed loop.

In terms of Christoffel symbols, the components of the Riemann tensor are given by: Rρσμν = ∂μΓρνσ - ∂νΓρμσ + ΓρμλΓλνσ - ΓρνλΓλμσ. This expression highlights that curvature depends on the first and second derivatives of the metric tensor (since Christoffel symbols depend on first derivatives of the metric). If all components of the Riemann tensor are zero, the manifold is flat (locally Euclidean).

The Riemann tensor possesses several crucial symmetries:

  1. Antisymmetry in the last two indices: Rρσμν = -Rρσνμ.
  2. Antisymmetry in the first two lower indices (after lowering the first index): Rρσμν = -Rσρμν.
  3. Symmetry across pairs of indices: Rρσμν = Rμνρσ.
  4. The Bianchi identity (or cyclic identity): Rρσμν + Rρμνσ + Rρνσμ = 0. This identity implies that not all components of the Riemann tensor are independent.

These symmetries significantly reduce the number of independent components. For an n-dimensional manifold, the number of independent components is n²(n²-1)/12. For example, in 4-dimensional spacetime, there are 20 independent components.

The Riemann tensor can be decomposed into simpler tensors, which have distinct physical interpretations:

  • Ricci Curvature Tensor (Rμν): This is obtained by contracting the Riemann tensor: Rμν = Rλμλν. It describes how the volume of a small ball of geodesics changes. In general relativity, the Ricci tensor is directly related to the distribution of matter and energy (via the Einstein Field Equations), representing the attractive nature of gravity.
  • Scalar Curvature (R): This is obtained by contracting the Ricci tensor with the inverse metric: R = gμνRμν. It's a scalar invariant that gives an overall measure of the curvature at a point.
  • Weyl Curvature Tensor (Cρσμν): This is the traceless part of the Riemann tensor, meaning it's what remains after subtracting the Ricci and scalar curvature contributions. It describes tidal forces and gravitational waves, representing the "free gravitational field" in vacuum. Unlike the Ricci tensor, the Weyl tensor can be non-zero even in empty space.

Understanding these components is vital for analyzing the geometry of spacetime and its physical implications, from the bending of light around massive objects to the dynamics of black holes and the expansion of the universe.

Fibre Bundles: Geometry Beyond Tangent Spaces

While Riemannian geometry primarily focuses on the tangent bundle of a manifold, the more general concept of a fibre bundle provides a powerful framework for understanding a wider array of geometric structures and their connections to physics, particularly in gauge theories. A fibre bundle is a space that locally looks like a product of a base space (our manifold M) and a fibre (a space F), but globally can be twisted.

Formally, a fibre bundle consists of a total space E, a base space M, a projection map π: E → M, and a fibre F, such that for every point x in M, there is an open neighborhood U of x and a homeomorphism φ: π⁻¹(U) → U × F. This homeomorphism is called a local trivialization. The key idea is that while E might be globally complex, locally it's simple. The tangent bundle TM (where the fibre is the tangent space TxM) and the cotangent bundle T*M are prime examples of vector bundles, which are a specific type of fibre bundle where the fibre is a vector space.

Beyond vector bundles, principal bundles are particularly important. A principal G-bundle (where G is a Lie group, the "structure group") is a fibre bundle where the fibre is G itself, and G acts freely and transitively on the fibre. The most common example is the frame bundle (or principal frame bundle) of a manifold. At each point x on the manifold, the fibre consists of all possible bases (frames) for the tangent space TxM. The general linear group GL(n, ℝ) acts on these frames. Principal bundles provide a natural setting for defining connections and curvature in a more general sense than just the Levi-Civita connection.

A connection on a fibre bundle can be thought of as a way to "lift" tangent vectors from the base space M to the total space E, or equivalently, a way to define parallel transport of the fibres. For principal bundles, a connection is often defined as a Lie algebra-valued 1-form on the total space. The curvature of this connection then measures the failure of parallel transport to be path-independent around closed loops in the base space. This generalizes the Riemann curvature tensor, which arises from a connection on the tangent bundle.

The significance of fibre bundles extends deeply into theoretical physics. In gauge theories (like electromagnetism, the weak force, and the strong force), the fundamental fields are often interpreted as connections on principal bundles over spacetime. The gauge group of the theory (e.g., U(1) for electromagnetism, SU(2) for the weak force, SU(3) for the strong force) is the structure group G of the bundle. The field strengths (like the electromagnetic field tensor Fμν) are precisely the curvature forms of these connections. This geometric interpretation provides a unified and elegant framework for understanding fundamental forces, where forces arise from the curvature of appropriate fibre bundles over spacetime. This abstract language allows physicists to describe interactions in a coordinate-independent and gauge-invariant manner, pushing the boundaries of our understanding of the universe's fundamental structure.

Common Traps in Advanced Differential Geometry

  • Confusing Christoffel Symbols with Tensors: Christoffel symbols (Γλμν) are *not* tensors. They transform inhomogeneously under coordinate changes, meaning their values depend on the specific coordinate system chosen, unlike tensors which have invariant physical meaning. This is a frequent point of confusion.
  • Misinterpreting the Role of the Metric Tensor: While the metric tensor gμν defines distances and angles, it also implicitly defines the connection (Christoffel symbols) and thus the curvature in Riemannian geometry. Forgetting this fundamental link can lead to errors in deriving geometric properties.
  • Incorrectly Applying Tensor Contraction: Contraction involves summing over one upper and one lower index. Incorrectly contracting indices (e.g., two upper or two lower) or contracting indices from different tensors without a proper tensor product can lead to non-tensorial results.
  • Overlooking the Symmetries of the Riemann Tensor: The Riemann curvature tensor has specific symmetries (e.g., antisymmetry in the last two indices, Bianchi identity). Failing to utilize these symmetries can lead to unnecessary calculations or incorrect deductions about the number of independent components.
  • Confusing Ricci Curvature with Weyl Curvature: While both are derived from the Riemann tensor, Ricci curvature (Rμν) relates to volume changes and matter/energy distribution (gravity's attractive component), whereas Weyl curvature (Cρσμν) describes tidal forces and gravitational waves (the "free" gravitational field in vacuum). They are distinct and represent different aspects of curvature.
  • Assuming Flatness from Zero Ricci Curvature: A manifold with zero Ricci curvature (Ricci-flat) is not necessarily flat (zero Riemann curvature). For example, a manifold with gravitational waves in vacuum is Ricci-flat but has non-zero Weyl curvature, meaning it is still curved. Only if the entire Riemann tensor is zero is the manifold flat.
  • Misunderstanding the Global vs. Local Nature of Fibre Bundles: Fibre bundles are locally trivial (look like a product space) but can be globally non-trivial (twisted). This global twisting is what allows for complex geometric structures and is crucial for understanding phenomena like magnetic monopoles in physics.

Modular Arithmetic and the Chinese Remainder Theorem

Modular arithmetic treats integers as residues modulo a positive integer m. Two numbers a and b are congruent modulo m (written a ≡ b (mod m)) when m divides a − b. This equivalence partitions the integers into m residue classes. Basic properties: if a ≡ b (mod m) and c ≡ d (mod m) then a + c ≡ b + d (mod m), a − c ≡ b − d (mod m), and a·c ≡ b·d (mod m). These rules allow simplification of large powers, e.g. 7100 (mod 10) reduces to 74 (mod 10) because φ(10)=4 (Euler’s theorem for coprime base).

The Chinese Remainder Theorem (CRT) states that for pairwise coprime moduli m₁, m₂, …, mₖ and any residues r₁, r₂, …, rₖ, there exists a unique solution modulo M = m₁·m₂·…·mₖ. Construction: compute Mᵢ = M / mᵢ, find the multiplicative inverse yᵢ of Mᵢ modulo mᵢ (i.e. Mᵢ·yᵢ ≡ 1 (mod mᵢ)), then the solution is x = Σ rᵢ·Mᵢ·yᵢ (mod M). CRT is indispensable for solving simultaneous congruences that appear in calendar problems, cryptography, and large‑number remainder questions.

Typical exam twists: moduli that are not coprime (then a solution exists only if residues agree on common divisors), or asking for the smallest positive integer satisfying several remainders. In such cases reduce each congruence by the gcd of the moduli before applying CRT. Another common variant asks for the last two digits of a huge exponent; this is exactly mod 100 and can be tackled by splitting into mod 4 and mod 25 (coprime) and recombining via CRT.

Key shortcuts

  • For an (mod m) with gcd(a,m)=1, reduce exponent modulo φ(m) (Euler) or λ(m) (Carmichael).
  • When m = 2k (k≥3), the group of units is cyclic of order 2k‑2; use this for powers of odd numbers.
  • To find inverse of a modulo m, run extended Euclidean algorithm; the coefficient of a is the inverse.

Advanced LCM and HCF with Fractions, Decimals, and Polynomials

The concepts of Least Common Multiple (LCM) and Highest Common Factor (HCF) extend beyond integers. For fractions a/b and c/d in lowest terms, LCM = LCM(a,c) / HCF(b,d) and HCF = HCF(a,c) / LCM(b,d). This follows from the definition that LCM is the smallest positive rational that is an integer multiple of each fraction, while HCF is the largest rational that divides both. Example: LCM of 2/3 and 3/4 = LCM(2,3)/HCF(3,4) = 6/1 = 6; HCF = HCF(2,3)/LCM(3,4) = 1/12.

For terminating decimals, convert to fractions with denominator a power of 10, then apply the fraction rule. For recurring decimals, express as a fraction using the standard algebraic method (e.g. 0.1̅6 = 1/6) before computing LCM/HCF. When decimals are mixed (some terminating, some recurring), bring all to a common fractional form first.

Polynomial LCM and HCF follow the same prime‑factor logic: factor each polynomial over the integers (or rationals), then LCM takes the highest power of each irreducible factor, HCF takes the lowest. For P(x) = x²−1 = (x−1)(x+1) and Q(x) = x²−x = x(x−1), HCF = (x−1), LCM = x(x−1)(x+1). This is directly useful in algebraic simplification and in solving rational equations where common denominators are required.

Exam patterns: a question may give three numbers in different forms (integer, fraction, decimal) and ask for LCM or HCF. The trick is to normalise everything to fractions in lowest terms, then apply the fraction formula. Another trap: asking for LCM of numbers that are not co‑prime but share a large common factor; the product‑over‑HCF shortcut (LCM·HCF = product) holds only for two numbers, not for three or more. For three numbers, compute pairwise or use prime factorisation.

Worked Example: CRT for Last Two Digits
Find the last two digits of 7222.
We need 7222 (mod 100). Since 100 = 4 × 25 and gcd(4,25)=1, compute modulo 4 and modulo 25 separately.
Modulo 4: 7 ≡ −1 (mod 4) ⇒ (−1)222 = 1 (mod 4).
Modulo 25: φ(25)=20, gcd(7,25)=1 ⇒ 720 ≡ 1 (mod 25). Reduce exponent: 222 = 20×11 + 2 ⇒ 7222 ≡ 7² = 49 ≡ −1 (mod 25).
Now solve x ≡ 1 (mod 4), x ≡ 24 (mod 25).
M = 100, M₁ = 25, M₂ = 4.
Inverse of 25 mod 4: 25 ≡ 1 ⇒ y₁ = 1.
Inverse of 4 mod 25: 4·19 = 76 ≡ 1 ⇒ y₂ = 19.
x = 1·25·1 + 24·4·19 = 25 + 1824 = 1849 ≡ 49 (mod 100).
Answer: 49.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a remainder question involves a composite modulus, factor it into coprime parts (e.g. 100 → 4 and 25, 1000 → 8 and 125). Solve each small congruence mentally, then recombine with CRT. Memorise the inverses of common pairs: 25⁻¹ (mod 4)=1, 4⁻¹ (mod 25)=19, 125⁻¹ (mod 8)=5, 8⁻¹ (mod 125)=47. This turns a 2‑minute calculation into a 15‑second one.

Componendo and Dividendo in Ratio and Proportion

Componendo and Dividendo are algebraic identities that transform a proportion into a new proportion, often simplifying the arithmetic. If a/b = c/d then:
Componendo: (a+b)/(a−b) = (c+d)/(c−d) (provided denominators non‑zero).
Dividendo: (a−b)/(a+b) = (c−d)/(c+d).
Combined (Componendo‑Dividendo): (a+b)/(a−b) = (c+d)/(c−d) and also (a/b) = (c/d) ⇒ (a+b)/(c+d) = (a−b)/(c−d).

These are derived by adding/subtracting 1 to both sides of the original proportion. They are powerful when the unknown appears in both numerator and denominator of a fraction. For instance, if (x+3)/(x−3) = 5/2, applying Componendo‑Dividendo gives ( (x+3)+(x−3) )/( (x+3)−(x−3) ) = (5+2)/(5−2) ⇒ (2x)/(6) = 7/3 ⇒ x = 7.

Extended forms: If a/b = c/d = e/f = k, then each ratio equals (a+c+e)/(b+d+f) (addendo) and also (a−c+e)/(b−d+f) (subtrahendo) provided denominators non‑zero. This is useful for problems with multiple equal ratios, such as finding a combined ratio of three quantities given pairwise ratios.

Exam twists: The proportion may be hidden inside a word problem (e.g. “the ratio of ages of A and B is 3:4, and the ratio of their ages 5 years ago was 2:3”). Set up the proportion, then apply Componendo‑Dividendo to avoid solving simultaneous linear equations. Another trap: applying the rule when a = b or c = d, which makes denominators zero; always check the condition a ≠ b and c ≠ d before using it.

Compound Interest with Variable Rates and Non‑Annual Compounding

Standard compound interest formula A = P(1 + r/100)t assumes a constant annual rate r and annual compounding. Real exam questions often vary the rate each year or change the compounding frequency. For variable rates r₁, r₂, …, rₙ over n years, the amount is A = P ∏ (1 + rᵢ/100). This product cannot be collapsed into a single effective rate unless the rates are equal; however, the overall effective annual rate R satisfies (1 + R/100)n = ∏ (1 + rᵢ/100).

When compounding is half‑yearly, quarterly, or monthly, the nominal annual rate r is divided by the number of periods per year m, and the exponent becomes m·t. Formula: A = P (1 + r/(100·m))m·t. The effective annual rate (EAR) is (1 + r/(100·m))m − 1. For continuous compounding, the limit as m → ∞ gives A = P ert/100 where e is Euler’s number.

Typical problem: “A sum of ₹10,000 is invested at 10% p.a. compounded half‑yearly for the first year and 12% p.a. compounded quarterly for the second year. Find the amount.” Compute first year: A₁ = 10000 (1 + 10/(200))2 = 10000 (1.05)² = 11025. Second year: new principal = 11025, rate 12% quarterly ⇒ A₂ = 11025 (1 + 12/(400))4 = 11025 (1.03)⁴ ≈ 11025 × 1.1255 ≈ 12407. Round as required.

Another variation: given the final amount and the varying rates, find the principal. Work backwards by dividing by each period’s growth factor. For continuous compounding, use natural logarithms: t = (100/r) ln(A/P). Exams rarely ask for e directly but may test the concept that continuous compounding yields the maximum possible amount for a given nominal rate.

Pipes, Cisterns, and Work Efficiency Variations

Pipe and cistern problems are direct applications of the work‑rate principle. A pipe that fills a tank in T hours has rate 1/T tank per hour. An outlet pipe that empties in E hours has rate −1/E. When multiple pipes operate together, net rate = Σ (fill rates) + Σ (empty rates). Time to fill = 1 / (net rate) provided net rate > 0.

Efficiency variations: “A is twice as efficient as B” means rateA = 2·rateB. If A and B together finish in 6 days, then (rateA + rateB) = 1/6 ⇒ 3·rateB = 1/6 ⇒ rateB = 1/18, rateA = 1/9. Hence A alone takes 9 days, B alone 18 days. This ratio method avoids solving simultaneous equations.

Leak problems: A cistern has a leak that would empty it in L hours. With a fill pipe open, it fills in F hours. The leak’s rate is −1/L, fill pipe’s rate is 1/F − (−1/L) = 1/F + 1/L. If the fill pipe alone were open, time = 1 / (1/F + 1/L) = FL/(F+L). This is a standard shortcut.

Alternate day work: A works on day 1, B on day 2, etc. Compute work done in each 2‑day cycle: rateA + rateB. Number of full cycles = floor(1 / (rateA+rateB)). Remaining work after full cycles is finished by the next worker in the sequence. Carefully handle the case where the remaining work is completed mid‑day; the answer may be a fractional day.

Exam patterns: multiple pipes with different opening/closing times (e.g. pipe A opens at 8 am, pipe B at 9 am, leak starts at 10 am). Break the timeline into intervals where the set of active pipes is constant, compute net rate for each interval, accumulate work until the tank is full. This piecewise approach is systematic and avoids guesswork.

  • Assuming LCM·HCF = product holds for three or more numbers; it only holds for two numbers.
  • Applying Componendo‑Dividendo when the numerator equals the denominator, causing division by zero.
  • Treating variable‑rate compound interest as a single effective rate without verifying the product of growth factors.
  • Forgetting to convert nominal rate to periodic rate when compounding frequency changes (e.g. using 10% instead of 2.5% per quarter).
  • In pipe problems, adding emptying rates as positive numbers instead of subtracting them.
  • Using the simple average of speeds for equal‑distance legs instead of the harmonic mean (2v₁v₂/(v₁+v₂)).
  • Ignoring the condition that CRT requires pairwise coprime moduli; forcing a solution when residues conflict on a common divisor.

Mastering these advanced arithmetic mechanisms equips you to handle the most twisted quantitative questions with confidence and speed.

hand/quantum-computing.html:
Quantum Phase Estimation and Its Role in Quantum Algorithms

Quantum Phase Estimation (QPE) is the subroutine that extracts the eigenvalue e2πiθ of a unitary operator U acting on an eigenstate |ψ⟩. The algorithm uses two registers: a control register of t qubits initialized in |0⟩⊗t and a target register prepared in |ψ⟩. After applying Hadamard gates to the control register, controlled‑U2k operations are performed for k = 0,…,\t−1. An inverse Quantum Fourier Transform on the control register then yields a binary approximation of the phase θ. The precision ε = 2−t determines the number of control qubits; achieving ε requires t = ⌈log₂(1/ε)⌉ qubits and O(t) controlled‑U calls. QPE is the engine behind Shor’s order‑finding (where U|x⟩ = |ax mod N⟩), the HHL linear‑systems algorithm, and quantum simulation of Hamiltonian dynamics via Trotter‑Suzuki decompositions. Kitaev’s original formulation used a single control qubit with iterative measurements, reducing space at the cost of repeated circuit executions. The algorithm’s runtime is polynomial in the number of qubits and the desired precision, placing phase estimation in BQP. However, QPE demands high‑fidelity controlled‑U operations and long coherence times, making it a benchmark for fault‑tolerant hardware.

Variational Quantum Algorithms: VQE and QAOA

Variational Quantum Algorithms (VQAs) replace deep, fixed circuits with shallow, parameterized ansätze optimized by a classical loop. The Variational Quantum Eigensolver (VQE) targets the ground‑state energy of a Hamiltonian H = Σi ci Pi (Pi Pauli strings). A trial state |ψ(θ⃗)⟩ = U(θ⃗)|0⟩ is prepared, the expectation ⟨ψ(θ⃗)|H|ψ(θ⃗)⟩ is measured by grouping commuting Pauli terms, and a classical optimizer (e.g., COBYLA, SPSA, gradient‑based methods) updates θ⃗. Hardware‑efficient ansätze use alternating layers of single‑qubit rotations and entangling gates native to the device; problem‑inspired ansätze such as unitary coupled‑cluster (UCCSD) encode chemical structure. The Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm (QAOA) solves combinatorial problems by alternating a problem Hamiltonian HC (diagonal in the computational basis) and a mixer Hamiltonian HM = Σ Xi. For depth p, the state is |γ⃗,β⃗⟩ = ∏k=1p e−iβkHM e−iγkHC |+⟩⊗n. As p → ∞, QAOA approaches the adiabatic limit and can achieve the optimal solution; for finite p it yields approximation ratios that often beat classical heuristics on MaxCut. Key challenges include barren plateaus (exponentially vanishing gradients for deep random circuits), noise‑induced bias in expectation values, and the combinatorial explosion of measurement settings for non‑commuting Pauli groups. Error mitigation techniques such as zero‑noise extrapolation and probabilistic error cancellation are routinely combined with VQAs on near‑term devices.

Worked Example: Choosing a VQE Ansatz for a 4‑Qubit Heisenberg Model
A student must design a VQE circuit to approximate the ground state of the 1D Heisenberg Hamiltonian H = Σi=13 (XiXi+1 + YiYi+1 + ZiZi+1) on four qubits with only nearest‑neighbor CNOT connectivity. Which ansatz family is most appropriate and why?
The problem‑inspired unitary coupled‑cluster (UCC) ansatz is overkill for a pure spin model and would require many non‑local gates. A hardware‑efficient ansatz with alternating layers of single‑qubit rotations (Rx, Ry, Rz) on each qubit followed by a ladder of CNOTs matching the linear connectivity (1→2, 2→3, 3→4) respects the device topology and can express the entanglement structure of the Heisenberg ground state. Two such layers (depth = 2) already provide sufficient variational freedom for a 4‑qubit system while keeping circuit depth low enough to mitigate decoherence. The student should also consider adding a final layer of single‑qubit rotations to capture local basis changes.
Exam‑Day Strategy for Variational Algorithms
When a question asks to compare VQE and QAOA, focus on three axes: (1) objective — VQE minimizes an energy expectation, QAOA maximizes a cost function; (2) ansatz structure — VQE uses problem‑agnostic or chemistry‑inspired layers, QAOA has a fixed alternating Hamiltonian form; (3) classical optimization — VQE requires a general‑purpose optimizer, QAOA’s parameters have a clear physical interpretation (γ, β) and often admit analytical gradients for small p. Memorize the barren‑plateau definition: gradient variance decays exponentially with qubit count for deep random circuits. Cite the 2018 McClean et al. paper if a reference is required.

Quantum Error Correction Beyond Surface Codes: Color Codes and LDPC Codes

The surface code dominates experimental roadmaps because its stabilizers are weight‑4 plaquette and star operators on a square lattice, requiring only nearest‑neighbor couplings and yielding a threshold near 1 %. Color codes generalize this idea to 2D lattices whose faces are three‑colorable (e.g., the 4.8.8 or 6.6.6 tilings). Each color class supports a set of stabilizers, and the code admits transversal implementation of the entire Clifford group, simplifying logical gate synthesis. Gauge fixing in subsystem color codes reduces the weight of measured stabilizers, easing experimental demands. Low‑Density Parity‑Check (LDPC) quantum codes go further: they maintain constant stabilizer weight while achieving a finite rate (k/n = constant) and, in recent constructions, linear distance d = Θ(n). The breakthrough by Panteleev and Kalachev (2021) produced a family of quantum LDPC codes with parameters [[n, Θ(n), Θ(n)]] based on a lifted product of classical expander codes. These codes promise thresholds comparable to the surface code but with far fewer physical qubits per logical qubit. The trade‑off is non‑local connectivity — stabilizers may couple qubits far apart on a planar chip — and more complex decoding (belief propagation, neural decoders). Hybrid architectures that embed LDPC codes in 3D or use modular interconnects are active research directions.

Quantum Communication Protocols: BB84, E91, and Quantum Repeaters

Quantum Key Distribution (QKD) provides information‑theoretic security grounded in the no‑cloning theorem and the disturbance‑measurement trade‑off. The BB84 protocol (Bennett & Brassard, 1984) encodes random bits in two conjugate bases (rectilinear and diagonal) of single photons. After transmission, Alice and Bob publicly announce their basis choices and keep only the matching‑basis outcomes, yielding a raw key. Error correction and privacy amplification then produce a secret key. Security proofs (Mayers 2001, Shor‑Preskill 2000) bound the eavesdropper’s information by the observed quantum bit error rate (QBER); a QBER above ~11 % aborts the protocol. The E91 protocol (Ekert 1991) uses entangled photon pairs and tests the CHSH Bell inequality; violation certifies the presence of genuine entanglement and bounds Eve’s knowledge device‑independently. Both protocols suffer exponential photon loss in optical fiber, limiting direct transmission to ~100–200 km. Quantum repeaters overcome this by segmenting the channel: entanglement is generated over elementary links, stored in quantum memories, purified via entanglement distillation, and swapped to extend the distance. The DLCZ protocol (Duan‑Lukin‑Cirac‑Zoller 2001) uses atomic ensembles and photon detection for heralded entanglement. Satellite‑based QKD (Micius, 2017) demonstrated intercontinental key exchange by exploiting free‑space loss scaling as 1/d² instead of exponential fiber loss. Trusted‑node networks (e.g., the Beijing‑Shanghai backbone) relay keys classically between secure nodes, while device‑independent QKD aims to remove trust assumptions on hardware.

Quantum Complexity Classes: BQP, QMA, and the Limits of Quantum Speedup

Bounded‑Error Quantum Polynomial Time (BQP) is the class of decision problems solvable by a uniform family of quantum circuits with polynomial size and error ≤ 1/3. It is known that P ⊆ BQP ⊆ PSPACE, and BQP ⊆ AWPP. The relationship to NP remains open; oracle separations (Simon’s problem, period finding) show that BQP can solve certain problems exponentially faster than any classical algorithm relative to an oracle, but no proof exists that NP ⊄ BQP. Quantum Merlin‑Arthur (QMA) is the quantum analogue of NP: a quantum verifier receives a polynomial‑size quantum witness and decides with bounded error. The k‑local Hamiltonian problem is QMA‑complete for k ≥ 2, establishing the hardness of estimating ground‑state energies. The quantum PCP conjecture posits that approximating the ground‑state energy of local Hamiltonians remains QMA‑hard even for constant relative error, with implications for the complexity of quantum many‑body physics. Grover’s algorithm gives a quadratic speedup for unstructured search, and the optimality proof (Bennett et al. 1997) shows that no quantum algorithm can achieve better than Ω(√N) queries. For NP‑complete problems, the best known quantum algorithms (e.g., quantum backtracking, quantum walk search) provide at most polynomial speedups; an exponential speedup would imply NP ⊆ BQP, which is widely believed false. Quantum supremacy experiments (Google Sycamore 2019, USTC Jiuzhang 2020) sample from random circuit or boson‑sampling distributions that are classically intractable under plausible complexity assumptions, but they do not solve decision problems in BQP. Understanding these boundaries guides expectations for near‑term quantum advantage.

  • Assuming QPE works with a single control qubit for high precision — iterative QPE requires many repetitions and coherent feedback, not a single shot.
  • Confusing VQE’s heuristic nature with a guarantee of finding the true ground state — convergence depends on ansatz expressibility and optimizer performance.
  • Believing color codes automatically have a higher threshold than the surface code — thresholds are comparable; the advantage lies in transversal Clifford gates.
  • Thinking quantum repeaters simply amplify photons like classical repeaters — they require quantum memories, entanglement purification, and swapping, not amplification.
  • Equating quantum supremacy with solving NP‑complete problems — supremacy demonstrates sampling hardness, not decision‑problem speedup.
  • Assuming BQP contains NP because Shor’s algorithm breaks RSA — factoring is in BQP but not known to be NP‑complete.
  • Remember to review these traps before the exam.
