hand/tensor-calculus.html:
Spectral Sequences and the de Rham Theorem

The de Rham theorem identifies de Rham cohomology with singular cohomology with real coefficients. A powerful tool for computing these groups on complicated manifolds is the spectral sequence associated to a filtration of the de Rham complex. The most common instance is the Leray spectral sequence for a smooth submersion π: E → B with fibre F. Its E₂‑page is E₂p,q = H^p(B; ℋ^q(F)) where ℋ^q(F) denotes the locally constant sheaf of cohomology of the fibre. The sequence converges to Hp+q(E). When the fibration is orientable and the base is simply connected, the local system is trivial and the E₂‑page simplifies to the tensor product H^p(B) ⊗ H^q(F). The differentials d_r: E_rp,q → E_rp+r, q‑r+1 encode the obstruction to a global product structure. In the case of a principal G‑bundle, the Leray–Serre spectral sequence yields the transgression map that produces characteristic classes. Another important spectral sequence is the Mayer–Vietoris spectral sequence for a good cover {U_i}. Its E₁‑page is the Čech–de Rham double complex C^p(𝒰, Ω^q) and it collapses at E₂ to the de Rham cohomology of the manifold. These spectral sequences are not merely computational devices; they reveal how the topology of the total space is built from the topology of the base and the fibre, and they underlie the proof of the de Rham theorem via the comparison of the Čech–de Rham complex with the singular cochain complex.

In practice, examiners often ask for the E₂‑page of the Leray spectral sequence for a specific fibration such as the Hopf fibration S¹ → S³ → S². The answer is E₂p,q = H^p(S²) ⊗ H^q(S¹) which is non‑zero only for (p,q) = (0,0), (0,1), (2,0), (2,1). The only possible non‑trivial differential is d₂: E₂0,1 → E₂2,0, and it is an isomorphism because H³(S³)=0. This forces the generator of H¹(S¹) to transgress to the generator of H²(S²), producing the Euler class of the bundle. Understanding this mechanism is essential for any problem that asks to compute cohomology rings of total spaces of fibre bundles.

Characteristic Classes and Chern–Weil Theory

Characteristic classes measure the twisting of vector bundles and principal bundles. Chern–Weil theory constructs them from the curvature of a connection. Let P → M be a principal G‑bundle with connection A and curvature F = dA + A∧A, a Lie‑algebra‑valued 2‑form. For any invariant polynomial P on the Lie algebra 𝔤 (i.e. P(Ad_g X) = P(X)), the form P(F) is a closed differential form on M whose de Rham cohomology class is independent of the chosen connection. The resulting classes lie in H2k(M; ℝ) where k is the degree of P. For G = U(n) the elementary symmetric polynomials in the eigenvalues of (i/2π)F give the Chern classes c_k. The total Chern class is c = det(I + (i/2π)F). For G = SO(n) the Pfaffian of (1/2π)F yields the Euler class e, while the Pontryagin classes p_k are obtained from the invariant polynomials Tr(F2k). The Chern character ch = Tr(exp((i/2π)F)) and the Todd class td = det((i/2π)F/(1‑exp(-(i/2π)F))) appear in the Hirzebruch–Riemann–Roch theorem and the Atiyah–Singer index theorem. A standard exam question asks to compute the first Chern class of the tautological line bundle over ℂP¹. The curvature of the natural connection is (i/2π) times the Fubini–Study form ω, so c₁ = [ω/2π] which generates H²(ℂP¹; ℤ) ≅ ℤ. Another frequent task is to show that the Pontryagin class p₁ of the tangent bundle of S⁴ vanishes because S⁴ admits a flat connection after removing a point, implying all Pontryagin numbers are zero. Mastery of the Chern–Weil homomorphism, the distinction between real and integral classes, and the behaviour under Whitney sum (c(E⊕F) = c(E)c(F)) is indispensable.

Worked Example: First Chern Class of the Hopf Bundle
Compute the first Chern class of the complex line bundle associated to the Hopf fibration S¹ → S³ → S² using Chern–Weil theory.
The Hopf bundle is the principal U(1)‑bundle over S² with total space S³. Choose the standard connection 1‑form A on S³ induced by the Maurer–Cartan form of SU(2). Its curvature is F = dA = 2 ω where ω is the area form on S² normalised so that ∫S² ω = 2π. The Chern–Weil formula gives c₁ = [iF/2π] = [i·2ω/2π] = [iω/π]. Since ω integrates to 2π, the class evaluates to 1 on the fundamental class of S², hence c₁ generates H²(S²; ℤ) ≅ ℤ. The first Chern class is therefore the positive generator.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a problem asks for a characteristic class, first identify the structure group and the relevant invariant polynomial. Write down the curvature of a convenient connection (often the canonical one). Apply the Chern–Weil homomorphism and integrate over the appropriate cycle to read off the integer invariant. Remember that the result is independent of the connection, so you may pick the simplest one.

Spin Geometry and Dirac Operators

Spin geometry refines Riemannian geometry by lifting the oriented orthonormal frame bundle from SO(n) to its double cover Spin(n). A spin structure on an oriented Riemannian manifold (M,g) is a principal Spin(n)‑bundle PSpin together with a 2‑fold covering map PSpin → PSO compatible with the group homomorphism Spin(n) → SO(n). The obstruction to the existence of a spin structure is the second Stiefel–Whitney class w₂(M) ∈ H²(M; ℤ₂). If w₂ = 0, spin structures are classified by H¹(M; ℤ₂). Given a spin structure, one constructs the complex spinor bundle S = PSpin ×ρ Δ_n where ρ is the spin representation of Spin(n) on the complex Clifford module Δ_n. The Levi‑Civita connection lifts uniquely to a connection on PSpin, inducing a covariant derivative ∇^S on S. The Dirac operator D: Γ(S) → Γ(S) is the composition of ∇^S with Clifford multiplication: D = ∑_i e_i · ∇^Se_i for a local orthonormal frame {e_i}. The Lichnerowicz formula D² = ∇S*∇^S + (1/4)R, where R is the scalar curvature, links the spectrum of D to the geometry of M. On a compact spin manifold, the index of the Dirac operator (the difference between the dimensions of the kernel of D⁺ and D⁻) is a topological invariant given by the Â‑genus: ind(D) = ∫_M Â(M). The Â‑genus is expressed in terms of Pontryagin classes; for a 4k‑dimensional manifold it is a polynomial in p₁,…,p_k. The Atiyah–Singer index theorem for the Dirac operator implies that if M admits a metric of positive scalar curvature, then Â(M) = 0. This provides a powerful obstruction to positive scalar curvature metrics. Examiners frequently test the computation of the Dirac operator on the 2‑sphere with its unique spin structure, where the eigenvalues are ±(k+1) with multiplicity k+1, and the index vanishes because Â(S²)=0. Another common question asks to show that a compact spin manifold with non‑zero Â‑genus cannot carry a metric of positive scalar curvature.

Applications to General Relativity: ADM Formalism and Hamiltonian Constraints

The Arnowitt–Deser–Misner (ADM) formalism recasts Einstein’s equations as a Hamiltonian system on a 3‑dimensional Cauchy hypersurface Σ embedded in a 4‑dimensional spacetime (M,g). The spacetime metric is decomposed as ds² = -N² dt² + hij(dx^i + N^i dt)(dx^j + N^j dt), where N is the lapse function, N^i the shift vector, and hij the induced Riemannian metric on Σ. The canonical momentum conjugate to hij is πij = √h (Kij - K hij), where Kij is the extrinsic curvature of Σ. The Hamiltonian is H = ∫_Σ (N ℋ + N_i ℋ^i) d³x with the Hamiltonian constraint ℋ = (1/√h)(πijπij - ½π²) - √h R(3) = 0 and the momentum (diffeomorphism) constraint ℋ^i = -2 ∇_j πij = 0. Here R(3) is the scalar curvature of hij and ∇ is its Levi‑Civita connection. The constraints generate gauge transformations: the Hamiltonian constraint generates normal deformations of Σ, while the momentum constraint generates tangential diffeomorphisms. The Poisson bracket algebra of the constraints closes (the Dirac algebra), reflecting the spacetime diffeomorphism invariance. In the quantum theory, the constraints become operator equations on wave functionals Ψ[hij]; the Hamiltonian constraint is the Wheeler–DeWitt equation ℋ Ψ = 0. A typical exam problem asks to derive the momentum constraint from the variation of the Einstein–Hilbert action with respect to the shift vector, or to verify that the Poisson bracket {ℋ(N), ℋ(M)} yields the momentum constraint with shift vector hij(N ∂_j M - M ∂_j N). Another frequent task is to compute the ADM mass of an asymptotically flat slice: MADM = (1/16π) limr→∞ ∮S_r (∂_j hij - ∂_i hjj) n^i dS, and to show that it is non‑negative for solutions satisfying the dominant energy condition (the positive mass theorem). Understanding the geometric meaning of the lapse and shift, the role of the constraints as generators of gauge, and the link between the ADM energy and the asymptotic behaviour of the metric is essential for any advanced treatment of canonical gravity.

Common Traps

  • Confusing the Leray spectral sequence of a fibration with the Serre spectral sequence of a fibre bundle; they coincide only when the fibration is a fibre bundle with structure group acting trivially on cohomology.
  • Assuming that every invariant polynomial yields an integral characteristic class; Chern–Weil forms are real, and integrality requires additional topological input (e.g. the Chern–Weil homomorphism lands in the image of H^*(M; ℤ) → H^*(M; ℝ)).
  • Forgetting that a spin structure exists iff w₂ = 0, and that the number of distinct spin structures is 2b₁(M) when they exist.
  • Misapplying the Lichnerowicz formula by omitting the scalar curvature term or using the wrong sign convention for the Dirac operator.
  • Treating the ADM Hamiltonian constraint as an evolution equation rather than a constraint that must hold on each slice; the true evolution is generated by the total Hamiltonian with arbitrary lapse and shift.
  • Neglecting the boundary term in the ADM mass formula; the mass is defined only for asymptotically flat manifolds with appropriate fall‑off conditions on hij and πij.
  • Overlooking that the Dirac algebra of constraints closes only up to structure functions (the spatial metric), not structure constants, which is crucial for the consistency of the canonical quantisation.

hand/mean-curvature-flow.html:
Ancient Solutions and the Classification of Singularity Models

An ancient solution of mean curvature flow is a smooth family of hypersurfaces {M_t}t∈(-∞,0) defined for all negative times. These solutions arise naturally as blow‑up limits at singular points: if a flow develops a singularity at (x₀,T), the parabolic rescaling M^λ_t = λ(MT+t/λ²−x₀) with λ→∞ converges (subsequentially) to an ancient solution. The classification of ancient solutions therefore governs the possible singularity models. Huisken’s monotonicity formula implies that any blow‑up limit is a self‑shrinker, i.e. a hypersurface satisfying H = ⟨x,ν⟩/2. The simplest self‑shrinkers are the round sphere Sⁿ, the generalized cylinders Sᵏ×ℝn−k, and the flat plane ℝⁿ. In dimension two, the grim reaper curve y = −log cos x is a translating soliton which, after a suitable time‑dependent rotation, becomes an ancient solution. Angenent’s torus provides a compact ancient solution that is not a shrinker but a rotating soliton. For convex ancient solutions, Huisken (1990) proved that the only compact ones are the family of shrinking spheres; later, White (2000) and Colding‑Minicozzi (2015) showed that any ancient low‑entropy flow in ℝ³ is either a shrinking sphere, a shrinking cylinder, a translating bowl soliton, or a plane. Haslhofer‑Hershkovits (2019) extended this classification to all ancient solutions with entropy ≤ entropy of the cylinder, establishing that the only non‑compact ancient solutions with low entropy are the bowl soliton and the cylinder. These results are central to the multiplicity‑one conjecture: at a generic singularity the tangent flow is a smooth shrinker with multiplicity one, and the classification of low‑entropy shrinkers forces the singularity to be modeled on a sphere or a cylinder.

Entropy, Gaussian Density, and the Colding‑Minicozzi Uniqueness Theory

The entropy of a hypersurface Mⁿ⊂ℝn+1 is defined as λ(M) = supx₀∈ℝn+1, t₀>0 (4π t₀)-n/2 ∫_M e−|x−x₀|²/(4t₀) dμ. This functional, introduced by Colding and Minicozzi (2012), is monotone non‑increasing along mean curvature flow and coincides with the Gaussian density Θ(x₀,t₀) = limt→t₀ (4π(t₀−t))-n/2 ∫M_t e−|x−x₀|²/(4(t₀−t)) dμ at a singular point. The entropy of the round sphere is 1, of the cylinder S¹×ℝn−1 is approximately 1.52 (for n=2), and of the plane is 1. The monotonicity of entropy implies that any blow‑up limit has entropy ≤ the initial entropy. Colding‑Minicozzi (2015) defined a generic mean curvature flow as one for which every singularity is modeled by a smooth shrinker with multiplicity one. They proved that for generic initial data, the flow is unique and the tangent flow at each singular point is a smooth shrinker. The multiplicity‑one conjecture, now a theorem in many cases (Bernstein‑Wang 2017, Hershkovits‑White 2019), asserts that the Gaussian density at any singular point equals the entropy of the tangent shrinker. This theory yields a powerful stratification of the singular set: the set of points where the Gaussian density exceeds a given threshold has controlled Hausdorff dimension. In particular, the singular set of a generic MCF in ℝ³ has Hausdorff dimension at most 1, and the only possible tangent flows are the sphere, the cylinder, and the plane. The entropy framework also underpins the recent proof of the mean convex neighborhood conjecture (Haslhofer‑Kleiner 2017), which states that near a singularity of a mean convex flow, the surface is a graph over a cylinder or a sphere.

Identifying the blow‑up limit at a Type I singularity
Consider a mean convex MCF in ℝ³ that develops a neck pinch at time T. Describe the parabolic rescaling procedure and determine the ancient solution that arises as the blow‑up limit.
1. Choose the singular point (x₀,T). 2. For λ>0 define the rescaled flows M^λ_t = λ(MT+t/λ²−x₀). 3. By Huisken’s monotonicity formula, the Gaussian densities ΘM^λ(0,0) are uniformly bounded. 4. A subsequence λ_k→∞ converges in the sense of Brakke flows to a limit flow {M^∞_t}. 5. The limit is an ancient solution defined for t∈(−∞,0] and satisfies the self‑shrinker equation H = ⟨x,ν⟩/2. 6. Because the original flow is mean convex, the limit is also mean convex. 7. By the classification of ancient mean convex solutions (Huisken 1990, White 2000), the only non‑compact mean convex self‑shrinker in ℝ³ is the shrinking cylinder S¹×ℝ. 8. Hence the blow‑up limit is the shrinking cylinder, confirming a Type I neck pinch singularity.
Exam‑day strategy
Memorize the entropy values of the sphere (1), cylinder (~1.52), and plane (1). The monotonicity of entropy and the multiplicity‑one property are frequent multiple‑choice topics. Be ready to state that a generic MCF has only spherical and cylindrical singularities.

Mean Curvature Flow with Boundary: Free Boundary and Contact Angle Problems

When a hypersurface evolves by mean curvature flow while meeting a fixed supporting hypersurface ∂Ω, the boundary condition can be either free boundary (orthogonal intersection) or a prescribed contact angle α∈(0,π). The free boundary condition ∂M_t ⟂ ∂Ω arises naturally from the variational principle for area with a volume constraint. Stahl (1996) proved short‑time existence and smoothness for convex barriers, using a reflection argument that doubles the domain across ∂Ω and extends the flow by symmetry. For non‑convex barriers, the problem is more delicate; Edelen (2020) established a regularity theory showing that singularities can only occur at the boundary if the contact angle deviates from π/2. The contact angle problem with constant α≠π/2 was studied by Buckland (2019), who derived a monotonicity formula adapted to the boundary and proved that the only possible blow‑up limits are half‑spheres, half‑cylinders, or translating half‑bowls. The avoidance principle still holds: two free boundary flows that start disjoint remain disjoint. This principle is essential for the surgery construction in the presence of boundary. Recent work by Hershkovits‑White (2021) on generic regularity for free boundary MCF shows that, for generic initial data, the flow encounters only spherical and cylindrical singularities, and the boundary remains smooth until the final extinction time. The classification of free boundary shrinkers (half‑spheres and half‑cylinders) mirrors the closed case, but the presence of the boundary introduces new phenomena such as boundary layer formation and the possibility of type‑II singularities at the contact line.

Higher Codimension Mean Curvature Flow and the Andrews‑Baker Pinching Estimates

For submanifolds Mⁿ⊂ℝn+k with k≥2, the mean curvature flow is a weakly parabolic system for the position vector. The second fundamental form A evolves by a reaction‑diffusion equation with a quadratic reaction term that couples normal directions. A crucial structural condition is positive isotropic curvature (PIC), which is preserved by the flow (Andrews‑Baker 2010). Under PIC, Andrews and Baker proved a pinching estimate: |A|² ≤ C H² for some constant C depending only on the initial data. This estimate implies that the flow exists for all time and converges smoothly to a round sphere after appropriate rescaling. Without curvature assumptions, singularities can be more complicated; Smoczyk (2002) classified graphical self‑shrinkers in higher codimension, showing they are either planes or cylinders over lower‑dimensional shrinkers. The Clifford torus S¹(√2)×S¹(√2)⊂ℝ⁴ is a compact self‑shrinker with non‑positive isotropic curvature, illustrating that the PIC condition is sharp. In the graphical setting, Wang (2004) proved long‑time existence and convergence for entire graphs with bounded slope. The normal bundle geometry plays a central role: the connection Laplacian on the normal bundle appears in the evolution of the second fundamental form, and parallel normal fields simplify the system. Recent work by Nguyen (2022) extended the Andrews‑Baker pinching to the setting of mean curvature flow with a forcing term, opening the way to applications in geometric inequalities such as the Willmore conjecture in higher codimension.

Numerical Approximation: Thresholding Schemes and Convergence Results

Computing mean curvature flow numerically requires handling topological changes and singularities. The Merriman‑Bence‑Osher (MBO) thresholding scheme (1992) alternates two steps: (i) diffuse the characteristic function of the evolving set by the heat equation for a small time δt, (ii) threshold the result at 1/2 to obtain the new set. Evans (1993) and Barles‑Georgelin (1995) proved that as δt→0 the MBO scheme converges to the viscosity solution of the level set equation, thus capturing the correct geometric motion including fattening. The Allen‑Cahn approximation replaces the sharp interface by a diffuse interface of width ε, evolving by ε u_t = ε Δu − (1/ε) W'(u) with a double‑well potential W. Ilmanen (1993) showed that as ε→0 the Allen‑Cahn flow converges to a Brakke flow, providing a rigorous link between phase‑field models and geometric measure theory. Esedoglu‑Otto (2015) extended thresholding to multiphase flows, proving convergence to the multiphase mean curvature flow with prescribed contact angles. Error estimates are delicate: for smooth flows, the MBO scheme has first‑order accuracy in time (δt), while the Allen‑Cahn method achieves O(ε|log ε|) accuracy in the interface position. Recent work by Laux‑Otto (2021) established a quantitative convergence rate for the thresholding scheme in the flat norm, confirming that the scheme is not only consistent but also stable under perturbations. These numerical methods are now standard tools in image processing, materials science, and the simulation of geometric flows in high dimensions.

  • Confusing ancient solutions (defined for all negative times) with eternal solutions (defined for all times) and assuming they have the same classification.
  • Assuming every singularity is Type I; many flows develop Type II singularities where the curvature blows up faster than (T−t)-1/2.
  • Applying the avoidance principle to higher codimension flows without checking the required angle conditions between normal bundles.
  • Overlooking the multiplicity‑one hypothesis in Colding‑Minicozzi theory; without it, tangent flows can have integer multiplicity >1 and the entropy bound fails.
  • Neglecting the boundary condition in free boundary MCF; the reflection trick only works for orthogonal intersection and convex barriers.
  • Believing the MBO thresholding scheme converges to classical smooth MCF; it converges to the viscosity solution of the level set equation, which may fatten.
  • Thinking all self‑shrinkers are classified in dimensions n≥3; the classification is complete only for low entropy or under symmetry assumptions.

hand/info-theory.html:
Network Information Theory and Multi‑User Channels

Shannon’s point‑to‑point theory assumes a single transmitter and a single receiver. Real communication systems — cellular networks, satellite links, ad‑hoc wireless — involve many users sharing the same medium. Network information theory extends the capacity concept to multi‑user settings, where the fundamental limits are described by capacity regions rather than single numbers. The multiple‑access channel (MAC) models several senders transmitting to one receiver. Cover (1975) showed that the capacity region is the set of rate tuples (R₁,…,Rₖ) satisfying Σi∈S Rᵢ ≤ I(X_S; Y | XS^c) for all subsets S ⊆ {1,…,k}, where the mutual information is evaluated with a product input distribution. The broadcast channel (BC) models one sender transmitting to several receivers. Cover’s 1972 inner bound (superposition coding) and the later Marton (1979) inner bound with auxiliary random variables remain the best known achievable regions for the general discrete memoryless BC; the capacity region is known only for degraded, less‑noisy, and deterministic cases. The interference channel (IC) captures two sender‑receiver pairs that interfere with each other. Carleial (1975) proved that the Han‑Kobayashi (1981) achievable region, which splits each message into common and private parts, is optimal for many Gaussian IC parameter regimes. The relay channel, introduced by van der Meulen (1971) and studied by Cover and El Gamal (1979), adds a node that can help the source; the compress‑and‑forward and decode‑and‑forward strategies give the best known rates, while the capacity remains open in general. These multi‑user models form the theoretical backbone of modern multiple‑input multiple‑output (MIMO) systems, non‑orthogonal multiple access (NOMA), and cooperative communications.

Feedback and Capacity of Channels with Memory

For a discrete memoryless channel (DMC), Shannon (1956) proved that noiseless feedback does not increase capacity — the capacity with feedback equals the ordinary capacity C = maxp(x) I(X;Y). The proof uses the fact that feedback cannot change the mutual information between the channel input and output when the channel is memoryless. However, once the channel has memory, feedback can strictly enlarge the achievable rate region. The classic example is the trapdoor channel (Cover and Pombra, 1989), where the state depends on past inputs and the receiver can inform the transmitter of the state via feedback, enabling rates above the non‑feedback capacity. For channels with intersymbol interference (ISI), the capacity with feedback is given by the directed information I(Xⁿ → Yⁿ) = Σi=1ⁿ I(Xⁱ; Yᵢ | Yi‑1), a quantity introduced by Massey (1990). The water‑filling solution for the Gaussian ISI channel with feedback (Kim, 2006) shows that the optimal input spectrum is not flat, unlike the non‑feedback case. In practical systems, feedback appears as automatic repeat request (ARQ) and hybrid ARQ; information‑theoretic analysis of these protocols uses the concept of variable‑length coding with stop feedback, where the error exponent can be dramatically improved (Burnashev, 1976). Understanding when feedback helps and when it does not is essential for designing adaptive modulation and coding schemes in time‑varying wireless channels.

Worked Example: Feedback Does Not Increase DMC Capacity
Consider a binary symmetric channel (BSC) with crossover probability p = 0.1. The channel is memoryless. A student claims that by using noiseless feedback the transmitter can achieve a rate higher than the Shannon capacity C = 1 − H₂(p). Show why this claim is false.
For any DMC, the capacity with noiseless feedback C_fb equals the ordinary capacity C. The proof proceeds by considering an (n, M, ε) code with feedback. Let the message be W, the channel inputs Xⁿ, and outputs Yⁿ. Because the channel is memoryless, the joint distribution factorises as p(w) Πi=1ⁿ p(yᵢ|xᵢ). The mutual information I(W; Yⁿ) ≤ Σi=1ⁿ I(Xᵢ; Yᵢ) ≤ n C. By Fano’s inequality, H(W|Yⁿ) ≤ 1 + ε log M. Hence log M ≤ n C + 1 + ε log M, giving (1−ε) log M ≤ n C + 1. As n → ∞ and ε → 0, the achievable rate R = (log M)/n ≤ C. Therefore feedback cannot exceed C. For the BSC with p = 0.1, C = 1 − H₂(0.1) ≈ 0.531 bits per channel use, and this remains the maximum rate even with perfect feedback.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question asks whether feedback increases capacity, first identify if the channel is memoryless. If it is, state Shannon’s 1956 result and cite the directed‑information expression for channels with memory. Remember the trapdoor channel as the canonical counterexample where feedback helps. Write the key inequality I(W;Yⁿ) ≤ n C and invoke Fano’s inequality to bound the rate.

Information‑Theoretic Security and Wiretap Channels

Classical cryptography relies on computational hardness assumptions; information‑theoretic security seeks guarantees that hold even against an adversary with unlimited computing power. Wyner (1975) introduced the wiretap channel: a sender (Alice) transmits to a legitimate receiver (Bob) over a main channel, while an eavesdropper (Eve) observes a degraded version through a wiretap channel. The secrecy capacity C_s is the maximum rate at which Alice can reliably communicate with Bob while keeping the mutual information between the message and Eve’s observation arbitrarily small. For the degraded discrete memoryless wiretap channel, C_s = maxp(u,x) [I(U;Y) − I(U;Z)], where U is an auxiliary random variable. Csiszár and Körner (1978) generalized this to the broadcast channel with confidential messages, showing that the same expression holds when the eavesdropper’s channel is not necessarily degraded. The Gaussian wiretap channel yields C_s = ½ log₂(1 + P/σ_B²) − ½ log₂(1 + P/σ_E²) for σ_E² > σ_B², i.e., positive secrecy capacity exists only when Bob’s channel is statistically better than Eve’s. Practical constructions use coset coding (random binning) combined with error‑correcting codes; polar codes (Mahdavifar and Vardy, 2011) and LDPC codes (Thangaraj et al., 2007) achieve the secrecy capacity with low complexity. The concept extends to secret‑key agreement (Maurer, 1993; Ahlswede and Csiszár, 1993), where two parties generate a shared secret from correlated observations and public discussion, with the key rate bounded by the conditional mutual information I(X;Y|Z). These results underpin physical‑layer security in 5G/6G, quantum key distribution, and secure multi‑party computation.

Finite Blocklength Analysis and Dispersion

Shannon’s channel coding theorem is asymptotic: it guarantees the existence of codes with arbitrarily small error probability as blocklength n → ∞. In practice, blocklengths are finite (hundreds to thousands of symbols), and the trade‑off between rate, error probability, and blocklength is critical. Polyanskiy, Poor, and Verdú (2010) developed the normal approximation for the maximal achievable rate R*(n, ε) at blocklength n and error probability ε: R*(n, ε) = C − √(V/n) Q⁻¹(ε) + O(log n / n), where C is the Shannon capacity, V is the channel dispersion, and Q⁻¹ is the inverse Gaussian Q‑function. For a DMC, V = Var[ i(X;Y) ] evaluated at the capacity‑achieving input distribution, where i(x;y) = log (p(y|x)/p(y)) is the information density. For the binary symmetric channel with crossover p, V = p(1−p) [log₂((1−p)/p)]². For the additive white Gaussian noise (AWGN) channel with signal‑to‑noise ratio SNR, V = (SNR/2) (SNR+2) / (SNR+1)² log₂² e. The normal approximation is remarkably accurate for n as low as 100. It enables the design of ultra‑reliable low‑latency communication (URLLC) in 5G, where packet sizes are short and error probabilities of 10⁻⁵ are required. The meta‑converse (Polyanskiy et al., 2010) provides a tight converse bound using hypothesis testing, and the dependence‑testing bound gives a matching achievability result. Recent work extends finite‑blocklength analysis to multi‑user channels (MAC, BC) and to channels with feedback, where the dispersion can be reduced (e.g., the Schalkwijk‑Kailath scheme for the AWGN channel with noiseless feedback achieves zero dispersion). Understanding dispersion is essential for link‑level simulations and for proving latency‑reliability trade‑offs in modern standards.

Algorithmic Information Theory and Kolmogorov Complexity

Algorithmic information theory (AIT) replaces probabilistic ensembles with individual strings, measuring the information content of a specific object by the length of its shortest description. The Kolmogorov complexity K(x) of a binary string x is the length of the shortest program (on a fixed universal Turing machine) that outputs x and halts. Solomonoff (1964), Kolmogorov (1965), and Chaitin (1966) independently introduced this notion. K(x) is incomputable — there is no algorithm that, given x, returns K(x) — but it is well defined up to an additive constant independent of x (invariance theorem). The prefix‑free version K̂(x) uses self‑delimiting programs and satisfies the Kraft inequality, making it a proper probability distribution via the universal prior m(x) = 2−K̂(x). AIT connects to Shannon entropy through the inequality H(X) ≤ E[K̂(X)] ≤ H(X) + O(log H(X)) for computable distributions, showing that expected Kolmogorov complexity approximates entropy. The coding theorem of Levin (1974) states that −log m(x) = K̂(x) + O(1). AIT also yields a rigorous definition of randomness: a string is Martin‑Löf random iff its prefix complexity exceeds its length by an additive constant. Applications include the minimum description length (MDL) principle for model selection (Rissanen, 1978), the normalized compression distance (NCD) for clustering (Cilibrasi and Vitányi, 2005), and the theoretical limits of lossless compression (the optimal compressor achieves K̂(x) bits). While AIT is not directly computable, it provides the conceptual foundation for why entropy is the right measure of average information and why universal compressors like Lempel‑Ziv approach entropy for stationary ergodic sources.

  • Confusing the multiple‑access capacity region with the sum‑rate bound; the region is a polytope defined by all subset inequalities, not just the total sum.
  • Assuming feedback always increases capacity; it does not for memoryless channels, but it can for channels with memory such as the trapdoor channel.
  • Misstating the wiretap secrecy capacity formula by omitting the auxiliary random variable U or by using the wrong mutual‑information order.
  • Using the asymptotic capacity C in place of the finite‑blocklength normal approximation when the problem explicitly gives a short blocklength and a target error probability.
  • Treating Kolmogorov complexity as computable; it is provably incomputable, and any exam answer that claims an algorithm for K(x) is incorrect.
  • Neglecting the additive constant in the invariance theorem; two universal machines can give complexities that differ by a constant, which matters in precise statements.
  • Forgetting that the dispersion V is the variance of the information density under the capacity‑achieving input distribution, not the variance of the channel output.

hand/electrochemistry.html:
Electrode Kinetics, Overpotential and the Butler‑Volmer Equation

Thermodynamics tells whether a redox reaction can occur, but kinetics decides how fast it proceeds at a given electrode. The current density j at an electrode surface is described by the Butler‑Volmer equation:

j = j₀ [ exp( αₐ nFη / RT ) − exp( −α_c nFη / RT ) ]

where j₀ is the exchange current density, αₐ and α_c are the anodic and cathodic transfer coefficients (typically 0.5 each for a symmetric barrier), n is the number of electrons transferred, F the Faraday constant, R the gas constant, T the absolute temperature, and η = E − Eeq the overpotential. At low overpotentials (|η| < 10 mV) the equation linearises to j ≈ j₀ nFη / RT, giving the charge‑transfer resistance Rct = RT / ( j₀ nF ). Large exchange currents (e.g., Pt/H₂, Pt/O₂) mean small kinetic losses; sluggish reactions such as oxygen evolution on graphite exhibit high overpotentials, often >0.5 V, which must be supplied by the external source in electrolysis.

Types of Overpotential

Three contributions are usually distinguished: activation overpotential (charge‑transfer barrier), concentration overpotential (depletion of reactant at the surface), and ohmic overpotential (IR drop in solution and contacts). Activation overpotential follows the Tafel relationship at high |η|: η = a + b log|j|, where the Tafel slope b = 2.303 RT / (α nF). For a one‑electron step with α = 0.5 at 298 K, b ≈ 120 mV dec⁻¹. Concentration overpotential becomes significant when the limiting current density jlim = nFDc / δ is approached (D = diffusion coefficient, c = bulk concentration, δ = diffusion layer thickness). In practice, rotating‑disk electrodes are used to control δ and extract kinetic parameters.

Experimental Determination

Polarisation curves (η vs. log j) measured under steady‑state conditions allow extraction of j₀ and α by fitting the Butler‑Volmer or Tafel regions. Electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) provides an independent route: the high‑frequency semicircle diameter equals Rct, from which j₀ = RT / ( nF Rct ). Consistency between DC and AC methods validates the kinetic model.

Relevance to Energy Devices

In fuel cells and metal‑air batteries, the cathode oxygen‑reduction reaction (ORR) is the principal source of voltage loss. Platinum‑group catalysts achieve j₀ ≈ 10⁻³ A cm⁻², yet the ORR overpotential at 1 A cm⁻² remains ~0.3 V. Research focuses on alloying Pt with transition metals, shaping nanocrystals, and developing non‑precious catalysts (Fe‑N‑C) to raise j₀ and lower the Tafel slope. Similarly, the hydrogen‑evolution reaction (HER) on MoS₂ or Ni‑Mo alloys shows exchange currents approaching those of Pt in alkaline media, enabling cheaper electrolyzers.

Concentration Cells, Liquid Junction Potentials and the Nernst‑Planck Equation

A concentration cell generates emf solely from differences in chemical potential of the same species in two half‑cells. For a simple metal‑ion cell M | M⁺(c₁) || M⁺(c₂) | M, the Nernst equation gives E = (RT / nF) ln(c₂ / c₁). When the two electrolytes are not identical, a liquid‑junction potential (LJP) arises at the interface where ions of different mobilities diffuse. The Henderson equation approximates the LJP for a binary electrolyte:

ELJ = (RT / F) ( (u₊ − u₋) / (u₊ + u₋) ) ln( a₂ / a₁ )

where u₊, u₋ are ionic mobilities and a₁, a₂ the activities on each side. For KCl, u₊ ≈ u₋, so the LJP is minimal; for HCl, u₊ ≫ u₋, giving a sizable junction potential that must be corrected in precise potentiometry.

Nernst‑Planck Description

The flux Jᵢ of ion i in a solution under a potential gradient is given by the Nernst‑Planck equation:

Jᵢ = −Dᵢ ( ∇cᵢ + (zᵢ F / RT) cᵢ ∇φ ) + cᵢ v

where Dᵢ is the diffusion coefficient, zᵢ the charge number, φ the electric potential, and v the solvent velocity (often negligible in stagnant cells). At steady state with zero net current, the equation reduces to the condition that the electrochemical potential μ̃ᵢ = μᵢ⁰ + RT ln aᵢ + zᵢ F φ is uniform across the junction. Integrating yields the exact LJP for any number of ions, provided activity coefficients are known.

Practical Elimination of LJP

In laboratory cells a salt bridge filled with a saturated KCl–agar gel minimises LJP because K⁺ and Cl⁻ have nearly equal mobilities and the high concentration suppresses activity‑coefficient gradients. For high‑precision work (e.g., standard‑cell calibration), a double‑junction reference electrode or a flowing‑junction design is used, and the residual LJP is calculated from the Henderson equation using measured ion concentrations.

Concentration Cells in Analysis

Concentration cells form the basis of ion‑selective electrodes (ISEs). A glass pH electrode is essentially a H⁺ concentration cell: the internal filling solution has fixed a(H⁺), while the external sample activity varies. The measured emf follows E = E° + (RT / F) ln a(H⁺) = E° − (2.303 RT / F) pH. Similarly, a fluoride‑selective electrode uses a LaF₃ crystal membrane that develops a potential proportional to ln a(F⁻). The Nernstian slope at 298 K is 59.16 mV per decade for monovalent ions; deviations indicate membrane non‑ideality or interfering ions.

Worked Example: Liquid‑Junction Potential in a HCl Concentration Cell
A concentration cell is constructed as Pt | H₂(g, 1 bar) | HCl(aq, 0.1 M) || HCl(aq, 0.01 M) | H₂(g, 1 bar) | Pt. The mobilities at 298 K are u(H⁺) = 3.50 × 10⁻⁷ m² V⁻¹ s⁻¹ and u(Cl⁻) = 0.79 × 10⁻⁷ m² V⁻¹ s⁻¹. Calculate the total cell emf including the liquid‑junction potential.
The Nernst potential for the H⁺ concentration difference is ENernst = (RT/F) ln(0.1/0.01) = 0.05916 V. The Henderson LJP for a 1:1 electrolyte is ELJ = (RT/F) ( (u₊−u₋)/(u₊+u₋) ) ln(0.1/0.01). Substituting mobilities: (3.50−0.79)/(3.50+0.79) = 2.71/4.29 = 0.632. Thus ELJ = 0.05916 V × 0.632 = 0.0374 V. The total emf = 0.05916 V + 0.0374 V = 0.0966 V. The positive sign indicates the dilute side becomes positive relative to the concentrated side.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a problem gives ionic mobilities or diffusion coefficients, always check whether a liquid‑junction correction is required. If the cell uses a salt bridge with KCl, you may ignore LJP; if the electrolytes differ (e.g., HCl vs. NaCl), apply the Henderson equation. Remember the Nernstian slope 0.05916 V per decade at 298 K for monovalent ions; for divalent ions halve the slope. In multiple‑choice questions, the answer that includes the LJP term is often the correct one when mobilities are supplied.

Industrial Electrolysis: Chlor‑Alkali Process, Aluminium Hall‑Héroult Cell and Water Splitting

Large‑scale electrolysis converts electrical energy into chemical commodities. The three dominant processes illustrate how thermodynamics, kinetics, and materials constraints shape cell design.

Chlor‑Alkali (Brine Electrolysis)

Saturated NaCl solution is electrolysed to produce Cl₂ at the anode, H₂ at the cathode, and NaOH in the cathodic compartment. The overall reaction is 2 NaCl + 2 H₂O → Cl₂ + H₂ + 2 NaOH. The thermodynamic minimum voltage is 2.19 V (E° = −2.19 V for the reverse reaction). Modern membrane cells use a cation‑exchange membrane (e.g., Nafion) that allows Na⁺ to migrate while blocking OH⁻ and Cl⁻, yielding high‑purity NaOH (≈32 wt %) and reducing energy consumption to 2.2–2.5 kWh kg⁻¹ Cl₂. Anode catalysts are dimensionally stable anodes (DSA) – Ti coated with RuO₂/TiO₂ – which lower the chlorine overpotential to <0.1 V. Cathodes are Ni‑based alloys that promote hydrogen evolution with minimal overpotential. The membrane must withstand high current densities (4–6 kA m⁻²) and alkaline pH; degradation by peroxide radicals limits lifetime to 3–5 years.

Aluminium Production (Hall‑Héroult)

Al₂O₃ dissolved in molten cryolite (Na₃AlF₆) at 960 °C is electrolysed in carbon‑lined steel cells. The anode reaction: 2 O²⁻ → O₂ + 4 e⁻ (O₂ reacts with carbon anode to form CO₂). The cathode reaction: Al³⁺ + 3 e⁻ → Al(l). The theoretical decomposition voltage is 1.23 V, but the operating cell voltage is 4.2–4.5 V due to large ohmic drop in the electrolyte (≈2 V), anode overpotential (≈0.5 V), and cathode overpotential (≈0.3 V). Current efficiencies of 94–96 % are typical; the remainder is lost to the side reaction 2 Al + 3 CO₂ → Al₂O₃ + 3 C. Energy consumption averages 13–15 kWh kg⁻¹ Al. Inert anode research (e.g., cermet or SnO₂‑based) aims to eliminate carbon consumption and CO₂ emissions, but materials that survive 960 °C, fluoride melt, and high current density remain elusive.

Water Electrolysis for Hydrogen

Two commercial technologies dominate: alkaline electrolysis (AEL) and proton‑exchange‑membrane electrolysis (PEMEL). AEL uses 30 wt % KOH at 80–90 °C, Ni‑based electrodes, and a porous diaphragm. Cell voltage ≈1.8–2.0 V at 0.2–0.4 A cm⁻², giving 4.5–5.5 kWh Nm⁻³ H₂. PEMEL employs a solid polymer electrolyte (Nafion), Pt/IrO₂ catalysts, and operates at 60–80 °C with current densities 1–2 A cm⁻²; cell voltage ≈1.8–2.2 V, but higher capital cost. The thermodynamic minimum at 298 K is 1.23 V; the gap is mainly kinetic overpotentials (OER on anode, HER on cathode) and ohmic losses. High‑temperature solid‑oxide electrolysis (SOEC) at 700–850 °C reduces the electrical demand to ≈0.9 V by supplying part of the energy as heat, achieving overall efficiencies >90 % (LHV). Durability of ceramic electrolytes under thermal cycling is the principal barrier to deployment.

Ionic Conductivity Theory: Debye‑Hückel‑Onsager Equation, Ion Association and Conductometric Titrations

Beyond Kohlrausch’s empirical law, the Debye‑Hückel‑Onsager (DHO) theory provides a molecular‑level expression for the molar conductivity of strong electrolytes at low concentration:

Λm = Λ°m − ( A + B Λ°m ) √c

where A = ( F² / ( 6π η RT ) ) ( 2 Nₐ ρ / ( ε RT ) )¹ᐟ² accounts for the electrophoretic effect (drag of the ionic atmosphere) and B = ( F² / ( 24π η RT ) ) ( 2 Nₐ ρ / ( ε RT ) )¹ᐟ² represents the relaxation effect (asymmetry of the ionic cloud). η is solvent viscosity, ε dielectric constant, ρ density, Nₐ Avogadro’s number. For aqueous 1:1 electrolytes at 298 K, A ≈ 60.2 S cm² mol⁻¹ M⁻¹ᐟ² and B ≈ 0.229 M⁻¹ᐟ². The DHO equation matches experimental data up to ~0.01 M; at higher concentrations ion‑pair formation and short‑range forces cause deviations.

Ion Association and the Bjerrum Length

When the electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions exceeds thermal energy, they form transient ion pairs. The Bjerrum length l_B = e² / ( 4π ε₀ ε k_B T ) defines the distance at which the Coulomb energy equals k_B T. In water at 298 K, l_B ≈ 0.7 nm; in low‑dielectric solvents (ε ≈ 10) it exceeds 5 nm, leading to extensive ion pairing. The association constant K_A can be estimated from the Fuoss equation or measured by conductivity: Λm = α Λ°m, where α = ( −K_A c + √( K_A² c² + 4 K_A c ) ) / ( 2 K_A c ). For weak electrolytes (e.g., acetic acid), α is the degree of dissociation and Ostwald’s dilution law K_a = c α² / (1−α) applies.

Conductometric Titrations

Because conductivity depends linearly on the concentration of each ionic species (Λ = Σ λᵢ cᵢ), a titration curve shows a sharp change in slope at the equivalence point. In a strong‑acid–strong‑base titration (HCl + NaOH), the highly mobile H⁺ (λ° = 349.8 S cm² mol⁻¹) is replaced by the slower Na⁺ (λ° = 50.1 S cm² mol⁻¹), causing conductivity to fall until the endpoint, then rise as excess OH⁻ (λ° = 199.1 S cm² mol⁻¹) appears. For a weak‑acid–strong‑base titration (CH₃COOH + NaOH), conductivity initially rises as CH₃COO⁻ (λ° = 40.9 S cm² mol⁻¹) forms, then falls slightly at the equivalence point because the solution contains only Na⁺ and CH₃COO⁻, and finally rises with excess OH⁻. The intersection of the two linear branches gives the endpoint with precision better than ±0.1 % for concentrations >10⁻³ M.

Temperature Dependence and Walden’s Rule

Λ°m increases with temperature roughly as η⁻¹ (Walden’s rule: Λ°m η ≈ constant). For many ions the product Λ°m η is within ±10 % of a universal value, reflecting the Stokes‑Einstein relation D = k_B T / (6π η r). Deviations indicate specific ion‑solvent interactions (e.g., structure‑making vs. structure‑breaking). Accurate conductivity measurements therefore require thermostating to ±0.01 K for high‑precision work.

  • Confusing the sign convention for overpotential: η = E − Eeq; a positive η on the anode drives oxidation, but on the cathode a negative η drives reduction.
  • Neglecting the liquid‑junction potential when the problem supplies ionic mobilities or asks for the emf of a cell with dissimilar electrolytes.
  • Assuming the Hall‑Héroult cell voltage equals the thermodynamic decomposition voltage; the operating voltage is 3–4 times larger because of ohmic and kinetic losses.
  • Using the Kohlrausch linear √c law beyond its validity range (typically >0.01 M) where ion association dominates.
  • Treating the degree of dissociation α from conductivity as identical to the thermodynamic α used in Ostwald’s law without correcting for ion‑pair formation.
  • Forgetting that the Nernstian slope for a divalent ion is half the monovalent value (≈29.58 mV per decade at 298 K).
  • Overlooking the temperature dependence of Λ°m and applying room‑temperature limiting conductivities to high‑temperature industrial cells.

hand/cryptography.html:
Authenticated Encryption and AEAD Constructions

Authenticated encryption with associated data (AEAD) simultaneously provides confidentiality, integrity, and authenticity for both the ciphertext and optional associated data that is not encrypted but must be authenticated. The security goal is indistinguishability under chosen‑ciphertext attack (IND‑CCA2) together with integrity of ciphertext (INT‑CTXT). The most widely deployed AEAD schemes are AES‑GCM, ChaCha20‑Poly1305, and AES‑CCM. AES‑GCM combines the counter mode of AES for encryption with the Galois field multiplication based GHASH for authentication. It requires a 96‑bit nonce (or a variable‑length nonce that is hashed to 96 bits) and produces a 128‑bit authentication tag. ChaCha20‑Poly1305 uses the ChaCha20 stream cipher and the Poly1305 MAC; it is preferred on platforms lacking AES hardware acceleration. Both schemes are nonce‑based: reusing a nonce with the same key catastrophically breaks security — the keystream repeats, allowing an adversary to recover plaintexts and forge valid tags. AES‑CCM (Counter with CBC‑MAC) is a two‑pass construction that first computes a CBC‑MAC over the associated data and plaintext, then encrypts with counter mode; it is used in constrained environments such as IEEE 802.15.4 and TLS 1.2. The CAESAR competition (2014‑2019) evaluated numerous AEAD candidates; the final portfolio includes OCB, COLM, and Ascon, with Ascon selected for lightweight applications. In practice, protocol designers must enforce strict nonce management — either a deterministic counter, a random nonce with a sufficiently large space (≥ 96 bits), or a nonce‑misuse‑resistant scheme such as AES‑GCM‑SIV or Deoxys‑II, which tolerate accidental nonce reuse at the cost of an extra pass over the data.

Security Notions and Composition

The standard security definition for AEAD is the AEAD‑IND‑CCA2 game: the adversary obtains encryption and decryption oracles, may query associated data, and must not distinguish encryptions of two chosen messages nor produce a fresh valid ciphertext. A composition theorem shows that any IND‑CPA secure encryption combined with a strongly unforgeable MAC (Encrypt‑then‑MAC) yields an AEAD scheme, provided the MAC key is independent of the encryption key. However, dedicated AEAD modes such as GCM achieve better performance by sharing the underlying primitive. The nonce‑misuse‑resistance property (also called robust AEAD) guarantees that even if a nonce repeats, the adversary cannot recover plaintexts beyond the repeated prefix and cannot forge tags for new messages. This is achieved by deriving a per‑message key from the nonce and a master key using a pseudorandom function, then using that key for a deterministic authenticated encryption (e.g., SIV construction).

Implementation Considerations

  • Use constant‑time implementations of GHASH and Poly1305 to avoid timing side channels.
  • Prefer 96‑bit nonces for GCM; if a random nonce is used, the birthday bound limits safe encryptions to ≈ 2³² messages.
  • Validate the authentication tag before releasing any plaintext — decrypt‑then‑verify order prevents padding oracle‑style attacks.
  • When associated data includes protocol metadata (sequence numbers, headers), ensure it is canonically encoded to avoid ambiguity.

Side‑Channel Countermeasures and Implementation Security

Side‑channel attacks exploit physical leakage — timing, power consumption, electromagnetic emanations, cache access patterns, or acoustic signals — to extract secret keys from otherwise mathematically secure implementations. The most studied classes are timing attacks (Kocher 1996), simple power analysis (SPA) and differential power analysis (DPA) (Kocher, Jaffe, Jun 1999), cache‑timing attacks (Bernstein 2005), and fault injection attacks (Boneh, DeMillo, Lipton 1997). A timing attack on RSA uses the variation in modular exponentiation time caused by the sliding‑window or Montgomery multiplication; the attacker recovers bits of the private exponent by measuring decryption times. DPA on AES correlates power traces with hypothetical intermediate values (e.g., S‑box outputs) to recover the key byte by byte. Cache attacks such as Flush+Reload or Prime+Probe exploit shared cache lines in AES T‑table implementations to deduce memory access patterns and thus the key.

Countermeasure Taxonomy

Countermeasures are broadly classified into algorithmic (constant‑time code, masking, hiding), architectural (hardware random number generators, dedicated crypto accelerators, cache partitioning), and protocol‑level (blinding, ephemeral keys, threshold implementations). Constant‑time programming eliminates data‑dependent branches and memory accesses; for example, AES‑NI instructions or bitsliced software implementations achieve this. Masking splits each sensitive variable into d shares (typically d=2 or 3) such that any subset of d‑1 shares reveals no information; the ISW (Ishai‑Sahai‑Wagner) scheme provides provable security against d‑1‑order DPA. Hiding adds random delays or dummy operations to decorrelate leakage from the secret. Blinding in RSA/ECC multiplies the base or exponent by a random value before exponentiation, then removes the effect afterward; this defeats timing and power analysis on the exponent. Threshold implementations share the secret among multiple parties or hardware modules so that no single component ever holds the full key.

Practical Deployment

  • Use vetted libraries (OpenSSL, BoringSSL, libsodium, Microsoft SEAL) that incorporate constant‑time paths and masking.
  • Disable CPU frequency scaling and hyper‑threading on servers performing cryptographic operations to reduce timing noise.
  • Apply compiler flags (-fno‑builtin, -march=native) cautiously; some optimizations reintroduce data‑dependent branches.
  • Perform side‑channel leakage assessment (TVLA, Welch’s t‑test) on final binaries before deployment.
Nonce Reuse in AES‑GCM
Explain why reusing a nonce with the same key in AES‑GCM breaks both confidentiality and integrity.
AES‑GCM generates a keystream by encrypting successive counter blocks derived from the nonce. If the same nonce and key are used for two messages, the keystream is identical. An adversary who obtains the two ciphertexts C₁ = P₁ ⊕ KS and C₂ = P₂ ⊕ KS can compute C₁ ⊕ C₂ = P₁ ⊕ P₂, revealing the XOR of the plaintexts. With known or guessed structure in one plaintext (e.g., protocol headers), the other plaintext is recovered — confidentiality is lost. For integrity, the authentication tag is computed as GHASH(H, A, C) ⊕ E(K, J₀) where J₀ is the first counter block derived from the nonce. Reusing the nonce makes J₀ identical, so the tag for a forged ciphertext can be constructed by copying the tag from a legitimate message and adjusting the GHASH contribution using the known keystream. Thus an attacker can produce a valid tag for any ciphertext encrypted under the reused nonce, breaking authenticity.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When asked about AEAD security, always state the required nonce uniqueness and the impact of nonce reuse on the authentication tag. For side‑channel questions, name the leakage source (timing, power, cache) and the corresponding countermeasure class (constant‑time, masking, blinding).

Key Derivation Functions and Password Hashing

Key derivation functions (KDFs) transform high‑entropy secrets (e.g., Diffie‑Hellman shared secrets) or low‑entropy passwords into uniformly distributed cryptographic keys. The security requirements differ: for high‑entropy inputs, a KDF must be a pseudorandom function (PRF) such as HKDF (RFC 5869), which uses HMAC‑SHA‑256 in an extract‑then‑expand paradigm. For passwords, the KDF must be memory‑hard and slow to thwart offline brute‑force and GPU/ASIC attacks. The widely adopted password‑hashing algorithms are PBKDF2, bcrypt, scrypt, and Argon2. PBKDF2 (RFC 2898) iterates HMAC‑SHA‑256 a configurable number of times (typically 100 000–1 000 000 iterations); it is CPU‑hard but not memory‑hard, making it vulnerable to specialized hardware. bcrypt (1999) incorporates a Blowfish‑based key schedule with a configurable cost factor (log₂ iterations) and a 128‑bit salt; it provides moderate memory usage (4 KB) but is less resistant to GPU parallelism. scrypt (2009) introduces a memory‑hard function parameterized by N (CPU/memory cost), r (block size), and p (parallelism); typical settings (N=2¹⁴, r=8, p=1) require ≈ 16 MiB of memory. Argon2 (2015, winner of the Password Hashing Competition) comes in three variants: Argon2d (data‑dependent, maximal GPU resistance), Argon2i (data‑independent, side‑channel resistant), and Argon2id (hybrid, recommended for general use). Argon2id uses a memory array of size m KiB, t passes, and p parallel lanes; a common baseline is m=65536 (64 MiB), t=3, p=4.

Parameter Selection and Upgrade Paths

When deploying a password hash, choose parameters that make a single verification take 100–500 ms on the target hardware. Store the algorithm identifier, version, salt, and parameters alongside the hash (e.g., argon2idv=19$m=65536,t=3,p=4$) to enable future upgrades. A migration strategy: on successful login, verify with the current parameters, then re‑hash the password with stronger parameters and update the stored record. This avoids a flag‑day reset. For high‑entropy KDFs, HKDF‑SHA‑256 with a 256‑bit salt and info string binding the context (protocol, version) is standard; the output length can be any multiple of the hash output (256 bits). In TLS 1.3, the key schedule uses HKDF‑Expand‑Label with labels such as derived and handshake to derive traffic keys from the master secret.

Common Pitfalls

  • Using a fast hash (SHA‑256, MD5) directly on passwords — enables billions of guesses per second on GPUs.
  • Reusing salts across users — allows precomputation (rainbow tables) and parallel attacks.
  • Hard‑coding iteration counts that become too low as hardware improves — implement a configurable cost factor.
  • Deriving multiple keys from the same password without domain separation — use distinct info strings in HKDF or separate Argon2 instances.

Threshold Cryptography and Distributed Key Generation

Threshold cryptography splits a secret key into n shares such that any subset of size t (the threshold) can reconstruct the key or jointly perform cryptographic operations, while fewer than t shares reveal nothing. The foundational primitive is Shamir secret sharing (1979): a dealer chooses a random polynomial f(x) of degree t‑1 over a finite field with f(0) = secret; share i is f(i). Any t points uniquely determine the polynomial via Lagrange interpolation. For public‑key operations, the secret is the private exponent (RSA) or scalar (ECC). Distributed key generation (DKG) removes the trusted dealer: each participant acts as a dealer in a Feldman or Pedersen verifiable secret sharing (VSS) protocol, broadcasting commitments to their polynomial coefficients. The joint public key is the sum of individual commitments; the private key is the sum of the constant terms, never reconstructed in one place. Threshold signatures enable t parties to produce a valid signature without revealing their shares. For BLS signatures (pairing‑based), each party computes a partial signature σᵢ = H(m)skᵢ; the combiner aggregates using Lagrange coefficients λᵢ to obtain σ = ∏ σᵢλᵢ = H(m)∑ λᵢ skᵢ = H(m)sk. For ECDSA, threshold variants (GG18, GG20, Lindell‑Nof) use additive secret sharing of the nonce and private key, combined with zero‑knowledge proofs to prevent malicious behavior. Threshold decryption for ElGamal or RSA follows similar share‑combining techniques. Applications include cryptocurrency custody (multi‑sig wallets), HSM clusters, and secure multiparty computation (MPC) frameworks such as SPDZ, where threshold keys protect the MAC key.

Security Models and Robustness

The standard security model is static corruption (adversary chooses corrupted parties before protocol start) or adaptive corruption (adversary may corrupt during execution). A DKG is robust if it guarantees output delivery even when up to t‑1 parties are malicious; this requires a complaint and reconstruction phase. The Pedersen VSS adds a second random polynomial to hide the secret from the dealer, achieving information‑theoretic hiding. Proactive secret sharing periodically refreshes shares without changing the secret, limiting the window of exposure for long‑term keys. In the honest‑majority setting (t > n/2), protocols like SPDZ achieve active security with preprocessing; in the dishonest‑majority setting (t ≤ n/2), threshold signatures require additional assumptions (e.g., broadcast channel, PKI). The FROST (Flexible Round‑Optimized Schnorr Threshold) protocol (2020) provides a two‑round threshold Schnorr signature with identifiable abort, suitable for blockchain validators.

Implementation Checklist

  • Use a prime‑order group (e.g., secp256k1, Ristretto255) with a well‑tested library (libsecp256k1, dalek‑crypto).
  • Verify all VSS commitments before accepting shares; abort on any inconsistency.
  • Store shares in hardware‑isolated enclaves (TEE, HSM) to prevent extraction.
  • Implement proactive refresh at least annually for long‑lived keys.

Post‑Quantum Migration Strategies and Hybrid Schemes

The advent of large‑scale quantum computers threatens all widely deployed public‑key algorithms (RSA, DH, ECDSA, EdDSA) via Shor’s algorithm. Migration must preserve interoperability, avoid downgrade attacks, and provide a clear rollout timeline. The dominant approach is hybrid key exchange: combine a classical algorithm (X25519, P‑256) with a post‑quantum KEM (CRYSTALS‑Kyber) so that the session key is derived from both shared secrets. TLS 1.3 draft‑ietf‑tls‑hybrid‑design defines a named_group list containing both classical and PQ groups; the client sends a key_share for each, and the server selects one classical and one PQ group, returning both shares. The HKDF‑Extract step takes the concatenation of the two shared secrets as input, ensuring that breaking either component alone does not compromise the session key. Similar hybrid constructions are standardized for IKEv2 (RFC 9242) and SSH (draft‑ietf‑ssh‑hybrid‑kex). For digital signatures, hybrid certificates embed two public keys (e.g., RSA‑3072 and Dilithium‑3) and two signatures; a verifier accepts if either signature validates, providing backward compatibility while allowing relying parties to migrate verification logic incrementally. The NIST PQC standardization (2024) selected Kyber (KEM) and Dilithium (signatures) as primary algorithms, with Falcon and SPHINCS+ as alternatives. The migration timeline recommended by NIST and major browser vendors: 2025‑2026 — hybrid TLS deployed in browsers and servers; 2027 — PQ‑only TLS for internal services; 2030 — deprecation of classical‑only cipher suites in public PKI. Algorithm agility is critical: protocols must negotiate algorithm identifiers, support multiple concurrent versions, and allow seamless addition of future PQ candidates (e.g., BIKE, HQC) without breaking existing deployments.

Operational Considerations

  • Key sizes: Kyber‑768 public key 1184 bytes, ciphertext 1088 bytes; Dilithium‑3 public key 1952 bytes, signature 3293 bytes — plan for increased bandwidth and storage.
  • Performance: Kyber encapsulation/decapsulation ≈ 0.1 ms on modern CPUs; Dilithium signing ≈ 0.3 ms — acceptable for TLS handshakes but monitor CPU load on high‑traffic servers.
  • Certificate management: issue dual‑algorithm certificates (RSA + Dilithium) via ACME extensions; ensure OCSP/CRL responders handle larger responses.
  • Testing: use the Open Quantum Safe (OQS) provider for OpenSSL to experiment with hybrid groups in staging environments before production rollout.

Risk of Premature Deprecation

Deprecating classical algorithms before PQ implementations are widely validated introduces downgrade risk: an active attacker could force a fallback to a weak classical suite if the client or server misconfigures the supported groups. The hybrid‑only policy (require both classical and PQ shares) mitigates this, but demands that all endpoints support the PQ algorithm. A phased approach — first enable hybrid, monitor failure rates, then disable classical‑only — balances security and availability. Additionally, stateful hash‑based signatures (SPHINCS+, XMSS) require secure state management (used leaf indices); losing state leads to key reuse and catastrophic security loss. For most deployments, stateless lattice‑based signatures (Dilithium, Falcon) are preferred.

  • Assuming AES‑GCM remains secure under nonce reuse — it does not; nonce reuse breaks both confidentiality and integrity.
  • Believing constant‑time code alone defeats all side channels — microarchitectural effects (cache, branch predictor) may still leak.
  • Using PBKDF2 with a low iteration count (e.g., 1000) for password hashing — modern GPUs can test billions of candidates per second.
  • Thinking threshold schemes require a trusted dealer — DKG protocols eliminate the dealer entirely.
  • Expecting a single post‑quantum algorithm to replace RSA/ECC overnight — hybrid deployment and algorithm agility are mandatory for a safe transition.
  • Neglecting state management for hash‑based signatures — losing the used‑leaf index enables existential forgery.
  • Review these traps before the exam to avoid common misconceptions.

hand/surface-chemistry.html:
Adsorption Kinetics and Surface Heterogeneity

Beyond the equilibrium isotherms, the rate at which adsorbate molecules reach and occupy surface sites governs process design in separations, catalysis, and sensor technology. The kinetic models most frequently examined are the pseudo‑first‑order (Lagergren), pseudo‑second‑order (Ho‑McKay), and the intraparticle diffusion model (Weber‑Morris). The pseudo‑first‑order equation, ln(qₑ − qₜ) = ln qₑ − k₁t, assumes that the rate is proportional to the number of vacant sites, while the pseudo‑second‑order form, t/qₜ = 1/(k₂qₑ²) + t/qₑ, implies chemisorption involving valence forces. In practice, the pseudo‑second‑order model often fits chemisorption data better because it accounts for the activation energy barrier associated with electron sharing or transfer.

Surface heterogeneity introduces a distribution of site energies, which the classical Langmuir model ignores. The Freundlich isotherm, qₑ = K_F Cₑ^(1/n), empirically captures this heterogeneity through the exponent 1/n (0 < 1/n < 1). A more rigorous treatment is the Temkin isotherm, which assumes a linear decrease in adsorption heat with coverage: qₑ = (RT/b) ln(A Cₑ). The Dubinin‑Radushkevich (D‑R) model further distinguishes micropore filling from surface coverage by using the Polanyi potential, ε = RT ln(1 + 1/Cₑ), and yields a mean adsorption energy E = 1/√(2β) that discriminates physisorption (E < 8 kJ mol⁻¹) from chemisorption (E > 8 kJ mol⁻¹).

Experimental determination of kinetic parameters requires careful control of particle size, agitation speed, and temperature to isolate film diffusion, pore diffusion, and surface reaction steps. The Boyd plot (Bt vs t) and the Weber‑Morris plot (qₜ vs t^½) help identify the rate‑limiting step: a linear Boyd plot passing through the origin indicates particle‑diffusion control, whereas a multi‑linear Weber‑Morris plot with an intercept suggests boundary‑layer effects. Understanding these nuances allows the examiner to test whether a candidate can select the appropriate model for a given dataset and interpret the physical meaning of the fitted constants.

Catalyst Deactivation and Regeneration Strategies

Industrial catalysts lose activity over time through several concurrent mechanisms: sintering, coking (carbon deposition), poisoning, and mechanical attrition. Sintering is the thermally driven agglomeration of active metal crystallites, reducing the metal surface area; it follows an Arrhenius‑type dependence on temperature and is accelerated by the presence of steam or hydrogen. Coking results from hydrocarbon cracking and polymerisation on acidic sites, forming polyaromatic carbon that blocks pores and covers active centres. The rate of coke formation correlates with the acidity of the support (e.g., zeolites) and the partial pressure of olefinic feeds. Poisoning occurs when strong chemisorption of impurities (S, N, As, Pb) irreversibly occupies active sites; even ppm‑level contaminants can cause severe deactivation in noble‑metal catalysts.

Regeneration strategies are tailored to the deactivation mode. Oxidative regeneration (controlled combustion of coke in air or O₂/N₂ mixtures) restores activity for coked catalysts but must be temperature‑limited to avoid sintering or support collapse. For sulfur‑poisoned metal catalysts, high‑temperature hydrogen treatment (hydrodesulfurization) can strip sulfur as H₂S, though the metal‑sulfur bond strength often makes complete recovery difficult. In fluid catalytic cracking (FCC), continuous catalyst circulation through a regenerator where coke is burnt off at 650–750 °C maintains steady‑state activity. Promoters such as rare‑earth oxides (La, Ce) enhance the thermal stability of zeolite frameworks, delaying dealumination and preserving acidity. The examiner may ask to compare the economics of periodic shutdown regeneration versus continuous regeneration, requiring an understanding of catalyst lifetime, downtime costs, and the impact of regeneration severity on long‑term structural integrity.

Worked Example: Identifying Rate‑Limiting Step
A batch adsorption experiment for methylene blue onto activated carbon yields the following data: at t = 10 min, qₜ = 45 mg g⁻¹; at t = 30 min, qₜ = 78 mg g⁻¹; at t = 60 min, qₜ = 102 mg g⁻¹; at equilibrium qₑ = 120 mg g⁻¹. Using the pseudo‑second‑order model, calculate the rate constant k₂ and comment on the fit.
The linearised pseudo‑second‑order form is t/qₜ = 1/(k₂qₑ²) + t/qₑ. Compute t/qₜ for each point: 10/45 = 0.222, 30/78 = 0.385, 60/102 = 0.588. Plot t/qₜ versus t; the slope equals 1/qₑ = 1/120 = 0.00833 min g mg⁻¹, intercept = 1/(k₂qₑ²). Using the three points, linear regression gives slope ≈ 0.0083 (matching 1/qₑ) and intercept ≈ 0.14. Hence k₂ = 1/(intercept × qₑ²) = 1/(0.14 × 14400) ≈ 4.96 × 10⁻⁴ g mg⁻¹ min⁻¹. The high correlation coefficient (R² > 0.99) confirms that chemisorption controls the rate, consistent with the pseudo‑second‑order mechanism.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question provides kinetic data, first test the pseudo‑first‑order plot (ln(qₑ−qₜ) vs t). If the plot is non‑linear, switch to pseudo‑second‑order (t/qₜ vs t). Remember that the pseudo‑second‑order model inherently assumes qₑ from the equilibrium isotherm; if qₑ is unknown, use the non‑linear form and fit by iteration. Examiners often award marks for correctly identifying the linearised equation and stating the physical implication of the rate constant.

Colloidal Stability: DLVO Theory and Steric Effects

The Derjaguin‑Landau‑Verwey‑Overbeek (DLVO) framework quantifies the balance between van der Waals attraction and electrical double‑layer repulsion that governs the aggregation of lyophobic colloids. The total interaction energy V_T = V_A + V_R, where V_A = −A_H a/(12 H) for two identical spheres of radius a at surface‑to‑surface separation H (A_H is the Hamaker constant), and V_R = 2π ε a ζ² ln[1 + exp(−κH)] for constant surface potential ζ (ε is the permittivity of the medium, κ⁻¹ the Debye length). The energy barrier V_max must exceed ~15 k_BT to confer kinetic stability; otherwise rapid coagulation occurs. The critical coagulation concentration (CCC) follows the Schulze‑Hardy rule: CCC ∝ z⁻⁶ for indifferent electrolytes, where z is the counter‑ion valence. This explains why Al³⁺ (z = 3) coagulates a negatively charged sol at millimolar concentrations while Na⁺ (z = 1) requires molar levels.

Steric stabilization adds a non‑DLVO repulsive term when adsorbed polymer layers overlap. The steric repulsion V_S ≈ (2π a Γ² / ρ²) (δ − H)² for H < δ, where Γ is the adsorbed amount, ρ the polymer density, and δ the layer thickness. Effective steric stabilization requires the polymer to be strongly anchored, soluble in the dispersion medium, and of sufficient molecular weight to provide a thick adsorbed layer (typically > 10 nm). In contrast, bridging flocculation occurs when a single polymer chain adsorbs onto two particles, pulling them together; this is favoured at low polymer coverage and high molecular weight. The examiner may present a scenario where a colloidal dispersion is stable at low ionic strength but flocculates upon addition of a non‑ionic surfactant, testing the ability to distinguish between electrostatic and steric mechanisms.

Zeta potential measurement via electrophoresis provides a practical proxy for the surface potential ζ. The Smoluchowski equation, ζ = (η u_E)/ε, relates electrophoretic mobility u_E to ζ for thin double layers (κa ≫ 1). For small particles (κa ≪ 1), the Hückel equation ζ = (3η u_E)/(2ε) applies. Knowing which limit applies is essential for interpreting zeta potential data correctly. A typical exam trap is to give a mobility value and ask for ζ without specifying particle size or ionic strength, expecting the candidate to state the assumption (Smoluchowski vs Hückel) and its validity.

Emulsion Phase Inversion and Rheological Behavior

Phase inversion is the spontaneous transformation of an oil‑in‑water (O/W) emulsion into a water‑in‑oil (W/O) emulsion, or vice versa, triggered by changes in temperature, composition, or surfactant concentration. The hydrophilic‑lipophilic balance (HLB) of the emulsifier is the primary determinant: low HLB (3–6) favours W/O, high HLB (8–18) favours O/W. The phase inversion temperature (PIT) for non‑ionic surfactants occurs when the surfactant’s affinity for water and oil becomes equal; at the PIT the interfacial tension reaches a minimum and the emulsion type flips. The PIT can be predicted from the surfactant’s cloud point and the oil’s equivalent alkane carbon number (EACN) using the HLD (hydrophilic‑lipophilic difference) equation: HLD = ln S − k EACN + f(A) + C_c + T − α (EO − PO), where S is salinity, f(A) the alcohol contribution, C_c the surfactant concentration term, and α the temperature coefficient. When HLD = 0, the system is at the inversion point.

Two inversion pathways exist: catastrophic inversion, where a small change in a control variable (e.g., temperature) causes an abrupt flip with a dramatic viscosity drop, and transitional inversion, which proceeds through a bicontinuous microemulsion phase with a viscosity maximum. The rheology of concentrated emulsions is described by the Krieger‑Dougherty equation: η = η₀ (1 − φ/φ_m)^(−[η]φ_m), where φ is the dispersed‑phase volume fraction, φ_m the maximum packing fraction (~0.63 for random close packing), and [η] the intrinsic viscosity (2.5 for hard spheres). As φ approaches φ_m, viscosity diverges, leading to yield‑stress behaviour typical of mayonnaise or cosmetic creams. The presence of a yield stress is often modelled by the Herschel‑Bulkley equation: τ = τ_y + K γ̇^n. Understanding these relationships allows the formulation scientist to predict flow behaviour during processing and shelf life.

Demulsification techniques exploit the same principles: heating above the PIT, adding electrolytes to compress the double layer, or introducing a demulsifier with an HLB opposite to that of the original emulsifier. In crude oil dehydration, chemical demulsifiers (often polyoxyethylene‑polyoxypropylene block copolymers) displace the natural asphaltene film at the water‑oil interface, promoting coalescence. The examiner may ask to design a demulsification protocol for a given emulsion, requiring selection of the appropriate method based on the emulsion type, stability mechanism, and operational constraints.

Surface Chemistry in Environmental Remediation

Adsorption on engineered nanomaterials and natural minerals is a cornerstone of water and air purification. Activated carbon, with a surface area exceeding 1000 m² g⁻¹, removes organic micropollutants (pesticides, pharmaceuticals) via hydrophobic interactions and π‑π stacking. The adsorption capacity is often correlated with the octanol‑water partition coefficient (K_ow) of the solute; compounds with log K_ow > 3 show strong uptake. For heavy metals, surface complexation on iron‑oxide nanoparticles (Fe₃O₄, γ‑Fe₂O₃) follows the ligand‑exchange mechanism: ≡Fe–OH + M²⁺ ⇌ ≡Fe–OM⁺ + H⁺. The point of zero charge (pH_pzc) of the oxide dictates the pH window for cation versus anion adsorption; below pH_pzc the surface is positively charged and favours anion uptake (e.g., arsenate, phosphate), while above pH_pzc it is negative and binds cations (Pb²⁺, Cd²⁺).

Photocatalysis leverages semiconductor band‑gap excitation to generate electron‑hole pairs that drive redox reactions at the surface. TiO₂ (anatase, E_g ≈ 3.2 eV) under UV light oxidises organic pollutants to CO₂ and H₂O and reduces Cr(VI) to Cr(III). Doping with nitrogen or coupling with narrow‑bandgap semiconductors (e.g., g‑C₃N₄) extends activity into the visible region. The Langmuir‑Hinshelwood kinetic model, rate = (k K C)/(1 + K C), describes the surface‑reaction‑limited regime, where K is the adsorption equilibrium constant and k the surface reaction rate constant. At low concentrations (K C ≪ 1), the kinetics simplify to pseudo‑first‑order: rate = k_app C with k_app = k K.

Colloidal nanoparticles also serve as reactive barriers in permeable reactive walls. Zero‑valent iron (ZVI) nanoparticles reductively dechlorinate trichloroethylene (TCE) to ethene via sequential hydrogenolysis. The reaction proceeds through surface‑bound Fe⁰ corrosion products (Fe²⁺/Fe³⁺ oxides) that can passivate the surface; periodic acid washing or the addition of a bimetallic catalyst (Pd/Fe) restores reactivity. In oil‑spill response, surfactant‑stabilised emulsions enhance the bioavailability of hydrocarbons for microbial degradation, while solid‑stabilised Pickering emulsions (using silica or clay particles) can be engineered to sink oil droplets for benthic remediation. The examiner may ask to compare the advantages and limitations of adsorption versus photocatalysis for a specific contaminant, requiring an integrated understanding of surface area, light penetration, and regeneration feasibility.

  • Confusing the pseudo‑first‑order and pseudo‑second‑order linear forms and misassigning the rate‑limiting step.
  • Assuming the Langmuir isotherm applies to heterogeneous surfaces without checking the Freundlich exponent.
  • Neglecting the temperature dependence of sintering when proposing regeneration cycles for supported metal catalysts.
  • Applying the Schulze‑Hardy rule to specific adsorption (chemical) rather than indifferent electrolytes.
  • Using the Smoluchowski equation for zeta potential without verifying the κa ≫ 1 condition.
  • Overlooking the distinction between catastrophic and transitional phase inversion when interpreting viscosity‑temperature curves.
  • Treating all heavy‑metal adsorption as purely electrostatic while ignoring surface complexation and pH_pzc effects.
