hand/logarithmic-geometry.html:
Log Hodge Theory and the Kato–Nakayama Realization

Log Hodge theory extends the classical Hodge decomposition to varieties with normal crossing degenerations by replacing the underlying topological space with the Kato–Nakayama space Xlog. For a fine saturated log analytic space (X, MX) the space Xlog is a real‑analytic manifold with corners whose points are pairs (x, h) where x ∈ X and h : MX,xgp → S1 is a homomorphism compatible with the log structure. The projection Xlog → X is a proper surjection with fiber a real torus of rank equal to the rank of the characteristic monoid at x. Kato and Nakayama proved that the log Betti cohomology H•B(Xlog, ℚ) is canonically isomorphic to the log étale cohomology H•log‑ét(X, ℚ) via a comparison isomorphism that respects the weight filtration. This yields a mixed Hodge structure on the log cohomology of any log smooth variety over ℂ, where the Hodge filtration comes from the log de Rham complex Ω•X/ℂ(log) and the weight filtration is induced by the monodromy operator N = log(Tu) on the nearby cycles. The log Hodge numbers hp,q = dim GrpF Grp+qW Hp+qlog(X) satisfy the same symmetries as in the smooth projective case, and the log Hodge–de Rham spectral sequence E1p,q = Hq(X, ΩpX/ℂ(log)) ⇒ Hp+qlog(X, ℂ) degenerates at E1 (Kato–Usui). For a semistable degeneration f : X → Δ with central fiber Y = ∪Yi, the Clemens–Schmid exact sequence identifies the limit mixed Hodge structure on H•(Xη) with the log mixed Hodge structure on H•log(Y), making the Kato–Nakayama space the natural topological avatar of the degeneration.

Log Riemann–Hilbert Correspondence and Logarithmic D‑Modules

The logarithmic Riemann–Hilbert correspondence, developed by Kashiwara, Mochizuki, and Sabbah, establishes an equivalence between the derived category of regular holonomic logarithmic D‑modules on a log smooth variety (X, M) and the derived category of constructible sheaves on the associated Kato–Nakayama space Xlog. A logarithmic D‑module is a coherent sheaf of modules over the sheaf of logarithmic differential operators DX(log), which is generated by vector fields tangent to the divisor defined by the log structure. Regularity means that locally the module admits a good filtration whose characteristic variety is contained in the log cotangent bundle. The functor DRlog : Dbrh(DX(log)) → Dbc(Xlog, ℂ) sends a logarithmic D‑module M to the complex of log de Rham sections DRlog(M) = [ M → Ω1X(log) ⊗ M → … ] placed in degrees 0,…,dim X. Its quasi‑inverse is the solution functor Sollog(F) = RHomℂ(F, OXan) equipped with the natural logarithmic connection. This correspondence respects the weight filtration: the perverse t‑structure on constructible sheaves corresponds to the irregular Hodge filtration on logarithmic D‑modules introduced by Mochizuki. As a consequence, the log irregular Hodge numbers of a meromorphic connection with logarithmic poles along a normal crossing divisor can be read off from the monodromy weight filtration on the nearby cycles, providing a Hodge‑theoretic interpretation of the Stokes phenomenon in the logarithmic setting.

Worked Example: Logarithmic de Rham Cohomology of a Normal Crossing Divisor
Compute the log de Rham cohomology of the pair (𝔸², D) where D is the union of the coordinate axes, and identify the Hodge filtration.
Let X = 𝔸² with coordinates (x, y) and log structure given by the divisor D = {xy = 0}. The log de Rham complex Ω•X/ℂ(log) is generated by dx/x and dy/y. In degree 0 we have OX. In degree 1 we have OX·dx/x ⊕ OX·dy/y. In degree 2 we have OX·(dx/x)∧(dy/y). The differential d sends 1 ↦ 0, f ↦ (∂f/∂x) dx/x + (∂f/∂y) dy/y, and ω₁∧ω₂ ↦ 0 because d(dx/x) = 0. The cohomology groups are H⁰ = ℂ (constants), H¹ = ℂ·[dx/x] ⊕ ℂ·[dy/y] (classes of the logarithmic 1‑forms), H² = ℂ·[(dx/x)∧(dy/y)]. The Hodge filtration Fp is the stupid filtration: F⁰ = whole complex, F¹ = Ω≥1(log), F² = Ω≥2(log). Thus Gr0F H⁰ = ℂ, Gr1F H¹ = ℂ², Gr2F H² = ℂ, and all other graded pieces vanish. The log Hodge numbers are h⁰⁰ = 1, h¹⁰ = h⁰¹ = 1, h¹¹ = 1, matching the mixed Hodge structure on the punctured affine plane.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question asks for the log Hodge numbers of a semistable degeneration, first write down the Clemens–Schmid exact sequence, then read off the weight filtration from the monodromy operator N; the log Hodge numbers are the dimensions of the graded pieces of the Hodge filtration on the log de Rham complex of the special fiber.

Log Motivic Integration and Arc Spaces on Log Schemes

Log motivic integration, pioneered by Nicaise and Sebag, extends Denef–Loeser motivic integration to log smooth pairs (X, D) by working on the log arc space Llog(X). For a fine log scheme X over a field k, the log arc space is the functor that assigns to a k‑algebra R the set of morphisms Spec R[[t]] → X of log schemes, where Spec R[[t]] carries the standard log structure associated to the divisor {t = 0}. When X is log smooth, Llog(X) is representable by a formal scheme locally of finite type over the log jet schemes. The log motivic measure μlog takes values in a completed Grothendieck ring of log varieties K̂0(Varlog) and satisfies the change‑of‑variables formula: for a log étale morphism f : Y → X of relative dimension d, μlog(f(A)) = 𝕃−d μlog(A) where 𝕃 is the class of the affine line. This formalism yields a log version of the motivic nearby fiber ψlog(f) for a log smooth function f : X → 𝔸¹, which lives in K̂0(Varlog) and specializes to the log Hodge–Deligne polynomial. The log motivic Milnor fiber of a non‑degenerate polynomial with respect to its Newton polyhedron can be computed combinatorially via the log toric geometry of the associated fan, generalizing the classical formula of Varchenko. Moreover, the log motivic integration on the space of log arcs provides a geometric interpretation of the log motivic zeta function Zlog(f, T) = ∑n≥1 [ψlog(fn)] Tn, whose poles are controlled by the log canonical thresholds of the pair (X, D).

Log Prismatic Cohomology and p‑adic Hodge Theory for Log Schemes

Prismatic cohomology, introduced by Bhatt and Scholze, has a logarithmic extension developed by Drinfeld, Bhatt–Lurie, and others. For a log scheme (X, M) over a perfectoid base (S, MS) with a bounded prism (A, I) equipped with a log structure compatible with the divided powers on I, the log prismatic site (X/A)log‑prism is defined by log‑étale maps to X together with a lift of the log structure to the prism. The log prismatic complex Δlog(X/A) computes a cohomology theory that specializes to log crystalline cohomology after base change to A/I, to log de Rham cohomology after base change to A/(p), and to log étale cohomology after inverting p and completing. The log Nygaard filtration N≥• on Δlog induces the log Hodge–Tate filtration on the log prismatic cohomology modulo p. The log version of the prismatic comparison theorem states that for a proper log smooth formal scheme X over OC with C a p‑adic algebraically closed field, there is a canonical isomorphism Hilog‑ét(XC, ℤp) ⊗ℤp Ainf ≅ Hilog‑prism(X/Ainf) compatible with Frobenius, the Nygaard filtration, and the Galois action. This yields a log analogue of the Fontaine–Laffaille and Breuil–Kisin classifications: log Breuil–Kisin modules with a log Frobenius correspond to log crystalline representations of the Galois group of a p‑adic field with log ramification. The log prismatic approach also clarifies the Hyodo–Kato isomorphism: the log prismatic cohomology of the special fiber with its canonical log structure, after adjoining the period element log([ϖ]), recovers the log rigid cohomology of the generic fiber, and the monodromy operator N arises from the log Frobenius on the prismatic complex.

Log Geometric Langlands on the Fargues–Fontaine Curve

The Fargues–Scholze geometric Langlands program uses the stack BunG of G‑bundles on the Fargues–Fontaine curve XFF = Proj(⊕n≥0 BdR+/ξn) over a p‑adic field. Log geometry enters at two levels. First, the curve XFF carries a natural log structure given by the divisor at infinity (the “untilt” divisor), making it a log adic space. The stack BunG inherits a log structure from the universal bundle, and the Hecke correspondences become log smooth morphisms of log stacks. Second, the local Langlands correspondence for GLn is realized via the cohomology of the log shtuka space Shtlog(G, μ) which parametrizes modifications of G‑bundles with a log structure at the modification points. The log étale cohomology of these spaces carries an action of the Weil group and of the Langlands dual group LG, and the log version of the excursion operators constructed by Fargues–Scholze uses the log Kummer flat topology to define the relevant sheaves. The log geometric Satake equivalence identifies the category of log perverse sheaves on the log affine Grassmannian GrG,log with the category of representations of LG, where the log structure encodes the tame ramification data. This log enhancement is essential for the compatibility with the local Langlands correspondence for non‑split groups and for the construction of the spectral action on D‑modules on BunG. In particular, the log version of the categorical trace formula expresses the trace of Frobenius on the log étale cohomology of Shtlog in terms of orbital integrals on the log Lie algebra, providing a geometric proof of the log fundamental lemma.

  • Confusing the Kato–Nakayama space with the underlying analytic space; the former carries a torus fibration that encodes the log structure.
  • Assuming the log de Rham complex is the same as the usual de Rham complex of the complement; logarithmic forms have poles along the divisor and a different Hodge filtration.
  • Neglecting the weight filtration on log étale cohomology when applying the Clemens–Schmid sequence; the monodromy operator N must be computed on the nearby cycles.
  • Treating log D‑modules as ordinary D‑modules on the complement; the logarithmic condition imposes regularity along the divisor and changes the characteristic variety.
  • Overlooking the role of the log Kummer flat topology in defining log étale cohomology with ℤp-coefficients; the Kummer flat site is strictly finer than the étale site.
  • Misapplying the log motivic change‑of‑variables formula without checking that the morphism is log étale and of constant relative dimension.
  • Forgetting that the log prismatic Nygaard filtration reduces to the log Hodge filtration only after base change to A/(p), not integrally.

hand/homotopy-type-theory.html:
Cubical Type Theory and Computational Univalence

Cubical type theory (CTT) was introduced by Cohen, Coquand, Huber, and Mörtberg (2016) to give a constructive interpretation of the univalence axiom. Unlike the original simplicial set model, which validates univalence only propositionally, CTT equips the interval 𝕀 with primitive constructors 0, 1 and a composition operation that fills open boxes. Types are interpreted as cubical sets — presheaves on the cube category — and the identity type Path A a b is defined as a function 𝕀 → A sending 0 to a and 1 to b. The crucial ingredient is the Glue type former, which builds a type equivalent to a given type along a specified equivalence. Using Glue, one can define a term ua : Equiv A B → Path U A B that computes by reducing the equivalence to a path in the universe. This yields canonicity: closed terms of natural number type reduce to numerals even in the presence of univalence. The composition structure also supports higher inductive types directly: the circle S¹ is given by a point base and a path loop : Path S¹ base base whose endpoints are definitionally equal to base. CTT has been implemented in the proof assistants Cubical Agda and the cubical mode of Coq, enabling programmers to write programs that transport data along equivalences and to extract executable code from homotopy‑theoretic constructions.

The Simplicial Set Model and Its Role in Consistency

The simplicial set model, constructed by Voevodsky (2009) and later refined by Kapulkin and Lumsdaine, interprets Martin‑Löf type theory with a cumulative hierarchy of universes in the category of simplicial sets sSet. Types are interpreted as Kan complexes — fibrant objects in the standard Quillen model structure — and the identity type corresponds to the path space object XΔ¹. The universe Uₙ is interpreted as a Kan complex classifying small Kan fibrations; its points are codes for Kan fibrations with fibers of homotopy level < n. Univalence holds because the map idtoeqv : (A = B) → Equiv(A,B) is a weak equivalence of Kan complexes, a fact proved by constructing a homotopy inverse using the straightening‑unstraightening equivalence for Cartesian fibrations. This model establishes the relative consistency of HoTT with respect to ZFC + infinitely many inaccessible cardinals (one for each universe level). Moreover, the model validates function extensionality, propositional extensionality, and the existence of higher inductive types such as the circle, the torus, and general pushouts. The simplicial set model also clarifies the relationship between HoTT and classical homotopy theory: the synthetic homotopy groups of spheres computed in HoTT agree with the classical groups because the interpretation preserves the relevant homotopy‑theoretic structure.

Technique: Computing Transport Along a Path in Cubical Type Theory
Given a type family P : Bool → U with P false ≡ ℕ and P true ≡ ℕ, and an equivalence e : ℕ ≃ ℕ defined by e(n) = n + 1, construct the transport of 0 : ℕ along the path ua(e) : P false = P true in Cubical Agda.
In Cubical Agda the universe is a cubical type, so ua(e) reduces to a path λ i → Glue (P false) [ (i = 0) ↦ (P false , idEquiv) ; (i = 1) ↦ (P true , e) ]. Transport along this path is defined by composition in the Glue type. For the endpoint i = 0 we have the identity equivalence, for i = 1 we have e. The composition operation fills the open box with the given equivalences, yielding a term of type P true. Evaluating the composition at the element 0 : ℕ produces e(0) = 1. Hence transport (ua e) 0 ≡ 1 : ℕ.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question asks for the computational content of univalence, recall that cubical type theory provides a primitive composition operation; the answer should mention Glue types, the interval 𝕀, and the fact that transport reduces to applying the underlying equivalence. Do not confuse this with the simplicial set model, which only gives a semantic justification.

Higher Inductive‑Inductive Types and Quotient Types

Higher inductive‑inductive types (HIITs) extend HITs by allowing the simultaneous definition of a type and a family of types indexed by it, where constructors may refer to both the type and the family. A canonical example is the Cauchy real numbers: one defines a type ℝ together with a family of relations ≈ : ℝ → ℝ → U such that constructors generate both points (rational approximations) and paths (equivalence of Cauchy sequences). HIITs also give a native formulation of quotient types: for a type A and an equivalence relation R : A → A → U, the quotient A/R is a HIIT with a constructor q : A → A/R and a path constructor qeq : ∀ {x y}, R x y → q x = q y. The elimination principle states that any family P : A/R → U respecting R extends uniquely to a function out of the quotient. This construction avoids the need for set‑quotients in the meta‑theory and works uniformly for higher‑dimensional relations, enabling quotients of groupoids and ∞‑groupoids. In Cubical Agda, HIITs are supported natively, and the quotient construction computes: the canonical map from A to A/R is a surjection, and the induced map on identity types is an equivalence precisely when R is an equivalence relation. HIITs have been used to formalize the construction of the real numbers, the free group on a type, and the localization of a type at a family of maps.

Modalities, Cohesion, and Differential Cohesive HoTT

Modal type theory adds operators □ (necessity) and ◇ (possibility) satisfying certain axioms; in HoTT these become idempotent monads and comonads on the ∞‑topos of types. A cohesive modality consists of an adjoint quadruple Π ⊣ Disc ⊣ Γ ⊣ coDisc where Π preserves finite products and Disc, coDisc are fully faithful. This structure captures the idea of a “shape” functor Π sending a type to its fundamental ∞‑groupoid, while Disc embeds discrete types. Differential cohesion refines cohesion by adding an infinitesimal shape modality ℑ and a reduction modality ℜ, yielding a diagram of modalities that models synthetic differential geometry inside HoTT. The tangent bundle of a type X can be defined as the fiber of the unit X → ℑ X, and differential forms appear as maps into the de Rham coefficient object ♭dR BⁿU(1). These modalities have been formalized in the cohesive-hott library for Agda and used to prove synthetic versions of the Stokes theorem and the Chern‑Weil homomorphism. The presence of modalities also enables modal descent: a type is modal for a modality if the unit map is an equivalence, and many classical constructions (e.g., sheafification) become instances of modal reflection.

Formalization of Algebraic Topology in Lean and Agda: Case Studies

The Lean 4 library Mathlib now contains a substantial HoTT layer built on top of its dependent type theory with proof irrelevance. Using the Quotient and HIT mechanisms, Lean formalizes the fundamental groupoid of a type, the Seifert‑van Kampen theorem for pushouts of groupoids, and the construction of the universal cover of the circle. In Agda, the HoTT-Agda library provides a cubical kernel where the Brunerie number (π₄(S³) = ℤ/2) has been verified by a 2‑year computation that reduces the defining higher inductive type of S³ to a normal form. A second case study is the formal proof of the Blakers‑Massey theorem for general pushouts in the cubical library: the proof proceeds by constructing a cubical diagram of fibrations and applying the connectivity estimates of the join construction. Both Lean and Agda formalizations rely on univalence to identify equivalent fibrations, and on higher inductive types to present cell complexes synthetically. The experience shows that proof assistants with native cubical support (Cubical Agda, Lean’s cubical mode) give shorter proofs for homotopical statements because transport along equivalences computes definitionally, whereas in non‑cubical settings one must manually invoke path induction and coherence lemmas.

  • Confusing the simplicial set model (semantic) with cubical type theory (syntactic computational model).
  • Assuming univalence computes in plain Martin‑Löf type theory without a cubical or Glue extension.
  • Treating higher inductive‑inductive types as ordinary inductive types; they require simultaneous constructors for the type and its family.
  • Overlooking that modalities in cohesive HoTT are idempotent monads/comonads, not merely logical operators.
  • Believing that formalization of the Brunerie number in Agda uses classical reasoning; it is fully constructive in cubical type theory.
  • Neglecting that the quotient HIIT constructor qeq only yields a set‑quotient when the relation is an equivalence relation; otherwise the quotient is a higher groupoid.

hand/metallurgy.html:
Thermodynamic and Kinetic Controls in Smelting Operations

Smelting is the high‑temperature reduction of a metal oxide (or other compound) to the metallic state. While the Ellingham diagram tells whether a reduction is thermodynamically possible at a given temperature, the actual furnace performance depends on kinetic factors such as reaction rates, mass‑transfer limitations, and the stability of intermediate phases. For ironmaking in a blast furnace, the overall reaction Fe₂O₃ + 3CO → 2Fe + 3CO₂ is thermodynamically favourable above 700 °C, yet the rate‑determining step is the gas‑solid reduction of wüstite (FeO) to iron, which proceeds via the sequence Fe₂O₃ → Fe₃O₄ → FeO → Fe. The FeO → Fe step has the highest activation energy and therefore controls the furnace height required for complete reduction. In practice, the burden descent rate, gas flow distribution, and the presence of catalytic alkali vapours alter the effective kinetics. A similar kinetic bottleneck appears in the carbothermic reduction of SiO₂ to silicon: SiO₂ + 2C → Si + 2CO is thermodynamically allowed above 1600 °C, but the formation of a viscous SiO‑rich slag layer around the carbon particles limits CO diffusion, so industrial furnaces operate at 1900–2000 °C with excess carbon to maintain a high CO partial pressure and to keep the slag fluid. The concept of a “reduction window” — the temperature interval where both thermodynamics and kinetics are favourable — is central to process design. For manganese, the window is narrow because MnO reduction to Mn is fast only above 1300 °C, yet Mn vaporises appreciably above 1500 °C, leading to losses. Process engineers therefore adjust the carbon activity, use pre‑reduced agglomerates, or employ plasma‑assisted heating to widen the window. Understanding the interplay of ΔG°, activation energy, and transport phenomena enables the selection of furnace type (blast furnace, electric arc furnace, submerged‑arc furnace) and the optimisation of charge composition, blast temperature, and residence time.

Slag Chemistry, Flux Selection, and Phase Equilibria

Slag is not a waste product; it is a engineered liquid phase that controls impurity removal, protects the metal from re‑oxidation, and determines the thermal efficiency of the furnace. The primary function of a flux is to react with gangue oxides to form a low‑melting, fluid slag that can absorb acidic or basic impurities. In ironmaking, limestone (CaCO₃) decomposes to CaO, which combines with silica (SiO₂) from the ore to form calcium silicate (Ca₂SiO₄, CaSiO₃) slags. The CaO/SiO₂ ratio (basicity) is kept between 1.0 and 1.3 to obtain a slag liquidus near 1350 °C, ensuring fluidity at the furnace hearth temperature. If the ratio is too low, the slag becomes highly viscous, impeding sulfur transfer from metal to slag; if too high, the slag solidifies prematurely, causing scaffold formation. The MgO content is also critical: 5–8 % MgO reduces the liquidus temperature and improves slag fluidity, but excess MgO raises the melting point again. In non‑ferrous smelting, such as copper converting, the slag system is FeO–SiO₂–CaO–Al₂O₃. The FeO content is deliberately maintained at 30–40 % to provide a liquid slag that dissolves FeS and Cu₂S, while the CaO/SiO₂ ratio is adjusted to keep the slag basic enough to absorb acidic impurities (As₂O₃, Sb₂O₃) but not so basic that it attacks the refractory lining. Phase diagrams (e.g., the CaO–SiO₂–Al₂O₃ ternary) are used to predict the liquidus surface and to design flux additions that keep the slag in the homogeneous liquid region throughout the temperature cycle. Modern practice employs computational thermodynamics (FactSage, Thermo‑Calc) to model multicomponent slag equilibria, allowing real‑time flux optimisation and the prediction of spinel or melilite formation that could cause accretions. The slag also acts as a sink for sulfur: the distribution ratio L_S = (%S in slag)/(%S in metal) increases with slag basicity and oxygen potential, so controlling the FeO level and CaO/SiO₂ ratio directly influences desulfurisation efficiency. In secondary steelmaking, synthetic slags (CaO–Al₂O₃–SiO₂–MgO) are tailored for each ladle treatment to achieve target sulfur, phosphorus, and inclusion chemistry.

Worked Example: Slag Basicity Calculation
A blast furnace charge contains 1200 kg of SiO₂ gangue and 800 kg of Al₂O₃ gangue. Limestone (CaCO₃) is added to achieve a target CaO/SiO₂ mass ratio of 1.2 in the final slag. Assuming complete decomposition of limestone to CaO and no other CaO sources, calculate the mass of limestone required. (Molar masses: CaCO₃ = 100 g mol⁻¹, CaO = 56 g mol⁻¹, SiO₂ = 60 g mol⁻¹.)
First convert the SiO₂ mass to moles: 1200 kg = 1 200 000 g ÷ 60 g mol⁻¹ = 20 000 mol SiO₂. The target CaO/SiO₂ mass ratio of 1.2 means mass(CaO) = 1.2 × mass(SiO₂) = 1.2 × 1 200 000 g = 1 440 000 g CaO. Convert CaO mass to moles: 1 440 000 g ÷ 56 g mol⁻¹ = 25 714 mol CaO. Each mole of CaCO₃ yields one mole of CaO, so moles of limestone needed = 25 714 mol. Mass of limestone = 25 714 mol × 100 g mol⁻¹ = 2 571 400 g = 2 571 kg. Therefore, 2 571 kg of limestone must be charged.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question asks for flux quantity, always convert gangue oxides to moles, apply the required basicity ratio on a mass basis, and then back‑calculate the flux mass using its decomposition stoichiometry. Keep a mental table of common molar masses (CaCO₃, CaO, SiO₂, Al₂O₃, MgO) to avoid arithmetic errors under time pressure.

Electrochemical Extraction of Highly Reactive Metals

Metals that lie far down the Ellingham diagram (e.g., alkali, alkaline‑earth, aluminium, titanium) cannot be reduced by carbon at practical temperatures because their oxides are more stable than CO/CO₂. Their commercial production relies on electrolysis of molten salts where the metal is deposited at the cathode and oxygen (or chlorine) evolves at the anode. The Hall‑Héroult process for aluminium dissolves Al₂O₃ in a cryolite (Na₃AlF₆) melt at 950–960 °C. The electrolyte composition is critical: excess AlF₃ lowers the liquidus temperature and increases conductivity, while CaF₂ additions reduce the vapour pressure of NaF and improve current efficiency. The carbon anode reacts with oxide ions to form CO₂ (2O²⁻ + C → CO₂ + 4e⁻), consuming ~0.45 kg C per kg Al. Current efficiencies of 93–96 % are typical; losses arise from the back‑reaction of dissolved Al with CO₂ (the “metal fog” reaction) and from anode effects caused by insufficient alumina concentration. The Downs cell produces sodium by electrolysing molten NaCl (with CaCl₂ to lower the melting point to ~600 °C) using a steel cathode and a graphite anode. Chlorine gas evolves at the anode and is a valuable by‑product. The cell operates at 6–8 V with current densities of 5–7 kA m⁻². Magnesium is obtained either by the electrolysis of molten MgCl₂ (Dow process) or by the Pidgeon silicothermic reduction; the electrolytic route uses a molten mixture of MgCl₂, NaCl, and CaCl₂ at 700 °C with a graphite anode and a steel cathode, achieving current efficiencies above 90 %. Titanium is produced via the Kroll process (Mg reduction of TiCl₄) rather than direct electrolysis because TiCl₄ is a volatile liquid that can be purified by distillation, and the high melting point of TiO₂ (1840 °C) makes oxide electrolysis impractical. However, recent research on the FFC Cambridge process (electrolysis of solid TiO₂ in molten CaCl₂ at 900 °C) shows promise for a direct, lower‑cost route. In all these cells, the key design parameters are electrolyte composition (to maximise conductivity and minimise vapour pressure), electrode materials (to resist corrosion and minimise overpotential), and cell geometry (to ensure uniform current distribution and easy metal collection). Energy consumption is the dominant cost: aluminium requires ~13–15 kWh kg⁻¹, sodium ~2.5 kWh kg⁻¹, magnesium ~12–14 kWh kg⁻¹. Improvements focus on inert anodes (e.g., cermet or doped SnO₂) to eliminate carbon consumption and CO₂ emissions.

Hydrometallurgical Processing: Leaching, Solvent Extraction, and Electrowinning

Hydrometallurgy exploits aqueous chemistry to extract metals from low‑grade or complex ores where pyrometallurgy is uneconomic or environmentally prohibitive. The sequence typically involves (1) leaching — dissolution of the target metal into an aqueous solution, (2) solution purification and concentration — often by solvent extraction (SX) or ion exchange, and (3) metal recovery — by electrowinning (EW), precipitation, or crystallisation. For copper oxide ores and low‑grade sulfides, heap leaching with dilute sulfuric acid (pH 1.5–2.5) percolates through stacked ore, producing a pregnant leach solution (PLS) containing 2–5 g L⁻¹ Cu²⁺. The leaching kinetics are controlled by acid diffusion, ferric/ferrous redox cycling, and bacterial oxidation (Acidithiobacillus ferrooxidans) that regenerates Fe³⁺, the actual oxidant for sulfide dissolution. The PLS is then contacted with an organic extractant — typically a hydroxyoxime (e.g., LIX 984) diluted in kerosene — in mixer‑settler units. The extraction equilibrium Cu²⁺(aq) + 2HR(org) ⇌ CuR₂(org) + 2H⁺(aq) is pH‑dependent; operating at pH 1.8–2.2 gives high copper loading while limiting iron co‑extraction. The loaded organic is stripped with spent electrolyte (high acid, high Cu²⁺) to produce a rich electrolyte (40–50 g L⁻¹ Cu²⁺, 180–200 g L⁻¹ H₂SO₄) for electrowinning. In the EW cell, copper plates onto stainless‑steel cathodes at current densities of 250–350 A m⁻², with lead‑calcium‑tin anodes that evolve oxygen. Current efficiencies exceed 95 % and energy consumption is 1.8–2.2 kWh kg⁻¹ Cu. Zinc hydrometallurgy follows a similar route: roasted ZnS concentrate is leached in spent electrolyte (ZnSO₄/H₂SO₄) under controlled pH to precipitate iron as jarosite or goethite, followed by purification (cementation, solvent extraction with D2EHPA) and electrowinning from a neutral sulfate electrolyte using aluminium cathodes. Nickel laterites are treated by high‑pressure acid leaching (HPAL) at 250–270 °C, 40–50 bar, dissolving Ni and Co into solution; subsequent solvent extraction with organophosphinic acids separates Ni from Co, and both are recovered by electrowinning or hydrogen reduction. The advantages of hydrometallurgy include lower temperature operation, selective metal recovery, and the ability to process ores with <0.5 % metal. Challenges involve reagent consumption, waste‑water management, and the need for robust solid‑liquid separation at large scale.

Secondary Refining and Alloy Production: AOD, VOD, and Ladle Metallurgy

Primary steelmaking (basic oxygen furnace or electric arc furnace) yields crude steel with carbon, phosphorus, sulfur, and dissolved gases above specification limits. Secondary refining in the ladle adjusts composition, temperature, and cleanliness before casting. The Argon‑Oxygen Decarburisation (AOD) converter is the workhorse for stainless steel. Molten steel is charged, and a mixture of argon and oxygen is blown through submerged tuyeres. Argon dilutes the oxygen partial pressure, lowering the CO/CO₂ equilibrium and allowing carbon removal to <0.03 % without excessive chromium oxidation. Typical blowing sequences: high‑oxygen/low‑argon for rapid decarburisation, then low‑oxygen/high‑argon for chromium recovery. The process also reduces sulfur by forming CaS in a lime‑rich slag. Vacuum‑Oxygen Decarburisation (VOD) achieves similar results by applying a vacuum (0.5–1 mbar) during oxygen blowing, which reduces the CO partial pressure and drives decarburisation at lower oxygen potentials, preserving alloying elements such as Nb, Ti, and V. VOD is preferred for high‑alloy grades where argon cost is prohibitive. Ladle Furnace (LF) treatment provides reheating (by graphite electrodes) and alloy addition under a protective slag cover. The slag chemistry (CaO–Al₂O₃–SiO₂–MgO) is tailored to absorb inclusions (Al₂O₃, MnS) and to desulfurise via the reaction [S] + (CaO) → (CaS) + [O]. Calcium treatment (Ca‑Si wire injection) modifies sulfide morphology from elongated MnS to globular CaS, improving transverse ductility. Vacuum degassing (RH, DH) removes hydrogen and nitrogen to <2 ppm and <30 ppm respectively, preventing pinholes and hydrogen‑induced cracking. Inclusion engineering uses rare‑earth or calcium additions to form stable, fine oxides that act as nucleation sites for equiaxed solidification. The integration of these steps — AOD/VOD → LF → RH → continuous casting — defines the modern “clean steel” route. Process control relies on real‑time sensors (optical emission spectroscopy for composition, laser‑based temperature, off‑gas analysis for decarburisation rate) and thermodynamic models that predict slag‑metal equilibrium at each stage. Energy consumption for secondary refining is 150–250 kWh t⁻¹, a modest fraction of total steelmaking energy but critical for meeting stringent quality specifications in automotive, pipeline, and nuclear applications.

  • Confusing the thermodynamic feasibility shown by the Ellingham diagram with the actual kinetic rate of reduction in a furnace.
  • Assuming a single flux composition works for all ore types; neglecting the effect of MgO, Al₂O₃, and FeO on slag liquidus and viscosity.
  • Overlooking the role of anode reactions (carbon consumption, chlorine evolution) in the overall energy balance of electrolytic cells.
  • Treating solvent extraction as a simple partition without considering pH‑dependent loading, stripping efficiency, and organic phase degradation.
  • Believing that secondary refining only adjusts temperature; ignoring inclusion modification, gas removal, and slag‑metal equilibrium control.
  • Neglecting the impact of vacuum level and argon dilution on the decarburisation equilibrium in AOD/VOD processes.
  • Mastering these traps will improve accuracy in metallurgy questions.

hand/morse-theory.html:
Morse-Bott Theory and Degenerate Critical Manifolds

Morse-Bott theory extends classical Morse theory to smooth functions whose critical sets are non‑degenerate submanifolds rather than isolated points. A smooth function f on a manifold M is Morse‑Bott if its critical set Crit(f) is a disjoint union of closed submanifolds C_i and the Hessian of f is non‑degenerate in the normal directions to each C_i. The index of a critical submanifold C is the dimension of the negative eigenspace of the normal Hessian; the nullity equals dim C. This framework preserves the handle‑body picture: a neighbourhood of C is diffeomorphic to the total space of the negative normal bundle, and attaching a handle of index λ along C corresponds to attaching a λ‑handle bundle over C. The Morse‑Bott inequalities replace the usual Morse inequalities by summing Betti numbers of the critical submanifolds weighted by the Poincaré polynomials of their normal bundles. Bott’s original 1954 paper applied this to the energy functional on the loop space ΩG of a compact Lie group G, yielding the celebrated Bott periodicity theorem π_k(U) ≅ πk+2(U). In symplectic geometry, Morse‑Bott functions appear naturally as moment maps for Hamiltonian torus actions; the Kirwan surjectivity theorem uses Morse‑Bott techniques to compute the cohomology of symplectic quotients. The Witten deformation of the de Rham complex also adapts to the Morse‑Bott setting, where small eigenvalues of the deformed Laplacian concentrate near the critical submanifolds, giving a spectral proof of the Morse‑Bott inequalities.

Cerf Theory and the Classification of Morse Functions

Cerf theory studies the space of Morse functions on a fixed manifold and the bifurcations that occur when a function ceases to be Morse. A generic one‑parameter family f_t of smooth functions on a closed manifold M has only two types of singularities: birth‑death of a pair of critical points of adjacent index (a quadratic tangency) and a transverse crossing of critical values. Cerf’s 1970 theorem states that for dim M ≥ 5 the space of Morse functions is connected; any two Morse functions can be joined by a Cerf‑generic path. The critical point cancellation lemma used in the h‑cobordism proof is precisely the inverse of a birth event. In dimension four, Cerf theory encounters exotic phenomena: the failure of the Whitney trick means that certain birth‑death sequences cannot be realised by isotopies, leading to the existence of exotic smooth structures on ℝ⁴. The Cerf diagram — a graphic of critical values versus the parameter t — encodes the handle‑body decomposition of the cobordism traced by the family. The group of pseudo‑isotopies of M is isomorphic to the fundamental group of the space of Morse functions, linking Cerf theory to algebraic K‑theory via the Igusa stability theorem. Modern applications include the classification of Lefschetz fibrations and the study of stability of symplectic structures under deformations.

Worked Example: Birth‑Death Cancellation in a Cerf Family
Consider a smooth family f_t : S² → ℝ, t ∈ [−1,1], where f_t(x,y,z) = z + t z² − z³ on the unit sphere. For t < 0 the function has two non‑degenerate critical points (a maximum and a saddle); at t = 0 a birth‑death occurs creating a degenerate critical point of index 1; for t > 0 the degenerate point splits into a saddle and a minimum. Show that the total number of critical points changes by two and that the Morse inequalities hold for each t.
For t < 0 the critical points are solutions of ∇f_t = 0 restricted to S². The cubic term −z³ gives a maximum near the north pole (index 2) and a saddle near the equator (index 1). At t = 0 the Hessian at the saddle acquires a zero eigenvalue, producing a degenerate critical point of nullity 1. For t > 0 the degenerate point splits into a saddle (index 1) and a minimum (index 0). Thus the critical point count goes from 2 to 3, a net increase of one pair (index 1 and index 0). The Morse inequalities for t < 0: b₀=1, b₁=0, b₂=1; critical points c₀=0, c₁=1, c₂=1 satisfy c₀ ≥ b₀, c₀−c₁+c₂ = 0 = χ(S²). For t > 0: c₀=1, c₁=1, c₂=1; the alternating sum remains 1, matching χ(S²). The birth‑death adds a cancelling pair (index 0 and 1) which does not alter the Euler characteristic, illustrating the Cerf principle that topology is invariant under generic bifurcations.
Exam Strategy
When a question asks about the effect of a birth‑death singularity on handle decompositions, remember that a birth adds a λ‑handle and a (λ+1)‑handle whose attaching spheres intersect in a single point; a death removes such a pair. The Euler characteristic and homology are unchanged. Sketch the Cerf diagram to visualise the parameter interval where the pair exists.

Morse Theory on Manifolds with Boundary and Relative Handle Decompositions

When a manifold M has non‑empty boundary ∂M, a Morse function f : M → ℝ is required to have no critical points on ∂M and to be constant on each boundary component. The gradient flow then defines a handle decomposition of M relative to ∂M. Handles are attached along framed spheres in the level sets of f, but the attaching regions now lie in the interior of the boundary of the sublevel set. The relative Morse lemma guarantees that near a critical point of index λ the function takes the form f = f(p) − x₁² − … − x_λ² + xλ+1² + … + x_n² with the boundary given by a coordinate hyperplane. This yields a relative handlebody (W, ∂₋W) where ∂₋W is the part of ∂M where f attains its minimum. The relative Morse inequalities involve the relative homology groups H_*(M, ∂₋W). A fundamental result of Smale (1962) states that if (W, ∂₋W) is a simply connected cobordism of dimension ≥ 6 with ∂₋W → W a homology equivalence, then W is diffeomorphic to ∂₋W × [0,1] relative to ∂₋W. This relative h‑cobordism theorem underlies the proof of the generalized Poincaré conjecture for manifolds with boundary. In symplectic geometry, Liouville domains provide a natural class of manifolds with contact boundary; a Morse function that is plurisubharmonic yields a handle decomposition by Weinstein handles, which are symplectic analogues of smooth handles. The flexibility of Weinstein handles (indices ≤ n) is central to the h‑principle for Stein manifolds.

Applications to Symplectic Topology and the Weinstein Conjecture

Morse theory on the loop space of a symplectic manifold leads to Floer homology, but finite‑dimensional Morse theory also plays a decisive role in symplectic topology. A Weinstein manifold is a symplectic manifold (W, ω) admitting a Liouville vector field X (ℒ_X ω = ω) that is gradient‑like for an exhausting Morse function φ : W → ℝ. The critical points of φ correspond to the cores of symplectic handles; the index of a critical point is at most half the dimension of W. Weinstein’s 1991 construction shows that any Stein manifold carries a Weinstein structure, and conversely every Weinstein manifold is homotopy equivalent to a CW complex of dimension ≤ n. The Weinstein conjecture (proved by Viterbo for subcritical Stein manifolds and by Taubes in dimension three using Seiberg‑Witten theory) asserts that every contact type hypersurface in a symplectic manifold carries a closed Reeb orbit. Morse‑Bott techniques applied to the contact action functional give a chain complex whose homology is the contact homology; the differential counts pseudoholomorphic curves in the symplectization. The existence of a closed Reeb orbit follows from the non‑vanishing of the contact homology unit. In higher dimensions, the flexible/rigid dichotomy for Weinstein handles (indices < n versus index n) governs the h‑principle: subcritical Weinstein manifolds are classified up to deformation by their homotopy type, while critical handles encode symplectic rigidity. This interplay between Morse theory, handle decompositions, and pseudoholomorphic curves is the engine behind modern symplectic topology.

Computational Morse Theory and Discrete Morse Functions

Discrete Morse theory, introduced by Forman in 1998, translates smooth Morse theory to finite cell complexes. A discrete Morse function on a regular CW complex K assigns a real number to each cell such that for every cell σ the number of faces τ ⊂ σ with f(τ) ≥ f(σ) is at most one, and the number of cofaces σ ⊃ τ with f(σ) ≤ f(τ) is at most one. Critical cells are those where both counts are zero. The discrete Morse inequalities state that the number of critical cells of dimension k is at least the k‑th Betti number of K. A discrete gradient vector field is a collection of pairs (τ, σ) with τ a face of σ, each cell appearing in at most one pair; the unpaired cells are precisely the critical cells. Forman proved that a discrete gradient vector field determines a homotopy equivalence between K and a CW complex having one cell for each critical cell. This yields an algorithmic way to simplify complexes: by cancelling pairs of critical cells connected by a unique gradient path one obtains a smaller complex with the same homology. In computational topology, discrete Morse theory underpins persistent homology software (e.g., Dionysus, PHAT) where a filtration of simplicial complexes is reduced by discrete Morse collapses before computing persistence diagrams. The theory also extends to Morse‑Bott discrete functions where critical sets are subcomplexes, and to multi‑parameter filtrations via discrete Morse‑Bott theory. Recent work connects discrete Morse theory to the combinatorial Laplacian and to the Witten deformation on finite graphs, providing a fully finite‑dimensional analogue of the analytic proofs of the Morse inequalities.

  • Confusing Morse‑Bott critical submanifolds with degenerate isolated critical points — the Hessian must be non‑degenerate in normal directions.
  • Assuming Cerf theory works in dimension four exactly as in higher dimensions; the failure of the Whitney trick creates exotic phenomena.
  • Neglecting the relative boundary conditions when applying Morse theory to manifolds with boundary; the attaching spheres lie in the interior of the boundary of the sublevel set.
  • Thinking every symplectic handle is a Weinstein handle — only indices ≤ n occur, and critical handles (index n) are rigid.
  • Believing discrete Morse theory requires a triangulation; it works on any regular CW complex, including cubical complexes used in image analysis.
  • Overlooking that the discrete Morse inequalities are equalities for a perfect discrete Morse function, which exists for collapsible complexes.
  • Misapplying the h‑cobordism theorem to non‑simply‑connected cobordisms without invoking the s‑cobordism theorem and Whitehead torsion.

hand/etale-cohomology.html:
The Six Operations Formalism and Constructible Sheaves

The Grothendieck six operations — f*, f!, f*, f!, ⊗, and Hom — form the categorical backbone of étale cohomology. For a morphism f: X → Y of schemes, the derived functors Rf* and Rf! map the bounded derived category of constructible ℓ-adic sheaves Dcb(X, ℚℓ) to Dcb(Y, ℚℓ). The functors f* and f! are their left and right adjoints respectively. The tensor product ⊗ and internal Hom provide a symmetric monoidal structure compatible with the adjunctions. Constructible sheaves are those whose stalks are finite-dimensional ℚℓ-vector spaces and which become locally constant on a stratification by locally closed subschemes. This class is stable under all six operations, a theorem proved by Deligne in SGA 4½ and SGA 5. The proper base change theorem asserts that for a proper morphism f, the natural map g*Rf* → Rf'*g'* is an isomorphism for any cartesian square. The smooth base change theorem gives a similar isomorphism for smooth morphisms, but with f* replaced by f! up to a Tate twist. The projection formula Rf*(K ⊗ f*L) ≅ Rf*K ⊗ L holds for K ∈ Dcb(X) and L ∈ Dcb(Y). Verdier duality provides a canonical isomorphism Rf! ≅ DYRf*DX, where D denotes the dualizing functor. These formalism allow one to compute cohomology of complicated varieties by decomposing them into simpler pieces via stratifications and excision sequences.

Weights, Purity, and the Theory of Mixed Sheaves

Deligne's theory of weights, developed in Weil II, assigns to each constructible ℓ-adic sheaf a weight filtration compatible with the six operations. A sheaf is pure of weight w if all eigenvalues of geometric Frobenius on its stalks are algebraic numbers whose complex absolute values equal qw/2 for every finite field 𝔽q over which the sheaf is defined. The constant sheaf ℚℓ on a smooth projective variety is pure of weight 0. The Tate twist ℚℓ(1) has weight −2. For a smooth projective variety X of dimension n, the cohomology groups Hi(X, ℚℓ) are pure of weight i. Mixed sheaves are those admitting a finite filtration whose graded pieces are pure of successive weights. The category of mixed sheaves is abelian and stable under the six operations. The weight spectral sequence associated to a simplicial resolution of a variety converges to the cohomology of the variety and degenerates at E2 for proper varieties. This machinery underlies Deligne's proof of the Weil conjectures: the hard Lefschetz theorem and the Hodge-Riemann bilinear relations are replaced by the existence of a Lefschetz operator on the weight filtration and the positivity of the induced pairing on primitive parts. The theory also yields the decomposition theorem for proper maps: Rf*ℚℓ splits as a direct sum of shifted intersection cohomology complexes, each pure of a known weight.

Worked Example: Weight of a Tate Twist
Let X be a smooth projective curve over 𝔽q. Determine the weight of the sheaf ℚℓ(1) on X and explain how it affects the eigenvalues of Frobenius on H1(X, ℚℓ(1)).
The Tate twist ℚℓ(1) is defined as the inverse limit of the ℓ-power roots of unity tensored with ℚℓ. Its weight is −2 because the cyclotomic character χℓ: Gal(𝔽̄q/𝔽q) → ℤℓ× sends geometric Frobenius to q−1, so the eigenvalues on ℚℓ(1) are q−1, whose absolute value is q−1 = q(−2)/2. By the Künneth formula and the fact that H1(X, ℚℓ) is pure of weight 1, the twist shifts the weight by −2, making H1(X, ℚℓ(1)) pure of weight −1. Consequently, the eigenvalues of Frobenius on this group have absolute value q−1/2.
Exam Strategy
When a question asks for the weight of a cohomology group with a Tate twist, remember that each twist by (1) subtracts 2 from the weight. For a smooth projective variety of dimension n, Hi(X, ℚℓ(m)) has weight i − 2m. This rule applies even when the variety is not defined over a finite field, provided one works with the appropriate Galois representation.

Nearby Cycles, Vanishing Cycles, and the Monodromy Filtration

Let f: X → S be a morphism with S the spectrum of a henselian discrete valuation ring, generic point η and closed point s. The nearby cycles functor Ψf and vanishing cycles functor Φf relate the étale cohomology of the generic fibre Xη to that of the special fibre Xs. For a sheaf F on Xη, ΨfF is a sheaf on Xs equipped with an action of the inertia group I. The vanishing cycles ΦfF fits into a distinguished triangle ΨfF → ΦfF → i*F → ΨfF[1], where i: Xs → X is the inclusion. The monodromy operator N = log(Tu) (with Tu the unipotent part of the inertia action) is nilpotent and defines the monodromy filtration M• on ΨfF. The weight filtration on the nearby cycles coincides with the monodromy filtration shifted by the relative dimension, a result known as the weight-monodromy conjecture, proved by Rapoport-Zink for abelian varieties and by Ito for semi-stable reduction. In the semi-stable case, the Clemens-Schmid exact sequence connects the cohomology of the generic fibre, the special fibre, and the vanishing cycles, mirroring the classical topology of degenerations. These tools are essential for studying the ℓ-adic cohomology of families of varieties and for proving local-global compatibility in the Langlands program.

Comparison Theorems: Étale, Crystalline, and de Rham Cohomology

For a smooth proper variety X over a p-adic field K with ring of integers OK and residue field k, several cohomology theories coexist: ℓ-adic étale cohomology Hiét(XK̄, ℚℓ) for ℓ ≠ p, crystalline cohomology Hicrys(Xk/W(k)) ⊗ ℚp, and de Rham cohomology HidR(X/K). The Fontaine-Messing and Faltings comparison theorems provide canonical, Galois-equivariant isomorphisms Hiét(XK̄, ℚp) ⊗ℚp Bcrys ≅ Hicrys(Xk/W(k)) ⊗W(k) Bcrys and Hiét(XK̄, ℚp) ⊗ℚp BdR ≅ HidR(X/K) ⊗K BdR, where Bcrys and BdR are Fontaine's period rings. These isomorphisms respect filtrations, Frobenius, and monodromy operators. The Hodge-Tate decomposition Hiét(XK̄, ℚp) ⊗ ℂp ≅ ⊕j Hi−j(X, Ωj) ⊗ ℂp(−j) follows from the de Rham comparison. For varieties with good reduction, the crystalline comparison shows that the ℓ-adic representation is crystalline, hence potentially semi-stable. The p-adic Hodge theory of Fontaine classifies such representations via filtered (φ, N)-modules. These comparisons are the arithmetic analogue of the classical comparison between singular and de Rham cohomology over ℂ, and they underpin the proof of the local Langlands correspondence for GLn and the modularity of Galois representations.

The Tate Conjecture, Galois Representations, and the Langlands Correspondence over Function Fields

The Tate conjecture predicts that for a smooth projective variety X over a finitely generated field k, the cycle class map CHc(X) ⊗ ℚℓ → H2cét(Xk̄, ℚℓ(c))Gk is surjective. In other words, every Galois-invariant cohomology class of the appropriate weight comes from an algebraic cycle. This is known for abelian varieties (Faltings), K3 surfaces over finite fields (Nygaard-Ogus), and certain Shimura varieties (Kisin). The conjecture is equivalent to the semisimplicity of the Galois representation on the ℓ-adic cohomology and to the finite generation of the Chow groups modulo homological equivalence. Over function fields, the Langlands correspondence, proved by Drinfeld for GL2 and by Lafforgue for GLn, establishes a bijection between irreducible ℓ-adic local systems on a curve and automorphic representations of GLn over the function field. The geometric Langlands program, formulated by Beilinson and Drinfeld, replaces ℓ-adic sheaves by D-modules on the moduli stack of bundles. The cohomology of Shimura varieties carries an action of the Hecke algebra and the Galois group, realizing the local Langlands correspondence in the cohomology of the special fibre (Harris-Taylor, Scholze). The trace formula for stacks and the theory of perverse sheaves on the moduli stack of shtukas are the modern tools that connect the Tate conjecture to the Langlands program. These deep interactions show that étale cohomology is not merely a cohomology theory but a bridge between arithmetic geometry, representation theory, and number theory.

  • Confusing the weight of a Tate twist: each (1) subtracts 2, not 1.
  • Assuming the six operations hold for all sheaves; they require constructibility.
  • Neglecting the monodromy filtration when applying nearby cycles; the weight-monodromy conjecture is not a theorem in general.
  • Mixing ℓ-adic and p-adic comparison theorems without checking the reduction type (good, semi-stable, etc.).
  • Stating the Tate conjecture as a theorem for all varieties; it remains open in general.
  • Overlooking the role of the inertia group in the nearby cycles functor; the action is essential for the monodromy operator.
  • These traps illustrate the subtlety of the subject.

hand/category-theory.html:
Monoidal Categories and Coherence

A monoidal category equips a category C with a bifunctor ⊗ : C × C → C, a unit object I, and natural isomorphisms expressing associativity (α), left unit (λ) and right unit (ρ). The coherence theorem of Mac Lane (1963) states that any diagram built from α, λ, ρ and identities commutes, so one may treat ⊗ as strictly associative and unital for calculational purposes. This strictification underlies the graphical language of string diagrams used in quantum information and topological quantum field theory.

Strict vs. Weak Monoidal Structures

A strict monoidal category has α, λ, ρ as identities. Every monoidal category is monoidally equivalent to a strict one (Mac Lane’s strictification). In practice, the weak structure is essential: the category of vector spaces with the usual tensor product is not strict because (U ⊗ V) ⊗ W and U ⊗ (V ⊗ W) are canonically isomorphic but not equal. The associator αU,V,W : (U ⊗ V) ⊗ W → U ⊗ (V ⊗ W) is the canonical linear isomorphism sending (u ⊗ v) ⊗ w to u ⊗ (v ⊗ w).

Braided and Symmetric Monoidal Categories

A braiding is a natural isomorphism βX,Y : X ⊗ Y → Y ⊗ X satisfying the hexagon axioms. If βY,X ∘ βX,Y = idX⊗Y the braiding is symmetric. The category of representations of a quantum group is braided but not symmetric; the category of finite‑dimensional vector spaces over a field with the usual tensor product is symmetric. Braided monoidal categories give rise to invariants of knots and links via the Reshetikhin–Turaev construction.

Monoidal Functors and Monoid Objects

A lax monoidal functor (F, φ, φ₀) between monoidal categories preserves the tensor product up to coherent morphisms φX,Y : F(X) ⊗ F(Y) → F(X ⊗ Y) and φ₀ : I → F(I). A monoid object in a monoidal category (C, ⊗, I) consists of an object M with multiplication μ : M ⊗ M → M and unit η : I → M satisfying associativity and unit diagrams. In Set with cartesian product, monoid objects are ordinary monoids; in Ab with tensor product, they are rings; in Cat with cartesian product, they are strict monoidal categories.

Kan Extensions and the Yoneda Embedding

Given functors F : C → D and K : C → E, a left Kan extension Lan_K F : E → D is a functor equipped with a universal natural transformation η : F → (Lan_K F) ∘ K. Dually, a right Kan extension Ran_K F satisfies a universal property with a transformation ε : (Ran_K F) ∘ K → F. When they exist, Kan extensions are unique up to unique isomorphism. They subsume limits, colimits, adjoints, and the Yoneda embedding.

Pointwise Formula

If D is cocomplete, the left Kan extension can be computed pointwise as a colimit: (Lan_K F)(e) ≅ colim(c, u : K(c) → e) F(c). Dually, if D is complete, (Ran_K F)(e) ≅ lim(c, u : e → K(c)) F(c). These formulas show that Kan extensions are “best approximations” of F along K, extending the idea of extending a function defined on a subset to the whole set.

Yoneda Embedding as a Kan Extension

The Yoneda embedding y : C → [C^op, Set] sends an object c to the representable functor Hom_C(−, c). It is the left Kan extension of the identity functor id_C : C → C along itself: y ≅ Lanid_C id_C. This perspective explains why representables are “free” cocompletions: the presheaf category [C^op, Set] is the free cocompletion of C, and y is the universal functor from C into a cocomplete category.

Adjoints via Kan Extensions

A functor G : D → C has a left adjoint F iff the left Kan extension Lan_G id_D exists and is preserved by G; then F ≅ Lan_G id_D. Similarly, a right adjoint exists iff the right Kan extension Ran_G id_D exists and is preserved by G. This characterisation makes the adjoint functor theorems concrete: existence of certain (co)limits guarantees adjoints.

Worked Example: Computing a Left Kan Extension
Let C be the category with two objects 0,1 and a single non‑identity arrow f : 0 → 1. Let D = Set. Define F : C → Set by F(0) = {a}, F(1) = {b,c}, and F(f)(a) = b. Let K : C → E be the inclusion of C into the category E which adds a new object 2 and an arrow g : 1 → 2 (no other new arrows). Compute (Lan_K F)(2).
The comma category (K ↓ 2) has objects (c, u : K(c) → 2). Since K is inclusion, the only arrows to 2 in E are g : 1 → 2 and the composite g∘f : 0 → 2. Thus objects are (1, g) and (0, g∘f). There is a unique morphism (0, g∘f) → (1, g) induced by f. The diagram for the colimit is F(0) → F(1) sending a ↦ b. The colimit of this diagram in Set is the coequaliser of the two parallel maps from the coproduct F(0) ⊔ F(1) to the quotient identifying a with b. Concretely, the colimit set is {b,c} with a identified to b, i.e. a two‑element set {b,c}. Hence (Lan_K F)(2) ≅ {b,c}.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question asks for a Kan extension, first check whether the target category has the required (co)limits. If it does, write the pointwise (co)limit formula; the universal property then guarantees the answer. Remember that the Yoneda embedding is the left Kan extension of the identity along itself — this single fact often unlocks several sub‑questions.

Topos Theory and Internal Logic

A topos is a category that behaves like the category of sets: it has finite limits, exponentials, and a subobject classifier Ω. The prototypical example is Set; other examples include presheaf categories [C^op, Set], sheaf categories on a topological space, and the effective topos. Lawvere and Tierney (1970s) showed that every topos carries an internal higher‑order intuitionistic logic, allowing one to reason “as if” one were in Set while the external semantics may be vastly different.

Subobject Classifier and Truth Values

The subobject classifier Ω is an object equipped with a monomorphism true : 1 → Ω such that for every monomorphism m : A → X there is a unique characteristic morphism χ_m : X → Ω making a pullback square. In Set, Ω = {0,1} and true picks out 1. In a presheaf topos, Ω assigns to each object c the set of sieves on c; truth values become “local” and vary with context.

Internal Language and Mitchell–Bénabou Semantics

The internal language of a topos is a typed λ‑calculus with dependent types, where types correspond to objects, terms to morphisms, and propositions to subobjects. The logical connectives are interpreted via the Heyting algebra structure on Sub(X) for each X. Quantifiers arise from adjoints to pullback functors: ∃_f ⊣ f^* ⊣ ∀_f for a morphism f : X → Y. This makes it possible to prove theorems in a topos by ordinary logical deduction, then interpret the proof externally.

Geometric Morphisms and Classifying Toposes

A geometric morphism f : E → F consists of an adjoint pair (f^*, f_*) with f^* left exact. Geometric morphisms are the “maps” between toposes; they correspond to models of geometric theories. For any geometric theory T, there is a classifying topos Set[T] such that geometric morphisms E → Set[T] correspond to T‑models in E. This bridges syntax and semantics: the topos of sheaves on the Zariski site classifies local rings, the topos of G‑sets classifies groups with a G‑action, etc.

Higher Categories and ∞‑Groupoids

Ordinary categories have objects and 1‑morphisms. A 2‑category adds 2‑morphisms between 1‑morphisms, with vertical and horizontal composition satisfying interchange. Iterating yields n‑categories. The limit n → ∞ gives ∞‑categories, where all higher morphisms are invertible up to coherent equivalence — these are ∞‑groupoids. By the homotopy hypothesis (Grothendieck, 1983; proved by Joyal–Tierney, Lurie), ∞‑groupoids model homotopy types of topological spaces.

Quasi‑Categories and the Joyal Model Structure

A quasi‑category is a simplicial set satisfying the inner horn filling condition: every inner horn Λ^n_k → X (0 < k < n) extends to an n‑simplex. This encodes composition of 1‑morphisms up to coherent higher homotopies. The Joyal model structure on simplicial sets has quasi‑categories as fibrant objects; weak equivalences are categorical equivalences. This provides a concrete combinatorial model for (∞,1)‑categories used in derived algebraic geometry and higher algebra.

∞‑Topoi and Higher Sheaf Theory

An ∞‑topos is an ∞‑category of sheaves of ∞‑groupoids on an ∞‑site. Lurie’s “Higher Topos Theory” (2009) develops the analogue of Grothendieck topoi: ∞‑topoi have all small limits and colimits, a subobject classifier (now an object of ∞‑groupoids), and an internal higher‑order logic with homotopy‑type‑theoretic interpretation. The ∞‑topos of sheaves on a topological space X with values in ∞‑groupoids recovers the classical homotopy theory of X, while the ∞‑topos of ∞‑groupoids itself is the “base” ∞‑topos.

Applications to Homotopy Type Theory

Homotopy type theory (HoTT) interprets Martin‑Löf type theory in ∞‑groupoids: types are ∞‑groupoids, terms are points, identity types are path spaces. The univalence axiom states that equivalence of types corresponds to equality, which holds in any ∞‑topos. This gives a synthetic foundation where higher‑dimensional mathematics (e.g., higher homotopy groups of spheres) can be formalised directly in a proof assistant such as Coq or Agda.

  • Confusing a monoidal category with a monoid object — the former is a category with a tensor product, the latter is an object inside such a category equipped with multiplication and unit.
  • Assuming every Kan extension exists — pointwise formulas require the target category to have the relevant (co)limits; without them the extension may not exist.
  • Treating the subobject classifier Ω as a two‑element set in every topos — in a general topos Ω can be a large Heyting algebra varying with context.
  • Believing that geometric morphisms are just functors preserving limits — the inverse image part must be left exact, and the direct image part is its right adjoint; both conditions are essential.
  • Equating ∞‑groupoids with ordinary groupoids — ∞‑groupoids contain non‑trivial higher homotopies (2‑morphisms, 3‑morphisms, …) that ordinary groupoids lack.
  • Thinking that the Yoneda embedding is always full and faithful only for locally small categories — it is full and faithful for any category, but the codomain [C^op, Set] may not be a set‑valued functor category if C is large.
  • Overlooking the coherence conditions for braided monoidal categories — the hexagon axioms are not automatic consequences of naturality; they must be verified.

These advanced topics form the backbone of modern categorical research and appear regularly in higher‑level examinations.

hand/acoustics.html:
Nonlinear Acoustic Phenomena and Shock Wave Formation

When the acoustic pressure amplitude becomes a significant fraction of the ambient pressure, the linear approximation that underlies the simple wave equation breaks down. The equation of state for a fluid relates pressure p and density ρ through the adiabatic bulk modulus B. For finite‑amplitude waves the local sound speed c = √(∂p/∂ρ) depends on the instantaneous pressure, so compressional parts of the waveform travel faster than rarefaction parts. This steepening leads to the formation of a discontinuity — a shock front — after a characteristic distance known as the shock formation distance Lsh = c³/(β ω p0), where β = (γ+1)/2 is the coefficient of nonlinearity for an ideal gas (γ = ratio of specific heats) and p0 is the peak pressure amplitude. In air at 20 °C, β ≈ 1.2. The shock thickness is set by dissipative mechanisms — classical viscosity, thermal conduction, and molecular relaxation — and typically lies in the micrometre range for audible frequencies. The Rankine‑Hugoniot jump conditions across a normal shock give the pressure ratio p2/p1 = 1 + 2γ/(γ+1) (M²−1), where M is the Mach number of the shock relative to the upstream medium. For weak shocks (M → 1) the pressure jump is linear in (M−1); for strong shocks the pressure rises sharply. Practical consequences include sonic booms from supersonic aircraft, the “N‑wave” signature measured on the ground, and the design of high‑intensity focused ultrasound (HIFU) where controlled shock formation enhances tissue ablation. Examiners often test the distinction between the acoustic Mach number Ma = u/c (particle velocity over sound speed) and the shock Mach number, and they may ask for the distance at which a 1 kHz, 150 dB source in air forms a shock (≈ 30 m).

Acoustic Impedance Matching and Transducer Design

The specific acoustic impedance Z = ρc of a medium determines how much of an incident wave is transmitted across a boundary. For a plane wave normally incident from medium 1 (impedance Z1) onto medium 2 (Z2), the pressure transmission coefficient is Tp = 2Z2/(Z1+Z2) and the intensity transmission coefficient is TI = 4Z1Z2/(Z1+Z2)². Maximum power transfer occurs when Z1 = Z2 (impedance matching). In medical ultrasound the piezoelectric ceramic (PZT) has Z ≈ 30 MRayl, while soft tissue is ≈ 1.5 MRayl; a single quarter‑wave matching layer of impedance √(ZPZTZtissue) ≈ 6.7 MRayl and thickness λ/4 at the centre frequency reduces the reflection coefficient from ≈ 0.9 to ≈ 0.1. Multi‑layer matching (binomial or Chebyshev designs) broadens the bandwidth. The electromechanical coupling coefficient kt of the piezoelectric material governs the fractional bandwidth Δf/f ≈ kt/√(1−kt²). For PZT‑5H, kt ≈ 0.5 giving ≈ 55 % fractional bandwidth. Backing material (often a tungsten‑epoxy composite) is chosen to absorb the backward‑propagating wave, setting the pulse length and thus axial resolution. The electrical impedance of the transducer near resonance is modelled by the Mason equivalent circuit: a motional branch (Lm, Cm, Rm) in parallel with the clamped capacitance C0. Matching the electrical impedance to the 50 Ω system using an inductive network maximises signal‑to‑noise ratio. Examiner traps include confusing the acoustic intensity transmission coefficient with the pressure transmission coefficient, and forgetting that the quarter‑wave condition holds only at the design frequency; off‑centre frequencies see a phase shift that degrades matching.

Worked Example: Quarter‑Wave Matching Layer
A 5 MHz ultrasound transducer uses a PZT ceramic (Z = 30 MRayl) coupled to soft tissue (Z = 1.5 MRayl). Determine the required acoustic impedance and physical thickness of a single quarter‑wave matching layer made of epoxy (sound speed 2500 m/s).
The optimal matching impedance is Zm = √(ZPZT·Ztissue) = √(30 × 1.5) MRayl = √45 MRayl ≈ 6.7 MRayl. The wavelength in epoxy at 5 MHz is λ = c/f = 2500 / 5×10⁶ = 0.5 mm. Quarter‑wave thickness = λ/4 = 0.125 mm = 125 µm. Thus a 125 µm epoxy layer with impedance ≈ 6.7 MRayl provides near‑perfect transmission at 5 MHz.
Exam‑Day Strategy
When a question asks for “maximum power transfer” across an acoustic interface, immediately write the impedance‑matching condition Z₁ = Z₂ and the intensity transmission formula. If a matching layer is mentioned, compute its impedance as the geometric mean and its thickness as λ/4 in that layer. Keep a mental table of typical impedances: air 0.0004 MRayl, water 1.5 MRayl, soft tissue 1.5 MRayl, bone 7.8 MRayl, PZT 30 MRayl. This avoids unit‑conversion errors under time pressure.

Environmental Noise Metrics and Assessment Standards

Environmental noise assessment relies on metrics that compress time‑varying sound pressure levels into single numbers suitable for regulation. The equivalent continuous sound level Leq,T = 10 log₁₀( (1/T) ∫₀ᵀ 10L(t)/10 dt ) averages energy over the measurement period T. For community noise the day‑evening‑night level Lden applies a 5 dB penalty to evening (19:00–23:00) and a 10 dB penalty to night (23:00–07:00) periods: Lden = 10 log₁₀( (12·10Lday/10 + 4·10(Leve+5)/10 + 8·10(Lnight+10)/10) / 24 ). The day‑night level Ldn used in the United States applies only a 10 dB night penalty. Percentile levels LN (e.g., L10, L50, L90) describe the statistical distribution; L10 approximates the level exceeded 10 % of the time (traffic peaks), while L90 represents the background. The sound exposure level SEL = Leq + 10 log₁₀(T/T₀) normalises a transient event to a 1‑second reference, enabling comparison of aircraft flyovers or construction blasts. Standards such as ISO 1996‑2, ISO 9613‑2 (outdoor propagation), and the EU Environmental Noise Directive (2002/49/EC) prescribe measurement procedures, microphone height (1.2–1.5 m), and weather corrections (wind ≤ 5 m/s, no rain). The propagation model in ISO 9613‑2 splits attenuation into geometric spreading (6 dB per doubling of distance for a point source), atmospheric absorption (frequency‑dependent, ≈ 1 dB/100 m at 1 kHz, 20 °C, 70 % RH), ground effect (interference between direct and reflected rays), and barrier diffraction (Fresnel number N = 2δ/λ, where δ is path‑length difference). Examiners frequently ask to compute Lden from given Lday, Leve, Lnight values, or to estimate the insertion loss of a 3 m high barrier for a 500 Hz tone at 50 m distance (≈ 10 dB using the Maekawa chart).

Psychoacoustic Modeling and Perceptual Coding

Human hearing does not respond linearly to physical intensity; the auditory system performs a frequency‑dependent, level‑dependent analysis that can be exploited for data compression. The critical band concept divides the cochlea into overlapping filters of bandwidth ≈ 100 Hz below 500 Hz and ≈ 1/3 octave above. Within a critical band, simultaneous tones mask each other; the masking threshold is raised by the masker level according to the spreading function (≈ 27 dB/octave upward, 10 dB/octave downward). Temporal masking occurs when a loud sound precedes (forward masking, up to 200 ms) or follows (backward masking, < 20 ms) a softer signal. The equal‑loudness contours (ISO 226:2003) define the phon scale: a 1 kHz tone at 40 dB SPL is 40 phon; other frequencies require different SPLs to match loudness. The sone scale linearises loudness: 1 sone = 40 phon, doubling of loudness ≈ 10 phon. Perceptual codecs (MP3, AAC, Opus) use a filter bank (MDCT) to transform blocks of 576 or 1024 samples into frequency coefficients, compute the masking threshold for each band using a psychoacoustic model (e.g., MPEG‑1 Layer III model 1), and quantise coefficients below the threshold to zero. Bit allocation follows the “water‑filling” principle: more bits to bands where the signal‑to‑mask ratio is high. Joint stereo coding exploits inter‑channel correlation (mid/side coding) and intensity stereo for high frequencies where binaural cues are less critical. The typical transparent bitrate for stereo music is 128–192 kbps (MP3) or 96–128 kbps (AAC). Examiner questions may ask to estimate the masking threshold for a 1 kHz, 60 dB SPL tone masking a 1.2 kHz probe (≈ 30 dB below masker), or to explain why MP3 at 64 kbps produces audible pre‑echo on transient signals (insufficient time resolution of the long MDCT window).

Acoustic Metamaterials and Negative Refraction

Acoustic metamaterials are engineered structures whose effective dynamic mass density ρeff(ω) and bulk modulus Beff(ω) can become simultaneously negative over a frequency band, yielding a negative refractive index n = √(ρeff/Beff) < 0. The simplest unit cell combines a Helmholtz resonator (providing negative Beff near its resonance) with a membrane‑type mass‑spring system (providing negative ρeff near its anti‑resonance). When both resonances overlap, the dispersion relation ω(k) bends backward: the group velocity vg = dω/dk points opposite to the phase velocity vp = ω/k. This enables sub‑wavelength imaging (superlensing) because evanescent components are amplified inside the slab. The first experimental demonstration (2004) used an array of split‑tube resonators in water, achieving n ≈ −1 at 40 kHz. Practical challenges include high losses (imaginary parts of ρeff and Beff), narrow bandwidth (Δf/f ≈ 0.05), and fabrication tolerances. Gradient‑index (GRIN) acoustic lenses built from spatially varying unit cells can focus sound beyond the diffraction limit, with applications in high‑resolution ultrasound and non‑destructive testing. Another class, space‑coiling metamaterials, folds the acoustic path into a compact volume, achieving an effective refractive index up to 50 while maintaining low loss. Examiner traps: confusing negative refractive index with negative group velocity alone (both ρeff and Beff must be negative), and assuming that a single Helmholtz resonator array yields negative refraction (it only gives negative bulk modulus). Questions may ask to sketch the dispersion diagram for a double‑negative metamaterial and indicate the backward‑wave region.

  • Confusing pressure transmission coefficient with intensity transmission coefficient at an impedance boundary.
  • Applying the quarter‑wave matching condition at frequencies far from the design centre frequency.
  • Mixing up Lden (5 dB evening + 10 dB night penalties) with Ldn (10 dB night only).
  • Assuming a single Helmholtz resonator provides negative refractive index; both effective density and bulk modulus must be negative.
  • Neglecting temporal masking asymmetry (forward masking lasts ≫ backward masking) in perceptual coding questions.
  • Using the free‑field 6 dB/doubling rule for line sources (which follow 3 dB/doubling) in outdoor propagation calculations.
  • Forgetting that the shock formation distance scales inversely with frequency and pressure amplitude, leading to order‑of‑magnitude errors in sonic‑boom estimates.
