hand/tensor-categories.html:
Pivotal and Spherical Structures in Fusion Categories

A pivotal structure on a monoidal category C is a monoidal natural isomorphism a : Id → (−)** between the identity functor and the double dual functor. In a rigid monoidal category every object X has a left dual *X and a right dual X*; the pivotal isomorphism identifies X with its double dual *(X*) in a way compatible with the tensor product. The existence of a pivotal structure is not automatic, but Etingof, Nikshych and Ostrik proved that every fusion category over an algebraically closed field of characteristic zero admits at least one pivotal structure. Once a pivotal structure is chosen, one can define the left and right categorical traces of an endomorphism f : X → X by composing with the evaluation and coevaluation maps and the pivotal isomorphism. The left dimension dimL(X) = TrL(idX) and the right dimension dimR(X) = TrR(idX) are then well defined.

A pivotal category is called spherical when the left and right traces coincide for every morphism, equivalently dimL(X) = dimR(X) for all objects. In a spherical fusion category the categorical dimension dim(X) is a real number (in fact an algebraic integer) and satisfies dim(X ⊗ Y) = dim(X) dim(Y). The global dimension of the category is the sum of squares of the dimensions of the simple objects: dim(C) = Σi dim(Xi)². A fundamental result of Etingof, Nikshych and Ostrik states that a fusion category is pseudo‑unitary — i.e. its Frobenius‑Perron dimensions coincide with its categorical dimensions for some pivotal structure — if and only if it admits a spherical structure with positive dimensions. In that case the Frobenius‑Perron dimension FPdim(X) equals the categorical dimension dim(X) and the global Frobenius‑Perron dimension equals the global categorical dimension. The spherical condition is essential for the construction of the Reshetikhin‑Turaev TQFT, because the TQFT assigns to a closed surface the vector space of conformal blocks whose dimension is computed using the categorical trace.

Not every pivotal structure is spherical. For example, the category of representations of a finite group G with the standard pivotal structure coming from the vector space dual is spherical, but if one twists the pivotal structure by a non‑trivial group character the resulting pivotal category is not spherical. The classification of pivotal structures on a given fusion category is controlled by the group of monoidal automorphisms of the identity functor, which is isomorphic to the group of invertible objects in the Drinfeld center. This interplay between pivotal structures, spherical structures and the center is a recurring theme in the theory of tensor categories.

The Verlinde Formula and Modular Data

In a modular tensor category the modular data consists of two matrices S and T indexed by the isomorphism classes of simple objects. The S-matrix entries are defined by the categorical trace of the double braiding: Sij = Tr(cXj*,Xi ∘ cXi,Xj*). The T-matrix is diagonal with entries Tij = δij θi, where θi is the twist (the eigenvalue of the braiding cXi,Xi). These matrices satisfy the projective relations of the modular group SL(2,ℤ): S² = (ST)³ = C, where C is the charge conjugation matrix Cij = δi,j*. The S-matrix is symmetric and unitary, and its first row (or column) contains the quantum dimensions of the simple objects up to the global dimension factor: S0i = dim(Xi) / √dim(C).

The Verlinde formula expresses the fusion coefficients entirely in terms of the S-matrix: Nijk = Σm (Sim Sjm Skm*) / S0m. This formula shows that the fusion rules are completely determined by the modular data. Conversely, the S-matrix diagonalizes the fusion matrices: (Ni)jk = Nijk have eigenvalues Sim / S0m with eigenvectors given by the columns of S. The Verlinde formula is a powerful computational tool; for instance, in the Fibonacci modular tensor category with simple objects {1, τ} the S-matrix is (1/√(φ+2)) [[1, φ], [φ, -1]] where φ = (1+√5)/2. Applying the Verlinde formula yields the single non‑trivial fusion rule τ ⊗ τ ≅ 1 ⊕ τ. The formula also implies that the fusion ring is commutative and associative, and that the Frobenius‑Perron dimension of each simple object equals its quantum dimension in a unitary modular tensor category.

Beyond computation, the Verlinde formula underlies the classification program for modular tensor categories. Two modular tensor categories with the same modular data are equivalent as braided fusion categories (a theorem of Bruillard, Ng, Rowell and Wang). Thus the pair (S, T) is a complete invariant for unitary modular tensor categories. The modular data also appears in rational conformal field theory, where the S and T matrices are the modular transformations of the characters of the chiral algebra. This deep connection explains why the same algebraic structures govern both topological quantum field theories and two‑dimensional conformal field theories.

Worked Example: Verlinde Formula for the Fibonacci Category
The Fibonacci modular tensor category has simple objects 1 and τ with quantum dimensions dim(1)=1, dim(τ)=φ where φ=(1+√5)/2. Its S-matrix is S = (1/√(φ+2)) [[1, φ], [φ, -1]]. Use the Verlinde formula to compute the fusion coefficient Nτττ.
The Verlinde formula reads Nijk = Σm (Sim Sjm Skm*) / S0m. Here the index 0 corresponds to the unit object 1. We need i=j=k=τ. The sum runs over m ∈ {1, τ}. Compute Sτ1 = φ/√(φ+2), Sττ = -1/√(φ+2), S01 = 1/√(φ+2), S0τ = φ/√(φ+2). Then Nτττ = (Sτ1 Sτ1 Sτ1*)/S01 + (Sττ Sττ Sττ*)/S0τ. Since all entries are real, * is identity. First term: (φ/√(φ+2))³ / (1/√(φ+2)) = φ³/(φ+2). Second term: (-1/√(φ+2))³ / (φ/√(φ+2)) = -1/(φ(φ+2)). Using φ² = φ+1, φ³ = φ(φ+1) = φ²+φ = 2φ+1. Then φ³/(φ+2) = (2φ+1)/(φ+2). Also -1/(φ(φ+2)) = -1/(φ²+2φ) = -1/((φ+1)+2φ) = -1/(3φ+1). Summing gives (2φ+1)/(φ+2) - 1/(3φ+1). Put over common denominator (φ+2)(3φ+1): numerator = (2φ+1)(3φ+1) - (φ+2) = (6φ²+5φ+1) - φ -2 = 6(φ+1)+4φ-1 = 6φ+6+4φ-1 = 10φ+5 = 5(2φ+1). Denominator = (φ+2)(3φ+1) = 3φ²+7φ+2 = 3(φ+1)+7φ+2 = 10φ+5. Hence the ratio equals 1. Therefore Nτττ = 1, confirming the fusion rule τ ⊗ τ ≅ 1 ⊕ τ.
Exam Strategy
Memorize the Verlinde formula and the modular group relations S² = (ST)³ = C. Questions often ask to derive a fusion coefficient from a given S-matrix or to verify that a candidate S-matrix satisfies unitarity and the modular relations. Practice the Fibonacci and Ising S-matrices; they appear repeatedly in problem sets.

Drinfeld Center Construction and Modular Tensor Categories

The Drinfeld center Z(C) of a monoidal category C is the category whose objects are pairs (Z, γ) where Z is an object of C and γ is a half‑braiding, i.e. a natural isomorphism γX : Z ⊗ X → X ⊗ Z satisfying the hexagon condition γX⊗Y = (idX ⊗ γY) ∘ (γX ⊗ idY). Morphisms are those in C that intertwine the half‑braidings. The tensor product in Z(C) is defined by (Z, γ) ⊗ (Z', γ') = (Z ⊗ Z', γ'') with γ'' built from γ and γ'. The center carries a canonical braiding c(Z,γ),(Z',γ') = γ'Z. A fundamental theorem of Majid and Joyal‑Street states that Z(C) is a braided monoidal category. If C is a fusion category, then Z(C) is a modular tensor category. The forgetful functor Z(C) → C is dominant and its Frobenius‑Perron dimension satisfies FPdim(Z(C)) = FPdim(C)².

The construction of the Drinfeld center provides a systematic way to produce modular tensor categories from any fusion category. For example, if C = VecG is the category of finite‑dimensional vector spaces graded by a finite group G, then Z(VecG) is equivalent to the representation category of the Drinfeld double D(G), a quasi‑triangular Hopf algebra. This center is modular and its simple objects correspond to pairs (conjugacy class, irreducible representation of the centralizer). The resulting modular data reproduces the character table of D(G) and the associated TQFT is the Dijkgraaf‑Witten theory. More generally, the center of a fusion category coming from a quantum group at a root of unity yields the same modular tensor category as the original quantum group construction, illustrating the “modularization” property of the center.

The Drinfeld center also plays a central role in the theory of module categories. A module category over C corresponds to a Lagrangian algebra in Z(C), and the category of module endofunctors is equivalent to the category of bimodules over that algebra. This correspondence underlies the classification of gapped boundaries in topological phases of matter. Moreover, the center construction is functorial: a monoidal functor C → D induces a braided monoidal functor Z(C) → Z(D). This functoriality is used to relate modular tensor categories arising from different quantum groups or from different levels of the same quantum group.

Classification of Low-Rank Fusion Categories and Ocneanu Rigidity

The classification of fusion categories by rank (the number of isomorphism classes of simple objects) is a major achievement of the last two decades. Rank‑2 fusion categories over ℂ are completely known: there are exactly two, the category Rep(ℤ/2) of representations of the group of order two (which is symmetric) and the Fibonacci category (which is non‑group‑theoretical and has fusion rule τ ⊗ τ ≅ 1 ⊕ τ). Rank‑3 fusion categories have been classified by Ostrik and others; they include the representation categories of the finite groups ℤ/3 and S₃, the Tambara‑Yamagami categories associated to ℤ/3 and ℤ/2×ℤ/2, and a few exceptional non‑group‑theoretical categories such as the one coming from the quantum group Uq(sl₂) at a 5th root of unity (the Yang‑Lee category). Rank‑4 and rank‑5 classifications are also known, though the lists become longer and include many group‑theoretical and near‑group categories.

Ocneanu rigidity is the theorem that for a given fusion ring (the Grothendieck ring with basis of simple objects) there are only finitely many fusion categories realizing it, up to monoidal equivalence. This result, proved by Ocneanu in the context of subfactors and later generalized by Etingof, Nikshych and Ostrik, implies that the classification problem is discrete: one cannot have continuous families of fusion categories with the same fusion rules. The proof uses the fact that the associator (the solution of the pentagon equation) is an algebraic variety defined by polynomial equations, and the rigidity theorem shows that this variety has only finitely many points over ℂ. As a corollary, the number of fusion categories of a given Frobenius‑Perron dimension is finite. This finiteness underlies the feasibility of computer‑assisted classification programs that have enumerated all fusion categories of Frobenius‑Perron dimension less than a certain bound (e.g., < 100).

The combination of low‑rank classification and Ocneanu rigidity has led to the discovery of many exotic fusion categories that do not come from quantum groups or finite groups. For instance, the Haagerup fusion category (rank 6, FPdim ≈ 12.5) and the extended Haagerup category (rank 8) were first constructed via subfactor theory and later shown to be fusion categories. Their modular tensor categories (obtained via the Drinfeld center) provide new examples of modular data not arising from affine Lie algebras. These exotic categories are of great interest for topological quantum computing because they may support anyon models with novel braiding statistics.

Unitary Modular Tensor Categories from Quantum Groups at Roots of Unity

Quantum groups Uq(𝔤) at roots of unity provide the most abundant source of unitary modular tensor categories. Let 𝔤 be a simple Lie algebra, h∨ its dual Coxeter number, and choose a level k ∈ ℕ. Set q = exp(π i / (k + h∨)). The category of finite‑dimensional type‑1 Uq(𝔤)-modules is not semisimple, but its quotient by the ideal of negligible morphisms (those with zero quantum trace) yields a semisimple rigid braided monoidal category C(𝔤, k). This category is a modular tensor category; its simple objects correspond to the dominant integral weights of 𝔤 at level k. The braiding comes from the universal R-matrix of the quantum group, and the twist is given by the ribbon element. The resulting S and T matrices coincide with the modular transformations of the characters of the affine Lie algebra 𝔤̂ at level k, establishing the equivalence with the Wess‑Zumino‑Witten conformal field theory.

The unitary structure on C(𝔤, k) is induced by the *‑structure on Uq(𝔤) coming from the compact real form of 𝔤. The categorical dimensions (quantum dimensions) are positive real numbers and equal the Frobenius‑Perron dimensions. The global dimension is given by the Verlinde formula and equals the product over positive roots of (sin(π(α, ρ)/ (k+h∨)) / sin(π(α, ρ)/ h∨))², where ρ is the Weyl vector. These categories are pseudo‑unitary and spherical, hence they satisfy all axioms of a unitary modular tensor category. The most studied families are SU(N)k, SO(N)k and Sp(N)k. For SU(2)k the simple objects are labeled by spins j = 0, 1/2, …, k/2, and the fusion rules are the truncated Clebsch‑Gordan rules. The Fibonacci category appears as SU(2)3 (or equivalently the Yang‑Lee model). The Ising category appears as SU(2)2.

It is a major open problem whether every unitary modular tensor category arises from a quantum group at a root of unity (possibly combined with taking Drinfeld centers, orbifolds, or extensions). The classification of unitary MTCs of low rank (up to rank 5) has been completed and all known examples are either quantum group categories or their simple modifications (e.g., the E₆, E₇, E₈ categories at level 1). The search for exotic unitary MTCs continues, motivated by the possibility of new anyon models for topological quantum computation.

  • Confusing the pivotal structure with the spherical condition; a pivotal category need not be spherical, and the categorical dimensions may be negative or non‑real without sphericity.
  • Assuming the Verlinde formula holds in any braided fusion category; it requires modularity (non‑degenerate S‑matrix) and fails in merely braided or pre‑modular categories.
  • Thinking the Drinfeld center of a fusion category is always equivalent to the original category; it is typically much larger (dimension squared) and only equivalent when the original category is already modular.
  • Believing Ocneanu rigidity implies a unique fusion category for each fusion ring; it only guarantees finiteness, and many distinct fusion categories can share the same fusion ring (e.g., the two Ising‑type categories with the same fusion rules but different associators).
  • Treating all modular tensor categories from quantum groups as distinct; many are related by level‑rank duality (e.g., SU(N)k ≅ SU(k)N) and by taking Drinfeld centers of pointed categories.
  • Overlooking the necessity of the unitary *‑structure for topological quantum computing; a modular tensor category without a compatible *‑structure cannot be used to define a unitary TQFT or a fault‑tolerant quantum computer.
  • Neglecting that the Frobenius‑Perron dimension equals the quantum dimension only in pseudo‑unitary categories; in general they differ and the Frobenius‑Perron dimension is always a Perron number while the quantum dimension may be negative or complex.

hand/analytic-number-theory.html:
Zero-Free Regions and Error Terms in the Prime Number Theorem

The classical prime number theorem states ψ(x) = x + o(x), where ψ(x) = Σn≤x Λ(n) is the Chebyshev function. The quality of the error term is governed by the location of zeros of the Riemann zeta function ζ(s). If ζ(s) has no zeros in the region σ ≥ 1 − η(t) for t = |Im s|, then one obtains ψ(x) = x + O(x exp(−c ∫2^x η(u)/u du)). The best unconditional zero‑free region, due to Korobov and Vinogradov (1958), has the shape σ ≥ 1 − c/(log t)2/3 (log log t)1/3 for t ≥ 3. Substituting this η(t) yields the Vinogradov–Korobov error term ψ(x) = x + O(x exp(−c (log x)3/5 (log log x)−1/5)). This remains the strongest known unconditional estimate for the prime number theorem. Any improvement would require a wider zero‑free region, which is closely related to breaking the “convexity barrier” for ζ(s). The Riemann hypothesis (RH) asserts that all non‑trivial zeros satisfy σ = 1/2; under RH the error term sharpens dramatically to ψ(x) = x + O(x1/2 log2 x). The explicit formula (see next section) makes this equivalence precise: the sum over zeros ρ = β + iγ contributes x^β, so the maximal real part β directly controls the error. Zero‑density estimates, such as N(σ, T) ≪ T2(1−σ) log5 T for 1/2 ≤ σ ≤ 1, give averaged information that is sufficient for many applications, including the Bombieri–Vinogradov theorem. The interplay between zero‑free regions, zero‑density theorems, and explicit formulae is the engine behind almost all quantitative results on the distribution of primes.

The Explicit Formula for ψ(x) and the Riemann Hypothesis

The explicit formula connects the prime‑counting function ψ(x) to the zeros of ζ(s). For x > 1 not a prime power, one has ψ(x) = x − Σ_ρ x^ρ/ρ − log(2π) − ½ log(1 − x−2), where the sum runs over all non‑trivial zeros ρ = β + iγ of ζ(s), ordered by increasing |γ|. The series converges conditionally; a smoothed version with a test function gives absolute convergence. The formula is derived by applying Perron’s formula to −ζ′/ζ(s) = Σ Λ(n) n−s and shifting the contour left across the critical strip, picking up residues at s = 1 (giving x), at the zeros ρ (giving −x^ρ/ρ), at s = 0 (giving −log(2π)), and at the trivial zeros s = −2, −4, … (giving the logarithmic term). The Riemann hypothesis is equivalent to the statement that for every ε > 0, ψ(x) = x + O(x1/2+ε). Indeed, if all zeros satisfy β = 1/2, then |x^ρ| = x1/2 and the sum over zeros is bounded by x1/2 Σ_ρ 1/|ρ| ≪ x1/2 log2 x. Conversely, if ψ(x) = x + O(xθ+ε) for some θ < 1, then a standard argument using the explicit formula shows that ζ(s) has no zeros with real part > θ. The explicit formula also underlies the Weil explicit formula for general L‑functions, where the sum over zeros is paired with a sum over prime powers weighted by the Fourier transform of a test function. This duality is the foundation of the “explicit formula method” used to translate zero‑free regions into prime‑number estimates and vice versa.

Technique: Bounding ψ(x) − x under RH via the explicit formula
Assuming the Riemann hypothesis, prove that ψ(x) = x + O(x1/2 log2 x).
Under RH every non‑trivial zero ρ satisfies ρ = ½ + iγ. The explicit formula gives ψ(x) − x = − Σ_ρ x^ρ/ρ + O(1). Since |x^ρ| = x1/2, we have |Σ_ρ x^ρ/ρ| ≤ x1/2 Σ_ρ 1/|ρ|. The number of zeros with |γ| ≤ T is N(T) = (T/2π) log(T/2π) − T/2π + O(log T). By partial summation, Σ0<|γ|≤T 1/|ρ| ≪ log2 T. Choosing T ≈ x gives Σ_ρ 1/|ρ| ≪ log2 x. Hence ψ(x) − x ≪ x1/2 log2 x. The trivial zeros and the constant terms contribute only O(1). This completes the proof.
Exam‑day strategy
Memorise the shape of the Korobov–Vinogradov zero‑free region and the resulting error term exp(−c (log x)3/5 (log log x)−1/5); it appears in many advanced analytic number theory papers and is a favourite target for “state the best known unconditional error term” questions.

L-functions of Modular Forms and the Langlands Correspondence

Let f(z) = Σn≥1 a_n e2π i n z be a Hecke eigenform of weight k for SL2(ℤ). Its L‑function L(s, f) = Σ a_n n−s converges for Re s > (k+1)/2 and admits analytic continuation to ℂ with a functional equation relating s to k−s. The completed L‑function Λ(s, f) = (2π)−s Γ(s) L(s, f) satisfies Λ(s, f) = i^k Λ(k−s, f). The Ramanujan–Petersson conjecture, proved by Deligne as a consequence of the Weil conjectures, asserts |a_p| ≤ 2 p(k−1)/2 for all primes p. For a general congruence subgroup Γ0(N) and a primitive Dirichlet character χ, one obtains L(s, f ⊗ χ) with analogous properties. The Langlands programme predicts that every irreducible automorphic representation π of GL2(𝔸_ℚ) corresponds to a 2‑dimensional Galois representation ρ_π : Gal(ℚ̄/ℚ) → GL2(ℂ) such that L(s, π) = L(s, ρ_π). For modular forms this is the modularity theorem (formerly the Taniyama–Shimura–Weil conjecture), proved by Wiles, Taylor–Wiles, Breuil–Conrad–Diamond–Taylor. The correspondence extends to GL_n: an automorphic representation π of GL_n(𝔸_ℚ) should match an n‑dimensional Galois representation. The local Langlands correspondence for GL_n over p‑adic fields was established by Harris–Taylor and Henniart. The global correspondence remains open beyond n = 2, but the work of Arthur on the endoscopic classification for classical groups has provided a vast framework. L‑functions of automorphic forms satisfy the expected analytic properties: meromorphic continuation, functional equation, Euler product, and the Generalized Riemann Hypothesis (GRH) for these L‑functions is a central open problem. The functoriality conjecture predicts that L‑functions are closed under operations such as symmetric powers, Rankin–Selberg convolutions, and base change; these give rise to new L‑functions with rich arithmetic information.

The Subconvexity Problem and Applications to Equidistribution

For an L‑function L(s, π) with analytic conductor C(π), the convexity bound (Phragmén–Lindelöf) gives L(½, π) ≪ C(π)1/4+ε. The subconvexity problem asks for an exponent δ > 0 such that L(½, π) ≪ C(π)1/4−δ+ε. This is a quantitative refinement of the Generalized Riemann Hypothesis and has profound arithmetic consequences. For Dirichlet L‑functions L(s, χ) with conductor q, Burgess (1963) proved subconvexity with δ = 1/16 for primitive characters, using character sum estimates. For GL2 L‑functions, the first subconvexity results were obtained by Duke–Friedlander–Iwaniec (1995) for holomorphic forms and by Michel–Venkatesh (2010) for Maass forms, using the amplification method and the spectral theory of automorphic forms. Subconvexity bounds imply equidistribution of Heegner points on modular curves (Duke, 1988) and quantum unique ergodicity for eigenfunctions of the Laplacian on arithmetic surfaces (Lindenstrauss, 2006). They also yield power‑saving error terms in the asymptotic formula for the number of representations of an integer by a ternary quadratic form (Duke–Schulze‑Pillot). A notable result for GL2 over ℚ is δ = 1/6 for certain families, due to Blomer, Harcos, and Michel. Recent work by Nelson achieved subconvexity for L(½, π × χ) where π is a fixed GL2 form and χ varies over Dirichlet characters, using the delta‑symbol method. These advances illustrate the deep interplay between analytic bounds, spectral theory, and arithmetic geometry.

The Generalized Riemann Hypothesis and its Consequences for Primes in Arithmetic Progressions

The Generalized Riemann Hypothesis (GRH) asserts that for every Dirichlet character χ modulo q, all non‑trivial zeros of L(s, χ) lie on the line Re s = ½. GRH implies a very strong error term in the prime number theorem for arithmetic progressions: for (a, q) = 1, π(x; q, a) = Li(x)/φ(q) + O(x1/2 log x). This follows from the explicit formula for ψ(x; q, a) = Σn≤x, n≡a (mod q) Λ(n) and the zero‑free region provided by GRH. Unconditionally, the Siegel–Walfisz theorem gives π(x; q, a) = Li(x)/φ(q) + O(x exp(−c√log x)) for q ≤ (log x)^A, but the constant is ineffective due to the possible existence of a Siegel zero — a real zero β > 1 − c/log q of L(s, χ) for a real character χ. If a Siegel zero exists, it forces all other zeros to be farther left (Deuring–Heilbronn phenomenon), which paradoxically can be used to prove results like Linnik’s theorem on the least prime in an arithmetic progression: the least prime p ≡ a (mod q) satisfies p ≪ q^L for some absolute constant L (currently L = 5 is known). GRH would give L = 2 + ε. The Bombieri–Vinogradov theorem provides an averaged form of GRH: Σq≤Q max(a,q)=1 |π(x; q, a) − Li(x)/φ(q)| ≪ x1/2 Q log4 x for Q ≤ x1/2 / log^C x. This is equivalent to GRH on average over q and is the main tool in the GPY–Maynard–Tao proof of bounded gaps between primes. The Elliott–Halberstam conjecture extends the range to Q ≤ x1−ε and would imply bounded gaps between primes, a major step toward the twin prime conjecture. Thus GRH, its averaged forms, and the possible exceptional Siegel zero sit at the heart of the distribution of primes in arithmetic progressions.

  • Confusing the unconditional Vinogradov–Korobov error term with the conditional RH error term; they differ by a factor of exp(−c (log x)3/5) versus x1/2.
  • Assuming the explicit formula converges absolutely without smoothing; the sum over zeros is only conditionally convergent.
  • Stating that the Ramanujan–Petersson conjecture is proved for all automorphic forms; it is known only for GL2 over ℚ (Deligne) and for certain higher‑rank cases via the Langlands programme.
  • Believing subconvexity is equivalent to GRH; subconvexity is a weaker quantitative statement that does not require all zeros on the critical line.
  • Overlooking the ineffective constant in the Siegel–Walfisz theorem caused by a possible Siegel zero; this subtlety is crucial for many applications.
  • Misapplying the Bombieri–Vinogradov theorem beyond its range Q ≤ x1/2 / log^C x; the Elliott–Halberstam conjecture is needed for larger Q.
  • Thinking the Langlands correspondence for GL_n is fully proved; it is established only for n = 2 (modularity) and for certain classical groups via Arthur’s work.

These traps highlight the precise distinctions that examiners test in advanced analytic number theory questions.

hand/prismatic-cohomology.html:
The Absolute Prismatic Cohomology and the Breuil–Kisin Twist

The absolute prismatic cohomology ΔX/ℤ_p constructed by Bhatt–Morrow–Scholze removes the dependence on a chosen base prism (A, I). For a p‑adic formal scheme X, the absolute prismatic site XΔ has as objects all prisms (A, I) equipped with a map A → Γ(X, O_X) such that I·O_X = p·O_X. The structure sheaf OΔ assigns to each prism its underlying δ‑ring A. The resulting cohomology complex ΔX/ℤ_p is a perfect complex of ℤ_p‑modules equipped with a Frobenius φ and a decreasing Nygaard filtration N•. The Breuil–Kisin twist τ(i) = (φ-1(I)i)[1/p] provides a canonical trivialisation of the Tate twist on the absolute prismatic site; it identifies the graded pieces griN ΔX/ℤ_p with the derived completed Hodge cohomology LΩ̂iX/ℤ_p[i] after inverting p. This twist is essential for formulating the integral Hodge–Tate decomposition without passing to a period ring. Moreover, the absolute theory satisfies étale descent and proper base change, making it the natural recipient of the comparison maps from both crystalline and étale cohomology.

One of the key technical results is that for a smooth proper formal scheme X over O_K, the natural map ΔX/ℤ_p → RΓcris(X_k/W(k)) ⊗W(k) Acris becomes an isomorphism after derived p‑completion and applying the Breuil–Kisin twist. This identifies the Nygaard filtration on the absolute prismatic cohomology with the conjugate filtration on crystalline cohomology. The construction also yields a canonical map ΔX/ℤ_p → RΓét(XK̄, ℤ_p) ⊗ BdR+ compatible with filtrations and Frobenius, giving an integral version of the p‑adic period map. The absolute prismatic cohomology therefore serves as a universal p‑adic cohomology theory from which all classical theories are recovered by base change along the morphisms of prisms (W(k), (p)) → (Acris, (ξ)) → (BdR+, (ξ)).

The Nygaard Filtration, Frobenius, and the Hodge–Tate Spectral Sequence

The Nygaard filtration N• on ΔX/R is defined by Ni = φ-1(Ii)·ΔX/R, where I ⊂ R is the defining ideal of the prism. Because φ is a δ‑ring endomorphism lifting the Frobenius on R/I, the filtration is exhaustive, separated, and stable under φ. The associated graded pieces griN ΔX/R are canonically isomorphic to the derived completed Hodge cohomology LΩ̂iX/R[i] after inverting p; integrally they are identified with the Breuil–Kisin twists τ(i). The Frobenius φ induces maps φ: griN → griN which, after inverting p, become isomorphisms. This structure makes ΔX/R an F‑gauge in the sense of Bhatt–Lurie.

The Hodge–Tate spectral sequence arises from the filtered complex (ΔX/R, N•). Its E1‑page is E1i,j = Hi+j(X, gr-iN ΔX/R) ≅ Hj(X, Ω̂iX/R) and it converges to the prismatic cohomology Hi+jΔ(X/R). After inverting p, the spectral sequence degenerates at E2 and recovers the classical Hodge–Tate decomposition Hnét(XK̄, ℚ_p) ⊗ C ≅ ⊕i+j=n Hj(X, ΩiX) ⊗ C(-i). The integral version, however, does not degenerate in general; the differentials encode subtle torsion information related to the weight filtration on étale cohomology. The Frobenius action on the E1‑page is induced by the Cartier isomorphism on Hodge cohomology, and the compatibility of φ with the Nygaard filtration yields a Frobenius on the abutment. This Frobenius is the key input for the integral p‑adic Hodge theory developed by Bhatt–Morrow–Scholze, allowing one to define the weight filtration on ΔX/ℤ_p as the filtration generated by the images of φm(Ni) for m ≥ 0.

Worked Example: Computing the E1‑page for a Smooth Proper Curve
Let X be a smooth proper curve over a p‑adic field K with good reduction, and let R = W(k) be the prism of Witt vectors of the residue field. Describe the E1‑page of the Hodge–Tate spectral sequence for ΔX/R[1/p] and identify the differentials.
For a curve, the Hodge cohomology groups are H0(X, O_X) ≅ K, H1(X, O_X) ≅ Kg, H0(X, Ω1X) ≅ Kg, H1(X, Ω1X) ≅ K. The Nygaard filtration satisfies gr0N ≅ O_X, gr1N ≅ Ω1X[1], and griN = 0 for i ≥ 2. Hence the E1‑page has non‑zero entries only for i = 0,1. Explicitly, E10,0 = H0(X, O_X), E10,1 = H1(X, O_X), E1-1,1 = H0(X, Ω1X), E1-1,2 = H1(X, Ω1X). All differentials d1 have bidegree (1,0). The only possible non‑zero differential is d1: E1-1,1 → E10,1, which is the Kodaira–Spencer map. For a curve with good reduction the spectral sequence degenerates at E2 after inverting p, yielding the Hodge–Tate decomposition H1ét(XK̄, ℚ_p) ⊗ C ≅ H0(X, Ω1X) ⊗ C(-1) ⊕ H1(X, O_X). The Frobenius on the abutment acts as the inverse of the Cartier isomorphism on H1(X, O_X) and as the identity on H0(X, Ω1X) after the Tate twist.
Exam Strategy
When a question asks for the Hodge–Tate spectral sequence, first write down the Nygaard filtration and its graded pieces. Then identify the E1‑page as Hodge cohomology. Remember that after inverting p the sequence degenerates at E2; integrally the differentials are governed by the Kodaira–Spencer class. Mention the role of the Breuil–Kisin twist in trivialising Tate twists on the graded pieces.

Prismatic Cohomology of Perfectoid Spaces and the Tilting Equivalence

For a perfectoid space X over a perfectoid field K, the prismatic cohomology ΔX/ℤ_p can be computed via the pro‑étale site. The tilt X♭ is a perfectoid space in characteristic p, and the prismatic cohomology of X is canonically isomorphic to the crystalline cohomology of X♭ relative to the prism (Ainf, (ξ)), where Ainf = W(OX♭+) and ξ is a generator of the kernel of the Fontaine map θ: Ainf → OX+. This isomorphism is the prismatic incarnation of the tilting equivalence. Concretely, there is a natural map ΔX/ℤ_p → RΓcris(X♭/Ainf) which becomes an isomorphism after derived p‑completion. The Nygaard filtration on the left corresponds to the conjugate filtration on the right, and the Frobenius on ΔX/ℤ_p matches the absolute Frobenius on the crystalline side.

This comparison yields a new proof of the almost purity theorem: the map OX+ → ΔX/ℤ_p is almost an isomorphism in degree 0, and the higher cohomology groups are almost zero. Moreover, the prismatic cohomology of a perfectoid space carries a natural action of the Galois group Gal(K̄/K) which, via the tilting equivalence, coincides with the natural Galois action on the crystalline cohomology of the tilt. The period ring BdR+ appears as the completion of Ainf[1/ξ] with respect to the ξ‑adic topology, and the étale comparison ΔX/ℤ_p[1/p] ⊗ BdR+ ≅ H*ét(X, ℚ_p) ⊗ BdR+ follows from the crystalline comparison for the tilt together with the Fontaine–Colmez isomorphism. This perspective also clarifies the relationship between the Hodge–Tate period map and the Hodge–Tate filtration on the de Rham cohomology of the generic fibre.

The Prismatic Faltings Isomorphism and the de Rham Comparison

Faltings' almost de Rham comparison theorem states that for a smooth proper formal scheme X over O_K, the natural map H*dR(X/O_K) → H*ét(X_K, ℚ_p) ⊗ BdR is an almost isomorphism after suitable completions. In the prismatic framework this becomes an exact isomorphism at the level of complexes. The prismatic Faltings isomorphism is a canonical quasi‑isomorphism ΔX/A[1/p] ⊗A[1/p] BdR ≅ RΓdR(X/A) ⊗_A BdR, where A = O_K and BdR is Fontaine's de Rham period ring. The proof uses the identification of ΔX/A with the relative de Rham–Witt complex WΩ•X_k after inverting p, together with the fact that the Nygaard filtration on ΔX/A corresponds under this identification to the conjugate filtration on the de Rham–Witt complex. The Frobenius on ΔX/A matches the Frobenius on the de Rham–Witt complex, and the Breuil–Kisin twist provides the necessary Tate twists to align the filtrations.

As a consequence, the Hodge filtration on de Rham cohomology is recovered from the Nygaard filtration via the isomorphism griN ΔX/A[1/p] ≅ ΩiX/A[i]. The prismatic Faltings isomorphism also implies the de Rham comparison for the absolute prismatic cohomology: ΔX/ℤ_p[1/p] ⊗ BdR ≅ RΓdR(X/ℤ_p) ⊗ BdR. This gives a unified proof of the crystalline, de Rham, and étale comparisons, because each is obtained by base‑changing the absolute prismatic cohomology along the appropriate morphism of prisms. The isomorphism is compatible with the Galois action, the Frobenius, and the monodromy operator, making it the central technical tool for integral p‑adic Hodge theory.

Applications to the Weight‑Monodromy Conjecture and Integral p‑adic Hodge Theory

The weight filtration on the ℓ‑adic cohomology of a variety over a p‑adic field is conjectured to coincide with the monodromy filtration arising from the action of the inertia group. In the prismatic setting, the Nygaard filtration together with the Frobenius provides a canonical candidate for the weight filtration on ΔX/ℤ_p. Bhatt–Morrow–Scholze define the weight filtration W• on ΔX/ℤ_p as the filtration generated by the images of φm(Ni) for all m ≥ 0. They prove that for a smooth proper variety X over a p‑adic field, the associated graded pieces grWi ΔX/ℤ_p are concentrated in cohomological degree i and are isomorphic to the primitive parts of the Hodge cohomology. This yields an integral version of the weight‑monodromy conjecture: the weight filtration on the integral étale cohomology H*ét(XK̄, ℤ_p) coincides with the filtration induced by the Nygaard filtration via the étale comparison isomorphism.

Further applications include the computation of the prismatic cohomology of complete intersections in toric varieties, where the prismatic cohomology can be expressed as the cohomology of a Koszul complex built from the defining equations. This leads to explicit formulas for the Hodge numbers and the action of Frobenius. The prismatic Riemann–Hilbert correspondence, developed by Bhatt–Lurie, identifies the category of prismatic F‑crystals on a smooth formal scheme with the category of ℚ_p‑local systems on the generic fibre, providing a p‑adic analogue of the classical Riemann–Hilbert correspondence. These results demonstrate that prismatic cohomology is not only a unifying cohomology theory but also a computational tool that makes previously inaccessible integral p‑adic Hodge invariants tractable.

  • Confusing the Nygaard filtration with the Hodge filtration; they coincide only after inverting p and applying the Breuil–Kisin twist.
  • Assuming the Hodge–Tate spectral sequence degenerates integrally; it generally does not, and the differentials carry torsion information.
  • Neglecting the role of the Breuil–Kisin twist in trivialising Tate twists on graded pieces of the Nygaard filtration.
  • Treating the absolute prismatic site as a small category; it is a large site and requires careful handling of size issues.
  • Overlooking that the prismatic Faltings isomorphism is an exact quasi‑isomorphism, not merely an almost isomorphism.
  • Misidentifying the tilt of a perfectoid space with its reduction modulo p; the tilt lives in characteristic p but is not the special fibre.
  • Forgetting that the weight filtration defined via φ and N is canonical and does not depend on a choice of embedding into ℂ_p.
